The idea encouraged travelers concerned about aviation emissions to choose trains instead. Swedish flying fell by just over 4% in 2019 as interest in rail travel grew. Yet there was an obvious weakness in the argument: wanting to take the train and having a practical train to take were not always the same thing. That is what makes the current changes more interesting. The pitch today is less about guilt and more about convenience. A traveler can board in Stockholm and stay on the same train to Copenhagen or Hamburg. From Copenhagen, Berlin and Prague are now direct destinations. That may prove a stronger argument than flygskam ever was. Norway Looks Toward Europe Norway remains something of an outlier because of its geography, but changes are coming. The Meråker Line from Trondheim to the Swedish border was fully electrified this spring, allowing electric trains to operate across the border at Storlien. The work improves the prospects for international passenger services, although long-discussed direct Trondheim-Stockholm trains remain uncertain. Much more concrete is a new Oslo-Europe route planned for 2028. Norwegian operator Vy, Denmark’s DSB and Deutsche Bahn have announced two daily direct trains from Oslo through Copenhagen and Hamburg to Berlin. Vy says Oslo-Copenhagen should take about seven hours, with Oslo-Berlin around 14 to 15 hours. It will be the first direct train between Norway and Denmark in more than 20 years. Nordic Rail Network Still Under Construction The Nordic rail revival should not be overstated, however. The new Finland-Sweden service does not yet create a seamless Helsinki-to-Stockholm rail journey, some international services remain seasonal and trains can still struggle to compete with low-cost flights. Infrastructure remains a constraint too, but one major project could eventually transform the map. The Fehmarnbelt tunnel between Denmark and Germany is designed to cut Copenhagen-Hamburg rail journeys to about 2.5 hours, strengthening the main land route between Scandinavia and continental Europe. Although that remains a future promise, the more immediate change is already visible on timetables. Seven years after flygskam made Scandinavia the center of a global debate about flying less, travelers finally have a growing number of practical alternatives. The Nordic rail network is far from finished. For the first time in years, though, it increasingly looks like a network. MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: Why Wealthy Families Are Selling Their Iconic Private Islands
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.77
For over a hundred years, Hay Island off the Connecticut coast was owned by the Ziegler family, who built their fortune through Royal Baking Powder co-founder William Ziegler Sr. The family first used the 18-acre island as a summer getaway, then made it their home. Several generations spent their childhoods there, enjoying Long Island Sound, two private beaches, a guest house, and a large New England-style house. In November, the family sold Hay Island for $26.5 million. By that time, family members had moved across the country and the island was no longer as important to them. Just two years earlier, the Zieglers had sold Great Island, another family property nearby, to the town of Darien for $85 million. In 2015, Forbes estimated the Ziegler family’s fortune at $2.8 billion. The Zieglers are not the only ones selling private islands. In the Venice lagoon, an Italian island once owned by the late billionaire Gernot Langes-Swarovski is for sale at €24 million. Off Brazil, the family of famous plastic surgeon Ivo Pitanguy is selling his private island for $100 million, the first time it has been on the market in over fifty years. In England, music producer Nigel Frieda is selling Osea Island after owning it for twenty years. Each sale has its own story, but many of these properties share a common thread. Wealthy owners once used their resources and vision to build private retreats that reflected their personalities. Years later, their families have to decide if keeping these places is still the right choice. A few years ago, I noticed a similar trend while reporting on billionaire ranch owners selling off some of America's iconic properties. Even when the land still mattered to the family, younger generations often moved away and were less interested in managing such large properties. Private islands face these same challenges, but everything from hiring staff to handling repairs, utilities, and transportation gets even more complicated when the property is surrounded by water. A Massive Transfer Of Wealth The timing is interesting because a huge amount of property wealth is about to change hands. Coldwell Banker Global Luxury's 2026 Trend Report estimates Gen X and Millennials will inherit about $4.6 trillion in global real estate wealth over the next decade, including $2.4 trillion in the United States. Gen X is expected to receive the largest share soon, while Millennials will become more important as the transfer continues. Meanwhile, younger wealthy buyers seem to value what private islands have always provided: land, privacy, rarity, and control over their environment. According to Coldwell Banker’s 2026 Mid-Year Report, searches for unique properties like private islands went up by 146% compared to last year, and land searches rose by 97%. The company connects some of this demand to a trend it calls “landmaxxing,” where wealthy buyers look for bigger plots or nearby properties to gain more privacy, keep their views, and make space for extended family. When I interviewed Mary Lee Blaylock, President of Coldwell Banker Affiliates, she highlighted a broader shift in how wealthy families view real estate as both an investment and a legacy to pass down between generations. “The Coldwell Banker Global Luxury’s Mid-Year Report 2026 told us that luxury real estate more broadly is increasingly being viewed as a long-term wealth-management and legacy asset,” she said. “We’re seeing affluent families use real estate for geographic diversification, multigenerational living and estate planning, and that they’re placing particular value on attributes that are difficult to replicate, such as land, location, privacy and scarcity.” These four qualities matter a lot when it comes to private islands. They also help explain why a property that one generation lets go can still attract interest from the next. Isola Santa Cristina, Venice - €24 Million For almost 40 years, Santa Cristina served as Gernot Langes-Swarovski's private getaway in the Venice lagoon. In 1986, the great-grandson of Swarovski founder Daniel Swarovski bought the 72-acre island and spent years bringing it back to life. Rather than just building a lavish vacation home, he focused on restoring its agriculture and ecology. They planted vineyards and orchards, brought back historic fish farming, and worked with Ca' Foscari University on environmental projects. Over time, Santa Cristina turned into a self-sufficient family estate with a nine-bedroom villa, a farmhouse, vegetable gardens, olive trees, an apiary, a private chapel, a swimming pool, boats, and even helicopter access. Langes-Swarovski passed away in 2021, and the family's foundation took over ownership. The island is now for sale at €24 million, its first time on the market in about forty years. Santa Cristina stands out for more than just its connection to the Swarovski family. The island was closely tied to the man who restored it, which can make passing it on more challenging. The next generation of property owners not only inherits history and memories but also assumes the responsibility and costs of maintaining a place shaped by one person's vision. Pitanguy Island, Brazil - $100 Million Among the islands currently for sale, few make the point as clearly as the retreat created by the famous Brazilian plastic surgeon Dr. Ivo Pitanguy. Pitanguy bought the island in 1973 and spent years making it a private getaway for his family, friends, and guests. For over 50 years, it stayed out of the commercial spotlight and was never run as a typical resort. After Pitanguy passed away in 2016 and his wife Marilu in 2023, the family decided to sell the island for $100 million. This is the first time it has been for sale in more than 50 years. Located off the coast of Rio de Janeiro, the island offers nearly 15,000 square feet of buildings, including six bungalows and nine suites. It also features preserved forest, beaches, an airstrip, a helipad, and a marina pier. The family is presenting it as a private retreat or, with the right approvals, a possible ultra-luxury hospitality property. This shows how these properties can change after they leave the families who built them. Pitanguy’s personal sanctuary could one day become a luxury resort, much like other private estates that are now being used for wellness, conservation, or hospitality. Hay Island, Connecticut - Sold for $26.5 Million The Zieglers owned this 18-acre property for over a hundred years. Unlike most private islands, it connects to the mainland by a causeway, so residents have privacy but do not need a boat to get there. In the middle of the island stands a Colonial-style home with 8,684 square feet, plus a guest house, an infinity pool, and two beaches. For many years, the island was a place where the family gathered each year. Over time, though, family members moved away, and it became harder to keep up such a large estate in Connecticut. The family sold Hay Island in November 2025, after already selling nearby Great Island, a 60-acre property that the town of Darien bought for $85 million in 2023. These two sales clearly show how a family compound can lose its practical use, even if the family still feels attached to it. When a property is designed for one family's way of life, it can be hard to keep once future generations stop living or vacationing there. Hamilton Island, Australia - A $1.2 billion sale In 2003, Australian wine billionaire Bob Oatley bought the 2,800-acre Hamilton Island in Queensland's Whitsundays. Over the next few years, he transformed it into one of Australia’s best-known resort destinations, adding hotels, restaurants, a marina, homes, and even a commercial airport. In late 2025, the Oatley family sold Hamilton Island to Blackstone in a deal reported at roughly A$1.2 billion. I met with Bob's son, Sandy Oatley, during a visit to the island not long after his father passed away in 2016. “When Dad first sailed past here in 1983 as part of a Whitsundays charter, he fell in love with it and eventually built the family estate Balmoral Villa, which had not been used since his death,” he told me. Hamilton Island is different from Santa Cristina or Hay Island because it has grown into a major tourist destination. Still, the main question of succession remains. When one person shapes a property with their vision, the next generation has to decide whether to continue that legacy. In this case, instead of another wealthy family, one of the world’s largest investment firms became the new owner. Inchconnachan Island, Scotland - £2.5 Million When Soho House founder Nick Jones and his wife, broadcaster Kirsty Young, bought Inchconnachan in Scotland’s Loch Lomond in 2020, they intended to create a private family retreat on the 103-acre island. The couple paid £1.55 million and later secured planning permission for a substantial lodge, boathouse and jetty designed to sit carefully within the protected landscape. The plan changed after Jones underwent cancer treatment. Earlier this year, the couple put the island back on the market for £2.5 million, saying they had begun thinking differently about how they wanted to spend their time. Buyers can purchase the island and its approved plans, or pay about £10 million for Jones to oversee completion of the planned retreat. Inchconnachan is particularly relevant to the changing private-island market because this is not an inherited property being passed down through generations. It is an example of how even very wealthy owners can discover that the dream of creating an island retreat changes as their lives do. Jones and Young had already navigated the difficult part, buying the island and securing permission to build, before deciding that the project no longer suited the life they wanted. That leaves the next owner with something increasingly valuable in the private-island world: not simply land and privacy, but an approved path toward turning it into a finished retreat. Osea Island, England - £25 Million Osea Island sits in England's Blackwater Estuary and stands out from other private islands. Music producer Nigel Frieda has owned its 380 acres for about twenty years, turning it into a retreat, hospitality spot, recording studio, and event venue. Osea Island has attracted more celebrity attention than most private estates. Stormzy recorded his album This Is What I Mean there, and artists like Rihanna and Olly Murs have also visited. The island connects to the mainland by a causeway that gets covered by water at high tide, so it is cut off for part of each day. A New Generation Of Island Owners Many of today’s wealthy buyers at the top of the market come from backgrounds that are quite different from those of families who dominated luxury real estate 30 or 40 years ago. Some are young technology founders and entrepreneurs, while others work in finance, private equity, or family businesses. More buyers are also inheriting significant wealth in their 30s and 40s. However, having more money does not mean they are less selective. Blaylock explained that today’s affluent buyers pay close attention to the full financial picture when considering a luxury property. “Today’s affluent buyer is discerning across many fronts. Luxury Property Specialists told us that buyers are scrutinizing factors such as insurance costs, inflation, property condition and long-term resale strength more closely. In markets affected by climate events, environmental risk and insurance availability are becoming increasingly important considerations as well.” She also said this careful approach is seen even among the wealthiest buyers: “That selectivity extends even to ultra-high-net-worth buyers. They may have greater freedom to purchase what they want, but our research suggests they are still looking for properties that make sense from both a lifestyle and long-term financial perspective.” That scrutiny matters even more with islands, where infrastructure often taken for granted on the mainland can become a substantial part of the purchase. Farhad Vladi, founder of Vladi Private Islands and one of the world's most experienced private-island brokers, has seen the market broaden beyond the traditional stereotype of oligarchs and billionaires. “Owning a private island is no longer reserved for the ultra-wealthy,” he told me in an interview. “In many cases, it’s comparable to the price of a high-end luxury car.” He also sees clients test the lifestyle before committing. “We’re seeing a clear shift toward experiential luxury. Many clients prefer to rent first, immersing themselves in the island lifestyle before considering a purchase.” Motu Tane near Bora Bora offers a good example of how these personal retreats are being repositioned. The ten-acre former private island of NARS Cosmetics founder François Nars is listed for $37.5 million and includes 22 Polynesian-style structures with interiors by designer Christian Liaigre. It is marketed as both a private family estate and a potential high-end hospitality property. This reflects a broader shift in how buyers think about islands at this level. A property can remain intensely private when the owner wants, while still having the flexibility to generate income or evolve later. Why Billionaires Bought Islands For decades, private islands have been a status symbol among billionaires, especially entrepreneurs who want more than just another vacation home. In 2012, Larry Ellison bought almost all of Lānaʻi in Hawaii for about $300 million, acquiring most of its homes, businesses, and resorts. Since then, he has used the island for luxury hospitality, wellness, farming, and sustainability projects. Google co-founder Larry Page has chosen a more spread-out strategy. According to reports, he owns at least five islands in the Caribbean and South Pacific. One of them is Cayo Norte near Puerto Rico, which he bought through an LLC in 2018 for about $32 million. Richard Branson made Necker Island in the British Virgin Islands famous as a billionaire retreat. He was just 28 when he bought the 74-acre island in 1978 for $180,000. Nearly three decades later, in 2007, he acquired neighboring 125-acre Moskito Island, which was eventually divided into ten private estates. Branson retained one for his family and sold the others to private owners who share ownership of the island’s common property. Bernard Arnault, meanwhile, owns the 135-acre Indigo Island in the Bahamas. The LVMH chairman purchased it for €4 million in 1999 and reportedly invested about $30 million developing it into a private family retreat, where his extended family gathers for Christmas. These islands are good examples because they show that billionaires are interested in more than just having a private beach. Owning an island lets them control the whole environment, whether they use it for family, hospitality, conservation, or a mix of these purposes. The Real Cost Of Owning A Private Island The idea of owning a private island may seem appealing at first, but the reality of ongoing costs can quickly become overwhelming. A 2026 analysis by Private Island Market estimates that a modest, developed island can cost roughly $84,000 to $310,000 a year to operate, while annual expenses on a larger staffed property can exceed $500,000 before major capital projects are considered. Saltwater speeds up rust and wear, plants need regular care, docks face storms and tides, and equipment like generators, solar panels, and desalination systems will eventually need replacing. In remote areas, even basic building materials and heavy machinery often have to be brought in by boat. Insurance can also be costly or hard to get, especially in places prone to hurricanes. Blaylock warned that the asking price is just one part of the equation. “With a property as unique as a private island, value goes well beyond the asking price. Buyers need to consider the full ownership picture, including accessibility, infrastructure, utilities, permitting, staffing and ongoing maintenance, and understand what additional investment may be required to make the property work for their lifestyle. What looks inexpensive on paper can be very different once those factors are taken into account.” These expenses add up whether a family stays on the island for months or just a few weeks. Things can get even more complicated when several children or grandchildren inherit the property. One part of the family might visit every summer, while others hardly come at all, but everyone is still responsible for upkeep. Over time, a place that once felt like a family retreat can turn into a big financial and practical burden. For families who have owned these islands for decades, selling does not always mean giving up their legacy. Sometimes it just means recognizing that the next generation has different ways of living. Meanwhile, younger wealthy buyers are searching for exactly what these islands offer: privacy, space, and a break from the outside world. The islands themselves stay special. The difference is who gets to shape their future. MORE FROM FORBES Aging families selling private islands

item.title: How Did A Piece Of The Berlin Wall End Up In A St. Pete Parking Lot?
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.26
St. Petersburg, Florida, is best known for beaches, sunshine, arts, and baseball. But tucked into the city's Warehouse Arts District is a surprising piece of history that seems to come out of left field—sections of the Berlin Wall. Three sections of the wall stand outside the Morean Center for Clay at 420 22nd Street South, a working ceramics facility housed inside a historic 1926 freight depot. That’s about the best way to say it—they stand there, in the middle of the parking lot. No sign. No fanfare. No description. You could park in front of it, as many do, and never know its significance. So, what gives? Today, several locations in Florida preserve pieces of the wall, but the St. Pete installation is particularly puzzling given its unheralded location in an otherwise normal parking lot. Let’s take a look at how this piece of history ended up in St. Pete: How the Berlin Wall Ended Up In St. Pete, Florida The story centers on the Outdoor Arts Foundation, a St. Petersburg nonprofit that developed public-art projects around the city. In 2007, it acquired what was described at the time as one of the world’s largest private collections of material from the Berlin Wall, which included more than 100 painted sections as well as about 350 plain concrete slabs identified as sections of the Hinterlandmauer, or "hinterland wall," part of the barrier system on the East Berlin side. The Outdoor Arts Foundation had much bigger plans for the collection than keeping it in Florida. The organization intended to use the concrete to establish 100 Berlin Wall monuments across North America, with the project leading into the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall in 2009. Communities could acquire sections for public memorials, while other pieces would be given to artists to turn into works of art. But the project never developed on the scale its organizers envisioned. The foundation eventually turned its attention to exhibiting and selling the painted pieces, while much of the plain concrete wall pieces remained in Florida. When The Wall Was Installed After the collection arrived in the Tampa Bay area in July 2007, St. Pete was the first Florida community to erect a Berlin Wall monument using those concrete pieces. In the spring of 2008, three sections were installed at 420 22nd Street South, then home to the St. Petersburg Clay Company. The Morean Arts Center moved its ceramics program into the historic freight depot in 2009 and took over St. Pete Clay in 2012, establishing what is now the Morean Center for Clay. In other words, the Berlin Wall wasn’t placed outside the Morean Center that exists today—the Morean Center came to the Berlin Wall. What Are You Actually Looking At? The three sections in St. Pete are authentic pieces of the former East German border fortifications that divided Berlin during the Cold War. The individual slabs are approximately 10 feet long, three feet high, and four inches thick. Together, they stack to create a wall roughly nine feet high. The Berlin Wall surrounded West Berlin for approximately 96 miles, with roughly 27 miles of the barrier separating East and West Berlin. East German authorities began constructing it in August 1961 as part of an effort to stop people from leaving East Germany through West Berlin. The wall fell on November 9, 1989, amid sweeping political changes in East Germany and elsewhere in Eastern Europe. Large-scale dismantling of the wall followed in 1990, and its pieces scattered around the world. Where Else Can You See the Berlin Wall In Florida? St. Pete isn’t the only place in Florida with authentic Berlin Wall material. Pieces are held or displayed at locations elsewhere in the state, including Tampa, Orlando, Miami, and Sarasota. Berlin Wall sections can also be found throughout the United States and around the world, often at museums, universities, government buildings, and public memorials. What distinguishes the St. Pete installation is less the rarity of the artifact and more the setting. There is no museum exhibit explaining any history. There is no visitor center. There is no sign. Instead, three sections of the Berlin Wall just sit there, where they were installed in 2008, outside a pottery studio in a former railroad freight depot. Dare I say, art for the sake of art? Pop by and have a quick look as you explore the city.

item.title: Americans Spend an Average Of $360 On Pre-Wedding Bach Trips
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.97
If a request from Splitwise following a fun and indulgent long weekend makes your heart race, you’re not alone. Splitwise, the app used to track expenses and split shared costs pulled fresh data on the financial cost of bachelor and bachelorette weekends. Used across more than 32 million group trips, the appe found that the average attendee spends $410 per trip, excluding individual airfare and travel costs. Unsurprisingly, with 38% of Americans going into debt to attend weddings and the related events, the U.S. is among the world’s most expensive destinations for pre-wedding celebration travel, with the median per-person spend is $360, approximately 25% higher than the global median of $289. “Bachelor and bachelorette parties used to be one big night out, closer to the actual wedding date," says Liz Hernandez, VP of Marketing at Splitwise. “Over the past decade, these parties have grown, often becoming full weekend celebrations and three-day destination trips. ” According to Splitwise’s transaction data, the average trip lasts three days, with 92% of pre-wedding trips lasting two days or longer. The Real Cost of Bachelor and Bachelorette Trips Luckily for Americans, there is still one country that typically spends more on these 72-hour-long parties: Switzerland, where the average cost is $409 per person. Canada came in third for the highest costs at $315 per person, followed by Austria at $303 per person and France at $280 per person. “I think that social media has raised the bar for what these celebrations look like. People are coordinating matching outfits, planning elaborate activities and creating content as part of the celebration, rather than capturing one night out on a single-use camera,” says Hernandez. “We see that evolution reflected in the Splitwise data, where shared costs can include everything from matching shirts and daytime activities to private chefs and group stays. We wanted to understand what all of that actually means for the people paying to attend.” A new digital Splitwise tool allows users to see how the bach party they’re attending stacks up with the rest of spenders, showing the estimated average cost for extras depending on the size of the group, destination, and length of the trip. Of course, the United States is far from a monolith and a long weekend in Jackson Hole, Palm Springs, or East Hampton may rack up a larger bill than a getaway to Galena, Illinois or Door County, Wisconsin. “I hope this data can help people planning these trips gut-check their plans, see how their spending stacks up and, most importantly, create a celebration that their guests can comfortably afford,” says Hernandez.

item.title: The $60 Cup: Where Coffee Connoisseurs Are Traveling Now
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.95
I’m about twelve years old, standing barefoot in the tiled kitchen of my best friend’s Cuban household, witnessing the cafecito ritual. The smell of fried plantains sizzling on the stove comingles with steaming plates of cumin-spiced rice and black beans. For dessert, we will eat cold papaya swimming in syrup. But first, we get to sip real café Cubano from a stovetop moka. The first drops of espresso are vigorously whipped with sugar into a thick espumita froth inside the cup, before the rest is poured in, causing the caramelly-brown foam to rise to the top. It’s intensely strong and sweet — and made by the hands of people who escaped Fidel Castro to build a new life. This isn’t just caffeine delivery. Getting to participate was to be embraced by this family. This is how I was made a purist before I knew the word, and have traveled the world recognizing and reveling in coffee pouring ceremonies everywhere from Istanbul to Bushwick. At the high end, this can cost $60 a cup. I wanted to find out how something so beautifully basic could become so expensive. Brooklyn's $60 Pour-Over Curiosity led me to café Sey in Bushwick, which serves specialty coffees in a bright, minimalist-industrial space to people hunched over ceramic cups sipping and sniffing “notes” of melon, lime and jasmine. They speak the language of third-wave coffee (the next rung above pumpkin latté shops like Starbucks), which deals in gram scales, micro-lots, extractions, and varietals. The café experience feels like walking into a serious wine-tasting in a cellar, where you pretend you know what you’re doing while servers periodically remind you to cleanse your palate. Barista Lorenzo Mezzatesta, a very generous and knowledgeable guide, walked me through the high end of their menu. The $60 cup is Panamanian, and is typically a “Panama Gesha” or “Finca Sophia.” Depending on the year and harvest, these can retail for $40 to $100 a cup, and come in scarce, limited edition shipments. “They were harvested about three or four months ago, and need to go through the roasting process. We’re getting some in this fall and winter,” says Mezzatesta, manning the counter with practiced precision, like an omakase chef. This level of pricing is niche, but it’s a fast-growing market. Partners Coffee has four brick-and-mortar shops in New York, Hydrangea popped up in California, Aviary Coffee in Cleveland, The Picky Chemist in Belgium, and the sleek newcomer Watchhouse from the UK will open five stores in New York City this year. They’re all dependent on traveling “green buyers.” A green buyer sources, samples, and purchases unroasted (green) coffee beans, bridging the gap between farmers and retailers. Think of them like brokers who set premium specialty coffee market prices, which are still a part of traditional commodity markets. They just think their coffee tastes better. How a Cup Gets to $60 The high end is influenced by online auctions where roasters bid up rare and microlot coffees through the Alliance for Coffee Excellence (ACE) or the Best of Panama auction. Plain old “commodity” coffee (the raw material) is also more expensive than it used to be. Everything else is perceived value. - The auction ceiling: a 20-kilo washed Gesha lot from Hacienda La Esmeralda sold for $604,080 — $30,204/kg — at the Best of Panama auction, on a day commodity coffee traded at $2.98/lb. The buyer was Julith Coffee, a Dubai roastery. It’s the priciest example, but these are the kind of micro-lots supplying the luxury cafés selling cups for $50–$100. - The middle-market suckers: 2024–2026 has been the most expensive coffee market in fifty years, with arabica setting a record above $4.37/lb in October 2025, due to high tariffs and climate disruptions in Brazil and Vietnam. Everyone's coffee got more expensive; ‘Specialty Roasters’ simply created a premium category. - The takeaway: the $60 cup isn’t inflation — it’s coffee acquiring a champagne tier, with terroir, auctions, and provenance to match. Back at Sey’s counter, I order $21.50 worth of Ethiopian Landrace, with a Chiroso chaser from Colombia from David Berrio’s farm, La Casita. Evidently these have been “hand-picked at peak ripeness.” I drink them black from handmade ceramic bowls, which sit prettily beside laminated cheat-sheets. These colorful cards outline everything from delivery and duty costs to the buyer (to soften the blow?); tasting notes like white honey and key lime; and full descriptions of the origin farms, including the region, altitude, processing technique, date of harvest and the varietal you’re drinking. I can’t help but blurt out: What does $60 taste like?! Mezzatesta’s answer is a musical metaphor: “Panama is famous for a distinction of florality that few others have; It’s a very complex, floral, long finish that stays with you for a while. There’s a nice sweetness, nice acidity. And a loudness. Like a great, explosive glass of wine… It's kind of like a melody or a chord where sweetness, acidity, and even a little bit of bitterness occur at the same time. How loud or expressive is the profile? When you're already at that very high level, some coffees have a demonstrative difference. It's in our business to understand and chase that.” They know what they’re doing; Sey brews Geshas from Panama's Elida Estate, and Elida won Geisha Washed at the Best of Panama 2026. Across town in Williamsburg, you can get a damn fine cappuccino in the Roman café called “Little Fino” for $5.50, paired with impeccable pistachio cake for $7. It’s run by Chef Andrew Carmellini’s NoHo Hospitality Group (known for Café Carmellini), so you can expect La Colombe beans served in a polished Italian trattoria style. For sheer taste and value, it’s one of the best cups in Brooklyn; La Colombe is one of the few "third wave" coffee movement roasters with low pricing, because they built early and at-scale. These days, everyone claims ethical sourcing (read: no forced or child labor, which are serious, well-documented problems in the global coffee industry). The travel and time it takes to consistently vet plantations around the globe justifies the high price… or so the argument goes. So, what does plantation labor really look like? Welcome to Aprocetu, Costa Rica I visited a remote coffee plantation in the Costa Rican highlands to see for myself. The owner of Aprocetu coffee, Arnoldo Guerrero, runs his farm at an elevation of around 3,000 feet in a cloud forest full of cherries (the whole, fleshy outer fruit that grow on trees). They’ve had weeks without enough rain in March, but that’s not what worries him. It’s the heat. “10 years ago the area was cooler. Now it’s harder in the intense heat… Ojo de gallo from humidity,” says Guerrero in Spanish. “It’s a fungus that can kill coffee leaves,” explains Tonny, 29, a first-time tour guide from the neighboring eco-lodge Santa Lucia Jungle Hacienda. During harvest time (December / January), it requires the hands of eight indigenous communities in the surrounding area to hand pick about 240 kilograms per day. Many, Guerrero tells me, are from Venezuela: “The money means more to them, so they come.” Drying comes next. Aprocetu farmers rake the entire lot in the sun every hour of daylight. In ideal conditions, it takes 36 hours. I pick up a rake and get to work in 95 Farenheit; I’m drenched and ready to quit in 10 minutes; “Flavor depends on the sun!” Guerrero says, laughing as I wilt. Only five people actually manage the drying and hand sorting required for quality control; and they roast on-site. The result is a bright, citrusy Arabico called San Isidro, sold mostly in the U.S. One sack of his coffee sells to retailers like Starbucks for about $800 USD, and it’s destined to end up in a $7 latte. Costa Rican Hospitality Guerrero lives modestly on a dirt road, in a one bedroom house, only reachable on foot or risking mudslides on a motorbike. Pigs grunt and chickens squawk in the mist, laundry is hung out on the line, and air conditioning is non-existent. His son lives next door under a tin roof, pounded out by the tropical rain. His wife welcomes me into their open-air kitchen for coffee and tamal de maicena — homemade milk tarts made with cornstarch, which are unbelievably fresh and delicious. On the raw concrete walls, there are framed and fading pictures of mothers, fathers and children punctuated by wooden Catholic relics. Everyone within a 15 mile radius works for Aprocetu; family bonds bind it together. As if on cue, Guerrero’s 98 year old father hikes up the hill to greet us, with the aid of two walking sticks and a machete hanging from his makeshift belt. He looks remarkably robust, not at all winded from the hike; a broad smile on his weather-worn face. In a gesture of hospitality, father and son cut down sour oranges and green mangoes from high in their trees with machetes. They don’t have central plumbing, but they’re offering fresh fruit. It feels biblical. And sobering. Costa Rica's system is comparatively protective — ICAFE ensures farmers receive 80% of the FOB [Freight on Board] export price — but that only goes so far. Even in the best-case origin country, the money lives at the roasting-and-ritual end of the chain. Not up in the cloud forests. How Far Would You Go for the Best Cup? True coffee connoisseurs typically travel in one of three ways: they’re looking for great café culture, they need to meet with origin farmers, or they’re attending international coffee championships. This October, for the first time in Latin America, Panama will host the World of Coffee and the World Barista Championship. It’s the coffee world’s Best in Show moment. Can Eugene Levy narrate? A slurping competition couldn’t get me to an airport. But amazing cafés can. Because coffee purism isn't really about price point, it's about ritual. It’s about culture. And every great café culture pours differently. In Rome, you stand up at an espresso bar and shout for your right to be served, with shirt-sleeves rolled up, bankers elbowing brick layers, everyone jostling together. In Istanbul, grounds brewed in long copper cezves are read to you, like a fortune divined in a cup. In Athens, the finely-ground sediment called katakathi settles to the bottom, each pour heavy and dark, demanding patience and time. The Greeks do the two-hour sidewalk sit better than anyone. But it’s in Brooklyn at Sey where I realize the $60 cup and the $0.60 cups my childhood Cuban friends let me drink are, at their best, the same thing. This is love-as-attention, made drinkable. And I’m always craving more. More From Forbes

item.title: The World’s Best IPAs, According To The 2026 World Beer Awards
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.95
India Pale Ale might be the poster child for American craft beer these days, but there are some really interesting IPAs being brewed today far outside the United States. Case in point: when the World Beer Awards rolled out its 2026 winners, not a single American brewery cracked the top of the IPA heap. Instead, seven beers from five countries—Brazil, Japan, Germany, Canada, and China—claimed the World’s Best titles in their categories. If you needed proof that IPA has gone global, here it is. The World Beer Awards might not get the same buzz stateside as the Great American Beer Festival or the World Beer Cup, but that’s exactly what makes its results so fun to watch. American breweries do throw their hats in the ring, but this competition casts a much wider net, often shining a spotlight on beers and breweries that would otherwise get lost in the shuffle of bigger, U.S.-centric contests. Held annually since 2007, the World Beer Awards evaluates commercially available beers from around the globe. Entries are blind tasted and judged on taste and quality, with winners advancing from country-level competitions toward global awards in internationally recognized beer styles. This year’s IPA results are basically a treasure map for adventurous beer lovers. Here are the seven brews that took home World’s Best honors in their IPA categories. Landel Atrás do Bloco — World’s Best Milkshake IPA/New England IPA Brazil’s Landel brewery snagged the top IPA prize with Atrás do Bloco, which didn’t just win its category—it was crowned the overall World’s Best IPA. This 7.5% ABV hazy IPA is double dry-hopped with Mosaic, Cascade, and Citra, serving up that juicy, tropical, citrus-forward punch hazy fans crave. And this isn’t its first rodeo: Atrás do Bloco has racked up medals at Brazilian beer competitions for years, including a gold at the 2026 Concurso Brasileiro de Cerveja. Derailleur Brew Works WC IPA — World’s Best American Style IPA It’s hard not to smile at the irony: the World’s Best American Style IPA comes from Japan. Osaka’s Derailleur Brew Works channels classic West Coast vibes with its 7% ABV WC IPA. Brewed with three hop varieties, it leads with tropical and citrus aromas, then finishes with that crisp, assertive bitterness that made West Coast IPAs legends in the first place. Camba Black Shark — World’s Best Black IPA Germany’s Camba Bavaria didn’t hold back with Black Shark, an 8.5% ABV Imperial Black IPA that clocks in at a whopping 100 IBUs. This beer brings together the hop punch you expect from an IPA with the roasted malt flavors you’d usually find in a stout. Think coffee and dark chocolate swirling with fruit and bold hop notes. Black Shark is no stranger to the winner’s podium, either—it’s already picked up Gold and Silver at the World Beer Awards in years past. Therezópolis Jade — World’s Best English Style IPA Brazil scored a second win with Jade from Therezópolis. At 6.5% ABV and 50 IBUs, Jade tips its hat to classic English IPA roots but brings its own flair. This copper beauty serves up bold floral and citrus aromas, plus the signature IPA bitterness. Jade already snagged a World Beer Awards Gold in 2025 before leveling up to take a global crown this year. Archibald Double IPA — World’s Best Imperial/Double/DIPA Quebec’s Archibald brewery grabbed the Double IPA crown with a beer that pulls no punches on hops or booze. Their 8.5% ABV Double IPA is loaded with Amarillo, Simcoe, and El Dorado hops, bringing notes of citrus, nectarine, and pineapple, all riding on a wave of firm bitterness. It’s a textbook case of the bigger-is-better mindset that made Double IPAs a cult favorite among hopheads. RichKat Craft Brewing Rebound — World’s Best Session IPA One of the most intriguing winners hails from China’s fast-growing craft beer scene. RichKat Craft Brewing’s Rebound snagged the Session IPA title, outpacing beers from some of the world’s most established brewing hotspots. The Hong Kong brewery crafted Rebound as a lighter, more refreshing riff on a previous Double IPA, dialing back the booze but keeping all the hop punch that makes the style sing. Cervejaria Unika Orange Kush — World’s Best Specialty IPA Brazil wrapped up its stellar run with Cervejaria Unika’s Orange Kush, which took top honors in the wide-open Specialty IPA category. This is the playground for the style’s wildest experiments—think fruit, rye, Belgian, white, sour, and other off-the-beaten-path IPAs. Orange Kush’s win meant Brazilian breweries claimed three of the seven World’s Best IPA titles in 2026. And Unika’s brewing chops go beyond just this competition: two of its other beers medaled at the 2026 World Beer Cup, with Catharina Sour Caju Pytang grabbing Gold and The Famous Gose (Morango & Pitanga) picking up Silver. If you’re an American beer fan, you probably won’t spot most of these bottles chilling at your local shop—and honestly, that’s part of the fun. The World Beer Awards is a reminder that the IPA revolution America kicked off years ago has truly gone worldwide. Brewers from Brazil to Japan to China are putting their own spin on the style, and by all accounts, some of these beers are well worth the trip. So if you find yourself near any of these breweries, consider it a sign: go taste what some of the world’s best IPA makers are up to. Follow here for the most up to date information about the ever-changing beer, wine and spirits industry.

item.title: 5 Adventure Experts Share Their Favorite Crowd-Free Hiking Trails
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.77
As sweltering summer temperatures push vacationers to choose mountains over cities and coastlines, hiking has surged in popularity. Well-known trails and parks are even struggling with visitor numbers; a visitor cap was introduced for climbing Japan’s Mount Fuji, while Portugal’s Madeira island has increased fees on its most popular paths. If you’re keen to avoid overcrowding, here are recommendations from guides, researchers and experience designers at Norrøna Adventure. Beyond why they love each hike, they’ve included difficulty level and seasonal timing. Rago-round / Litlverivassforsen, Nordland, Norway Thea Langeland, Adventure Designer, describes Rago as wild, rough, and incredibly beautiful. “Very few people know about it, even Norwegians, which gives it a quiet, untouched feel that I love,” she says. Plus, it might not be what you expect from Norwegian nature, with its deep valleys, steep cliffs, waterfalls, lakes and a river winding its way below the viewpoints. The full loop is challenging, with tough terrain. But if you don’t want something quite so demanding, Langeland recommends walking up to Grisryggen and getting the view over the valley and waterfall (Litlverivassforsen). “It's steep at the start, but the reward at the top is well worth the sweat,” she says. Best Time to Go: Summer or early autumn (June, July, August, early September) Difficulty: Full loop = Challenging (23 km, 1400 meters ascent, 2 days) | Hike to Litlverivassfossen = Intermediate (11 km, 600 meter ascent, out and back) Bakkanosi, Norway Adventure guide Hanne Hollås has another Norway hike that should be on your radar. Bakkanosi is a mountain peak located 1,398 meters above sea level in Vestland. “It is a long but relatively easy hike up to the edge, where you can look 1,400 meters down to one of Norway’s most beautiful fjords, the UNESCO-listed Nærøyfjorden,” says Hollås. “The steep mountains drop straight down into the narrow fjord.” Best Time to Go: Summer (July–September) and Winter (March–May) Difficulty: Intermediate Mount Triglav, Triglav National Park, Slovenia Camilla Melbye-Nørbech, Research, Design and Development Manager, points hikers to Mount Triglav in Slovenia. “What made conquering Mount Triglav so unforgettable was the striking contrast of its remote, crowd-free peaks and pristine alpine nature, paired with the unique luxury of being just a short drive away from world-class vineyards and the Adriatic coast,” she says. Best Time to Go: June–September Difficulty: Intermediate Fish River Canyon & Tok Tokkie Trail, Namibia If you’re traveling to Namibia, Elise Koren, Norrøna Adventure Guide, suggests tackling the Fish River Canyon and Tok Tokkie Trail. “Extremely remote, few people, unique, darkest sky for stargazing ever, sunny, comfortable temperatures, best atmosphere I have had trekking, amazing people,” she says. Best Time to Go: July–August Difficulty: 3/6 Sykes Hot Springs via Pine Ridge Trail, Big Sur, California Mike Holley, Project Manager, recommends that visitors to California try the Pine Ridge Trail. “I love hiking the Sykes Hot Springs Trail because it leads through the wild, remote beauty of the Ventana Wilderness to natural hot springs that are perfect for a soak,” he says. “This is a rugged hike through the remote California coastal range, where towering ancient coastal redwoods, sweeping ridge-top views, and the chance to spot soaring California condors make the steep climbs and occasional poison oak well worth the effort.” Best Time to Go: Year-round Difficulty: 7/10

item.title: How Europe’s Flight Compensation Changes Will Affect Your Next Trip
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.52
When Sofia Calvin's flight to Spain landed about five hours late, she filed a claim under Europe's passenger rights law and was promised 400 euros (about $466). She spent a little over a year trying to collect the money. Her airline wouldn’t send the required compensation to her U.S. bank account. Calvin, who runs Storied Travel, a luxury agency in Brookline, Mass., finally opened a Revolut account so she could take the payment in euros. "Having a right to compensation and actually receiving that compensation can be two very different experiences," she says. Europe upgraded its airline consumer laws this summer to eliminate cases like hers. In June, negotiators for the European Parliament and the Council of the EU struck a deal on the first real overhaul of Regulation 261/2004 in more than two decades. The Council signed off on the revisions in July. The new rules enter into force 12 months and 20 days after publication in the Official Journal, which means they take effect late next summer. Airlines spent 13 years trying to weaken Europe's consumer protections. Some of what they got could cost you money, but many of the changes will help passengers bound for Europe next year. For Calvin, the changes would have required her airline to answer her within 30 days. But that's not the biggest change, by far. What the new EU 261 flight compensation rules change - Cash compensation doesn't change. Delays of three hours or more at your final destination still pay 250 to 600 euros depending on distance. Airlines pushed to raise that trigger as high as nine hours and they lost. - A nine-month filing deadline replaces the patchwork. Right now the clock runs on each country's limitation period, anywhere from a year to several years. - Airlines get 30 days to answer you. Today there's no deadline at all, which is how a claim disappears into a queue for a year. - Self-booked rerouting becomes reimbursable. If the airline can't get you moving within three hours of a cancellation, you can book your own flight, train or bus and claim up to 400 percent of your fare, payable within 14 days. - Skipping your outbound leg won't cancel your return. The no-show penalty is banned. - A carry-on has to be in the advertised fare. No more discovering the bag fee at checkout. - Sitting with your child under 14 is free. No seat-selection charge. Erika Josefsson, legal strategist and air passenger rights expert at AirHelp, says one of the most significant shifts involves self-booked rerouting. If an airline fails to offer a viable alternative within three hours of a cancellation, passengers can book their own ticket on a rival airline, train, or bus and claim reimbursement up to 400% of their original fare. "A passenger who paid $100 for a low-cost ticket could get back up to $400, which is often enough to cover a same-day alternative," Josefsson notes. "But a passenger who paid $25 for a heavily discounted fare would only be entitled to $100 back—and that frequently isn't enough to cover the cost of the replacement flight, train, or bus they actually need to book." Airlines will also have to tell you within 96 hours of a disruption that you may be owed money. And the rules governing food and hotels get specific: a refreshment for every two hours of waiting, a meal after three hours and then every five, plus hotels for overnight delays. Here's the concession to the airline industry that broke a 13-year deadlock: You'll have nine months from your departure date to file a compensation claim with the operating airline. (Today there's no EU-wide deadline.) Claims currently run on each member state's limitation period, which stretches from a year to several depending on where you file. German passengers have effectively had close to four years; Danish passengers, at least three. Where the airlines will dig in The airline industry isn’t hiding its displeasure. The European Regions Airline Association has argued the reform will push the annual cost of EU 261 compliance from 8.1 billion euros to more than 15 billion euros, and that passengers will pay for it in higher fares. Josefsson expects friction in a few places. The revision writes a list of extraordinary circumstances into the regulation, the narrow set of events that let an airline refuse to pay. The list codifies 20 years of European court rulings, which is progress. It's also non-exhaustive, and it leaves room to argue if a borderline case qualifies. AirHelp says airlines wrongly reject 58 percent of valid claims on first response, and Josefsson doesn't expect that to change. And she anticipates a wave of form rejections timed to the new deadline. "Airlines might resort to sending standard rejection emails on day 29 as a matter of course, putting the burden back on the passenger to appeal," she says. The mistake that costs American passengers the most Americans assume U.S. carriers aren’t bound by European law. But they are, at least in certain instances, and every new protection in the revision of the EU law applies. The moment a Delta, United or American Airlines flight lifts off from a runway in an EU country, it's subject to EU 261. So a delayed Delta flight from Rome to New York can qualify for up to 600 euros. But that same Delta flight from New York to Rome doesn't qualify. Thousands of travelers abandon legitimate claims on the flight home because nobody told them they had a valid claim. The second expensive mistake happens at the gate. Accept a meal voucher or a goodwill gift card, and the fine print can waive your right to cash compensation worth many times more. Amanda Persi, founder of The Getaway Co., says the damage rarely stops with the flight. A five-hour delay on the way to a group trip in Europe can mean a missed connection, a missed transfer, a lost first night, or arriving after everyone else has started without you. "They shouldn't have to become experts in aviation regulations to know what they're entitled to when things go wrong," Persi says. How to claim EU 261 compensation for a delayed flight The new European consumer protections may not take effect until 2027, but you can take steps now to keep your flight on track. - Photograph the departure board before you leave the airport. Take an image of the delay, flight number and time in one frame. - Ask a gate agent for the reason in writing. "Operational issues" is not a reason. Push for specifics. - Keep everything. Boarding passes, booking confirmation, airline emails and texts, claim numbers, receipts. - Note your actual arrival time at your final destination. You can do that on FlightAware or a similar app showing the flight's departure and arrival times. Compensation depends on when the door opened, not on the scheduled arrival time. - Refuse the voucher until you know what cash you're owed. Read the waiver language before you sign or tap anything. - File early, but no later than nine months from your departure date. Sooner is better, even under today's longer deadlines. - Treat the first rejection as an opening position. Appeal it, escalate to the national enforcement body, or bring in a claims service. What the new rules won't do for you The new rules are better than what they replace, but claiming the protection they offer still takes some homework. Europe told airlines to email you within 96 hours and answer you within 30 days. It didn’t tell them to stop saying no. Calvin finally got her 400 euros because she wouldn't go away. She had to open a foreign bank account to be paid what a regulation already said was hers. Next summer, airlines are betting you'll take the first no and get on with your life.

item.title: Blank Street Expands To Los Angeles, Adding Ice Cream To The Menu
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.49
Another New Yorker has gone bicoastal. Blank Street, the New York-based coffee chain with an estimated $500 million valuation, has opened its 106th shop, expanding its reach beyond the East Coast and UK to Los Angeles. The new Los Angeles cafe in Studio City will offer Blank Street’s standard menu, with new treats slated for later this year. At Blank Street Los Angeles, guests can choose from classics, signatures and seasonals coffee and matcha beverages. In celebration of the West Coast opening, the cafe is offering an exclusive drink: Cortado Cloud. Served with either matcha or espresso, the drink features Madagascan vanilla bean syrup in a sweet cream cloud, topped with vanilla bean powder. The cafe is located at 13273 Ventura Blvd. “Studio City felt right for our California debut," said Blank Street Co-Founder and CEO Issam Freiha. “Beyond the neighborhood’s charm and storied history, it has the creative spirit and strong sense of community that matters so much to us. There’s also something special about opening here with Evan [Mateen], one of our earliest team members, who grew up nearby. That personal connection makes this launch feel like a true homecoming for us.” Later this year, Blank Street is debuting a new product to Los Angeles: Ice Cream. The frozen treats menu was developed in partnership with Zen Ong, known for plant-based, Indonesian-inspired vegan ice cream at Awan in Los Angeles. Blank Street’s ice cream menu draws inspiration from some of its most popular beverage flavors: white chocolate matcha, vanilla bean affogato, mocha, and strawberry shortcake matcha. Each flavor pairs a base (matcha, espresso, vanilla bean, or strawberry) with a shell (chocolate, white chocolate, matcha, or espresso) and a garnish dusting. Blank Street Los Angeles’ interiors are inspired by the city’s Case Study houses. The building’s midcentury architecture is accentuated by steel, glass, and wood. The brand’s iconic shade of green punctuates the design on the booth textiles and terrazzo flooring that extends from the interior through to the outdoor patio. Blank Street is set to open a Beverly Hills location later this year in a standalone Tudor Revival building on Bedford Drive,

item.title: Would You Pay $1,250 To Escape From A Hurricane?
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.03
It’s the height of hurricane season. And when a hurricane is barreling toward you, one of the hardest parts of hurricane evacuation isn’t deciding whether to leave, it’s knowing when. Wait too long and highways become parking lots, flights sell out and airports may shut down. Leave too early and you may wonder if you overreacted. That’s exactly the problem a new Florida startup, PriorityEvac, is aiming to solve. The company has launched the country’s first membership-based hurricane air evacuation program. For $1,250 per person each year, members receive access to pre-arranged evacuation flights from six Florida airports before qualifying storms make travel difficult or impossible. The idea came to founder Jason Murgio after hearing a friend’s nightmare evacuation story in 2019. “His family had a real difficult time getting flights,” Murgio told me in an interview. “They weren’t on the same flights, the prices were astronomical and it was just mass chaos. I said, ‘There has to be a better way to do this.’” Murgio, an insurance investment banker, spent the next several years figuring out a better way to evacuate people in a hurricane. Florida’s geography posed an obvious challenge: It’s a long peninsula, and when a major storm approaches, much of the evacuation traffic is headed in the same direction: north. So he set out to create a model that could evacuate people at scale. He partnered with Miami-based Global Crossing Airlines to reserve aircraft before hurricane season begins each year, ensuring planes would be available if—and when—a qualifying storm threatens. Murgio also assembled a team with extensive disaster-response experience, including retired Air Force Colonel Tim Houston, former Chief of Operations for NORAD and USNORTHCOM, who previously coordinated large-scale hurricane evacuations. He also brought on former National Hurricane Center lead forecaster Wally Barnes, who helped develop the weather triggers that determine when flights should activate. How PriorityEvac Works PriorityEvac currently serves residents and seasonal homeowners in 12 counties across South Florida’s east and west coasts. Flights depart from Miami, Fort Lauderdale, West Palm Beach, Tampa, Sarasota and Fort Myers and fly members to Atlanta. The company uses National Hurricane Center forecasting criteria to decide when to activate flights. Once those thresholds are met, members receive phone calls, texts and emails from assigned case managers, who help coordinate every step of the evacuation, from confirming whether they’ll leave to directing them to the appropriate airport. The goal is to get members airborne roughly 30 to 72 hours before winds become strong enough to disrupt aviation, not necessarily right before landfall. “Everybody thinks about when a hurricane makes a landfall, but evacuations have to happen well before landfall, especially if you’re using aviation because winds drive the ability to fly,” says Murgio. Two qualifying evacuations are included with the annual membership. Members aren’t required to evacuate, but if the company activates flights for a qualifying storm, that counts as one of the two evacuations, even if they decide to leave another way. Atlanta was selected because it’s close enough for aircraft to shuttle back and forth multiple times while also offering one of the country’s largest airports, abundant hotels, rental cars and onward flight connections. If a storm threatens Atlanta, the company says it can divert flights to Charlotte or Nashville. Once members arrive, they are responsible for arranging accommodations and transportation home after the storm. Is There Really A Need? The obvious question is whether PriorityEvac solves a real problem or simply offers another way to do something people could arrange themselves. From Miami-based meteorologist Amanda Pappas’ perspective, the problem is very real. Pappas, a Certified Broadcast Meteorologist who has covered hurricanes in Florida for years, shares all kinds of weather advice on her social channels, from TikTok to Instagram. She says evacuations have become increasingly difficult as the state’s population has grown and more people have moved into vulnerable coastal communities. “Once those evacuation orders go into play, it’s a race to try to get out,” Pappas told me in an interview. “This gives people another option and maybe allows them to get out even sooner.” During a hurricane, Pappas says the biggest challenge isn’t logistics, it’s psychology. People routinely convince themselves they have more time than they actually do. “I have to act almost as a psychologist when a storm is coming,” she says. “A lot of people wait till the last absolute minute to evacuate.” She knows firsthand how dangerous that can be. While covering Hurricane Ian in Fort Myers in 2022, Pappas was trapped at her television station after staff decided not to evacuate. She had to move through floodwaters before the National Guard eventually rescued the group in the middle of the night. Her advice is simple: Prepare early and don’t wait until the last minute to leave. That’s one reason she sees value in PriorityEvac, which outsources part of that decision-making process to people who spend their careers thinking about hurricanes. “You get to take out the guesswork,” says Pappas. “The pressure’s not on you to make the decision of whether or not to evacuate. There are professionals there.” Who Is It For? PriorityEvac says early interest has come from several groups, including homeowners looking for a predetermined evacuation plan, adult children buying memberships for elderly parents who live in Florida and parents of college students attending school in the state. The company expects to cap membership at roughly 5,000 people during its first season to ensure it can accommodate everyone if flights are activated. If it reaches capacity, additional applicants will be placed on a waiting list. Is It Worth $1,250? Whether the membership is worth $1,250 ultimately depends on how you think about hurricane preparedness. “I would call it a preparedness investment,” says Murgio. “I’d put this in the same category as people buying home generators, storm shutters, elevated flood coverage.” In other words, it’s an investment you hope you will never need to use. He also points to the potential economics of a last-minute evacuation. During previous hurricanes, Murgio says his research found that one-way commercial airline tickets could cost $1,500 to $3,000, assuming seats were still available. “If you think about two qualifying events, that’s effectively $625, which is the cost of a commercial flight,” he says. “And certainly a lot less than what we saw when we started researching what commercial aviation was charging during hurricanes.” PriorityEvac also differs from evacuation membership companies such as Medjet and Global Rescue. Those services are generally designed to respond to a medical, security or other emergency after something has happened. PriorityEvac is intended to be proactive: The aircraft, activation criteria and support system are put in place before the hurricane arrives. The concept may eventually extend beyond its current locations in Florida. Murgio says PriorityEvac plans to expand farther into the state and ultimately into Gulf Coast states, Texas and the southern Atlantic region. He has also received inquiries from people in the Bahamas, Puerto Rico and other Caribbean destinations, although he says expanding to the islands would be more operationally complicated. For Murgio, though, what he’s selling isn’t really a hurricane evacuation flight. “They’re buying peace of mind,” he says. “They’re buying a plan.”

item.title: New Sixt Data Reveals The Most Road Trip-Worthy College Campuses In The U.S.
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 3.96
College campus tours aren’t reserved for students — in fact a lot of college campuses across the U.S. are historically relevant buildings with stunning landscapes, walking paths, and plenty to see and do. New data from SIXT has analysed more than 150 college campuses across the country to see which locations are the most road trip-worthy. The data included things like green spaces, historic preservation, Google reviews, and appearances in film and television to find the best options to visit on your next road trip. Here are the campuses that came out on top: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign The number one spot on the list is the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign mainly due to its impressive amount of green spaces and outdoor areas. The campus boasts open green spaces across 6,370 acres (or about 17.5 acres per 1,000 students). It also boasts historic architecture for visitors looking for both scenery and history as well. The Ohio State University The Ohio State University earned second place thanks to its 27 quads, over 125 walking paths, and 1,777 acres of green space in total. Its location in Columnus also makes it easy for visitor to pack in a great trip beyond the campus. Cornell University Located in Ithaca, New York, Cornell Universiry took third spot thanks to its picturesque setting. The ivy league school boasts 745 acres of green space and ten quads as well as close to 52 miles of walking paths to explore. It also has historic architecture that movie buffs will recognize from film and television. University of Wisconsin-Madison The University of Wisconsin-Madison came in fourth place with a scenic campus that spans nearly 936 acres across 12 quads and open areas. There are also over 67 miles of walking paths for visitors to check out. The data also showed that the university’s historic designation and high Google reviews make it a campus worth visiting. Stanford University In fifth place is Stanford University in California. The data does show that the campus has fewer total walking paths than some of the other schools on the list but the outdoor space is vast with over 448 acres of land per 1,000 students. It also has very distinct architecture and striking landscaping.

item.title: Hidden Travel Insurance Exclusions You Should Check Before Your Trip
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 3.79
Before Janice Lintz visited the South Pole, she asked her travel insurance company a simple question: Would their policies cover her? Nobody could tell her. "Sadly, many insurance representatives did not know where the South Pole was," says Lintz, a disability advocate from Washington, D.C. "No joke." But she kept asking. She learned that some insurers and rescue companies won't cover travel below the 60th parallel, which takes in most of Antarctica. Finally, she requested an answer in writing about coverage of South Pole travel. She also asked for a list of what she could and couldn't do once she arrived. Rock climbing was out. So were ice climbing, mountaineering and rappelling. Skiing, a snowmobile tour, ice tunnels and rope walking were fine, and so was walking. "Knowing this was helpful to ensure I didn't do an activity that voided my insurance," says Lintz. "This was key since I was rope walking and visiting ice tunnels." Almost nobody buys insurance like Lintz. Most travelers see a price at checkout and click a box. They never open the insurance certificate. That works fine until you clip into a via ferrata in the Dolomites and have an accident. It doesn’t matter if you are climbing Mount Everest, paragliding in the Everglades or scuba diving off a remote island shore, travelers are better off with protection that has no activity limitations,” said Bill McIntyre, director at Global Rescue. How travel insurance policies define hazardous activities The words in an insurance certificate might not mean what you think they mean. And that's where most coverage denials start. "Don't assume that the label tells you everything you need to know," says Alex Adekola, founder of ReadyAdjuster. "Just because an event is labeled as hazardous doesn't mean that loss is excluded. So the important question is what does your policy consider hazardous and what conditions apply to that exclusion." It goes the other way, too. An activity you'd never call extreme may be excluded, because the insurer wrote its own definition without telling you. "Check if the policy uses its own definition of an activity rather than relying on what you would ordinarily consider that activity to mean," says Adekola. The most common travel insurance exclusions Some exclusions turn up almost everywhere. Chrissy Valdez, senior director of operations at Squaremouth, says the common ones include: - Professional or organized sports. - Claims tied to negligence, illegal activity or reckless behavior. - Any injury caused by alcohol or drug use. - Routine or planned medical and dental care. - Pre-existing conditions (unless your policy provides a waiver). - Traveling against a doctor's orders. - Travel to countries with State Department Level 4 advisories. - Military action and acts of war. Buying the adventure policy doesn't clear all of that away, which trips up a lot of travelers. "Travelers often believe that if you buy an adventure or sports-specific travel insurance policy, all activities will be covered, but that is simply not the case," says Valdez. "Some sports such as hiking, mountaineering, distance running and scuba diving have specific coverage limits for altitudes, depths and distances." Put differently, a policy can name your sport and still walk away from your claim, because you dove deeper or climbed higher than the certificate allows. How the circumstances of an accident affect your claim But the activity is only half of it. Insurers also look at how the injury happened. "Circumstances such as whether you're properly licensed to operate a rented scooter or other vehicle, whether you're participating in a competition, or whether drugs or alcohol contributed to an incident can matter," says Raymond Yorke, a spokesman for Redpoint Travel Protection. "Think through what you actually plan to do on your vacation and read the relevant exclusions before you go." Sankalp Singh nearly found that out in Greece. He rented a scooter on a family trip and assumed the rental company's coverage was enough. He later discovered his travel policy classified mopeds as a hazardous activity and excluded them outright. "I didn't crash, but I sure read the certificate afterward like it was a contract for buying a house," says Singh, who runs a travel site called Chasing Whereabouts. Renting mopeds is a well-known travel insurance "gotcha." Sometimes they're covered, but often they aren't. And riding on a scooter (think a Grab ride in Thailand) is almost never covered. "We look at what happened in fact, look at the policy, and see if the facts of the loss fall under the exclusion that is being used," says Adekola. "Don't read your policy and assume that you're covered for any and all accidents, because the accident has to happen under a particular set of circumstances." Understanding medical vs. evacuation coverage Lintz ran into all of these while preparing for Antarctica. Medical and evacuation coverages are separate. "Some plans include only evacuation and not medical insurance," she says. "The assumption is that both are covered when that is incorrect." An evacuation benefit gets you to a hospital. It won't always pay the hospital. Don't forget the "free look" period. You have anywhere from 10 to 30 days to review your policy and do any due diligence you may have forgotten. After that the policy is nonrefundable. Lintz had the underwriters confirm in writing that her prior treatment wouldn't be a problem, allowing her to keep her coverage. Where you're standing can void the whole thing. Advisory levels move, and so do the geographic carve-outs. Lintz says she checked both before she left, then asked for confirmation in writing. When I visited the Antarctic a few years ago, insurance was a real open question. I had just sustained a serious ski injury and was still on crutches. Would my policy still cover me? It turns out I had to get medical clearance from a doctor and a policy that covered medical evacuations in Antarctica, which cost extra. But it was worth it. I spent almost two weeks exploring Antarctica on the HX's MS Fridtjof Nansen, a vessel built to withstand the harsh conditions found in polar waters. Interestingly, we did have a medical evacuation on board. A woman broke her leg, but instead of airlifting her, the ship simply turned around and she was hospitalized in Ushuaia, Argentina. How to buy the right travel insurance policy Pull up the certificate—not the marketing page—and search it for the words that decide claims: hazardous, extreme, motorized, altitude, depth, competition, licensed, intoxication. Next, write out your itinerary activity by activity, including the things you'd never think to declare, like the zip line the resort throws in for free. Check whether medical and evacuation are both there and what each is capped at. Then ask the insurer, in writing, about anything the certificate leaves ambiguous. Oh, and if they don't know where the South Pole is, maybe skip the insurance company. If the answer comes back over the phone, it's worthless. Lintz's coverage would have been effective because she made the underwriters put it on paper before she boarded. That's a good idea no matter where you're traveling this summer.

item.title: The Long Shadow of the Iran Shock
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 7.24
By almost any measure, the world should be suffering a far more severe energy crisis. The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies normally passes, has been largely closed for months. Yet when considered against the nightmare scenarios contemplated at the war’s outset, oil prices have remained low and natural gas markets have proved resilient. The global economy has so far avoided the kind of recession that many past energy shocks produced. It would be tempting to conclude that the dangers of energy supply disruptions have been overstated, but such complacency would be misguided. The Hormuz crisis has so far led to only modest oil price spikes thanks to an unusual combination of favorable market conditions and years of investment in energy security measures. Before the war began, oil markets were oversupplied, inventories were relatively high, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates had built pipelines around the strait, and governments and companies had amassed emergency and commercial stocks. In addition, China helped stabilize the global oil balance by reducing its imports, drawing on its immense capacity to curb how much oil it buys for stocks, holds in inventory, refines for export, and consumes domestically. These conditions may not endure. If the conflict enters a new phase of intense fighting that threatens to spill across borders and continues to block the strait, oil markets, now stressed by shortages of refined products such as diesel and jet fuel, could see crude oil prices surge higher. But even if hostilities in the region de-escalate, a persistent risk to traffic through the strait will likely remain, with passage either outright controlled by Iran or, at the very least, subject to Iranian disruption at any time. A more optimistic scenario in the next several months seems a chimera, barring major and unlikely change in Tehran. In preparing for these scenarios, as well as new crises in the more distant future, the world should not take solace in the relatively benign outcome of the last five months for energy markets. The cushions that helped the world manage those months are now more threadbare: inventories have been depleted, demand is recovering, alternative routes are becoming more vulnerable, and infrastructure continues to come under fire and, in some cases, will take years to repair. A second phase of the Hormuz crisis could prove substantially more damaging than the first. Moreover, the first phase of the crisis was not as painless as headline global oil prices suggested. The relatively modest movement in global benchmark prices concealed a strikingly uneven distribution of pain, as countries in Asia and Europe endured high prices, shortages, rationing, fiscal strain, and forced reductions in consumption, while the United States and China demonstrated newfound levels of insulation and influence. Delayed effects also loom on the horizon. Because of the crunch in refining, diesel and other crude products are priced much higher than they normally would be at current headline oil prices. And the shock is making it harder and more costly for Europe to replenish its natural gas inventories, leaving the continent with lower-than-usual storage levels and more vulnerable to energy and geopolitical coercion in the coming winter. The past five months have revealed not that the world has become immune to energy crises but that market forces, policy, and government investments in energy security have paid off. Without renewed efforts to rebuild, in today’s geopolitically fractured world that resilience will quickly erode. Before a next phase of this crisis unfolds, therefore, policymakers must analyze how this resilience came to be. Moreover, they must acknowledge that, as the energy system has changed since the 1970s, so too has the way energy shocks reverberate around the world, and the measures needed to safeguard against them. Understanding these dynamics will better position the world for the next inevitable energy shock. WHAT COULD HAVE BEEN When Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz days after U.S. and Israeli attacks in late February, the head of the International Energy Agency (IEA) called it the “the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.” But even as the strait remained almost entirely closed for nearly four months—until Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June—Brent crude averaged just over $100 per barrel, up from around $70 per barrel when the war began. The peak of $126 per barrel, in April, was far below the $200 per barrel that veteran analysts had warned was possible. Even after Tehran closed the strait to oil traffic again in July, after the cease-fire collapsed, the barrel price fell into the $80 range. Many factors contributed to this relatively muted price response. As would be expected, oil demand was forced to decrease, to match available supply.
