item.title: The Cost of Keeping China Out
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.08
Travelers returning from China often report having seen the future. The country’s advances in frontier commercial technologies are visible in the robots that make and serve food in restaurants; the drones that deliver food and medicine; and the deployment of industrial and humanoid robots on factory floors. Even outside China, most of the world is now familiar with Chinese electric vehicles that are as affordable as they are sleek, with massage chairs and swappable batteries winning over passengers from London to Santiago. Most Americans, however, are unaware of this future. Chinese EVs are effectively absent from the U.S. market, blocked by 250 percent tariffs and broad national security restrictions. And a bipartisan fear has prevented many frontier Chinese technologies, including drones and robots, from reaching U.S. shores. Apart from a handful of products, mostly consumer electronics, the U.S. market is largely oblivious to the fruits of China’s advanced manufacturing ecosystem. The United States has its reasons for this blind spot. As early as the second Obama administration, if not before, it became clear that China was not playing fairly in business. Successive administrations have used a slew of trade remedies and official complaints to the World Trade Organization to fight back against unfair subsidies, and rulings by the federal Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) have tried to prevent sensitive U.S. technologies from falling into the hands of Chinese actors. Since 2017, Chinese firms have also found themselves the targets of heightened security reviews. Today, many actors in Washington think the United States should do even more to disengage from Chinese business. Members of Congress are pressuring American pharmaceutical companies to discontinue clinical trials in China, for instance, citing concerns that China’s research and development ecosystem has ties to the People’s Liberation Army. Others are proposing legislation to ban Chinese ownership of U.S. farmland, ostensibly to protect the U.S. food supply and critical infrastructure. Calling out China’s gains as ill gotten is frequently justified. Defensive responses also feel satisfying—as if the United States could level the playing field and instantly create effective American competitors by locking out Chinese firms that have scaled up and advanced unfairly. Unfortunately, this approach does little to advance American economic and security interests. Chinese firms are no longer merely efficient producers or copycats; in terms of knowledge and production capability, they are increasingly global leaders in many industries. Denying them access to the American market harms U.S. competitiveness, hinders U.S. efforts to build industrial capacity at home, and ensures that U.S. industry and consumers remain far from the frontier of technological advancement. Instead, Americans must reckon honestly with the scale of China’s industrial and technological progress. The United States need not embrace Chinese imports and investment unconditionally, but it must recognize that its own long-term competitiveness depends on its companies and consumers being exposed to the cutting edge. U.S. President Donald Trump’s vague proposal for a joint “Board of Investment” with China, announced after his May summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, seemed to suggest Washington was moving in this direction. But nothing concrete has come from the board, and managing investment flows at the leader-to-leader level is certainly not efficient. A more mature strategy of selective openness is possible. The United States should permit carefully structured Chinese investment in areas in which the economic and technological benefits are substantial while imposing stringent safeguards to mitigate security risks. Building the political confidence to sustain a selectively open market for Chinese direct investments requires skilled, transparent, and thorough regulatory oversight. With such an approach, Washington can penalize some imports but still permit access to the U.S. market through investments in American production facilities. There is a clear precedent for this strategy. It is, in fact, exactly what China did to Western companies for decades. TROJAN HORSES? Since the 1990s, China has required global investors to operate under conditions that are designed to advance its national development goals. When foreign automakers or cellphone manufacturers wanted to take advantage of China’s cheap labor force, Beijing required that the firms use local supply chains, transfer technology, share management with Chinese firms, provide workforce training, and offer security protections (for example, localizing data and submitting to government oversight). The goal was always to ensure that foreign companies invested in ways that fostered a Chinese ecosystem. As Jeffrey Immelt, then chief executive of GE, said of China in 2010, “I am not sure that, in the end, they want any of us to win, or any of us to be successful.” Indeed, GE spent decades accessing the Chinese market through joint ventures that eventually seeded Chinese competitors. China is now home to both private and state-owned companies such as Midea, Haier, and State Grid that rose up to compete with GE in everything from home appliances to power generation and transmission. Many are even taking their strategies global—including to the United States. Chinese firms in frontier sectors like EVs, robotics, and life sciences especially want access to the vast U.S. consumer market. These firms face narrow profit margins at best at home—a result of the overcapacity and “involution” that came from excessive state investment and hypercompetition in specific sectors. If companies want to survive, they need foreign markets to prosper, and the United States remains the largest consumer market in the world. Companies such as the electronics and EV conglomerate Xiaomi and the battery maker CATL have publicly pined for U.S. market access, signaling that they would make significant investments in the United States in exchange for access. So far, however, the U.S. government has blocked such investments because of security concerns. An array of technologies are imagined to be modern Trojan horses. EVs, for instance, are not simply cars; they are traveling networks of sensors, software, computers, batteries, and communications systems capable of collecting data, mapping cities and infrastructure, and integrating with national grids. The fears range from reasonable (Chinese-connected vehicles mapping U.S. critical infrastructure) to far-fetched (remote control and even weaponization of vehicles on the road). These realities require vigilance. But the answer is not to reject all Chinese investment unless it poses zero security concerns. Such an approach risks isolating the United States economically. If American firms don’t have to compete against the global leaders, they will increasingly sell things only to Americans. The United States will end up an island of legacy firms and practices, and the isolation will weaken American dynamism, reduce competitiveness, and erode broader economic security. A SMARTER GATEKEEPING Instead, the United States can adopt strategic terms for investment, as China did. Trump’s Board of Investment remains something of a mystery—a talking point only, so far—but it is not difficult to imagine it drawing from the many regulatory tools in Washington to create and sustain an overall investment structure for Chinese companies. In fact, imposing such a regime should be fairly simple for Washington because it already has much of the institutional sophistication to implement such terms. In addition to CFIUS, the United States has a substantial arsenal of tools to monitor, selectively ban, and condition Chinese investments. A host of regulatory agencies, including the Food and Drug Administration, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and the Federal Communications Commission, can make targeted rules for firms in specific sectors, like life sciences, networked EVs, and robotics. Rules about data localization, required local partnerships, and supply chain diversification can help ensure that Chinese supply chains are not just imported into U.S. production. Washington can and should upgrade these tools to shape Chinese investment on its terms. CFIUS, for example, imagines the most far-fetched risk scenarios and judges whether they can be mitigated. The interagency committee’s approvals for sensitive investments and acquisitions frequently involve “national security agreements”—special corporate governance arrangements devised collaboratively between firms and CFIUS personnel with provisions for cybersecurity protection, data management, and continuous monitoring of firm decisions by national security specialists appointed to boards. This is a good beginning for a robust investment control system, but these agreements focus only on protecting national security—not enhancing economic benefits. To be more aggressive, they could also mandate that companies with Chinese investment have special corporate governance boards that monitor and execute economic requirements, including workforce training, diversification of suppliers, technology transfers, and more. While the specific administrative solution may evolve with experimentation, the central task is clear: Washington needs more systematic assessment and coordination. It needs a structure that is both more open and more targeted in mitigation and governance. This requires greater coordination among industry-specific regulators. Indeed, given that multinationals have complex corporate supply chains and ownership patterns, even deciding the national identity of firms requires coordination across the U.S. government. CFIUS may not think a company is controlled by Chinese interests, for instance, but Commerce may deem it sufficiently connected to a “foreign adversary.” The ability to resolve these regulatory complexities is important, since it is only through good bureaucratic coordination that Washington can both recognize the risks of technologies and also harness their benefits. THE TESLA MODEL China’s playbook for EVs is especially instructive. Beijing began encouraging domestic EV and large battery production in the early 2000s, largely through subsidies and industrial policy. Private companies like CATL and BYD made progress with batteries, but the industry, especially large state-owned producers, needed competitive pressure to upgrade the cars they made to meet consumer tastes. In 2019, Beijing decided to balance the risks and rewards of inviting Tesla, then the global leader in EV manufacturing, into the Chinese market at scale. They lifted the joint-venture requirement, and Tesla became the first global automaker to operate a production facility in China with no local partner. The Shanghai government offered impressive incentives for Tesla’s Gigafactory 3 in Shanghai, including land and subsidized loans. But the Chinese government, which was wary of having an American company mapping roads and collecting data on Chinese nationals in cars, insisted that Tesla store all the personal data of Chinese drivers in China. In 2024, it also required that Tesla use a Chinese company—the Internet giant Baidu—for navigation services inside China and that it localize all mapping data in the country. Tesla’s production in China soared; even during the COVID-19 pandemic, the Shanghai factory was producing 140,000 cars a year, and localization of supply chains (85 percent by 2020) brought costs down. Tesla became profitable in 2020 for the first time on the strength of the Chinese market, and Shanghai had become an export hub for the rest of Asia and Europe by 2022. Baidu, meanwhile, used its time working with Tesla to develop frontier autonomous driving technologies and has now deployed “robotaxis” in Switzerland, the United Arab Emirates, and beyond. Perhaps most important, the success of Tesla in the Chinese market helped propel the EV industry there and served as inspiration for homegrown challengers such as BYD, pushing them to focus especially on design and consumer experience. BYD now sells more EVs globally than Tesla does, and Tesla is pushing a cheaper version of the Model Y to compete with companies like BYD and Xiaomi. For the United States, this is the great irony: the investment and manufacturing expertise it needs to compete with China can increasingly come only from China. For years, analysts have instead proposed working with allies and third countries to construct a scaled market outside China—one with common rules that can serve as a counterweight to China’s sheer size and operate parallel to it. This idea is at least a decade old and has taken many forms, from the Obama-era Trans-Pacific Partnership trade agreement, to the first Trump administration’s campaign to rally allies to exclude Chinese telecom companies, to the Biden era’s Indo-Pacific Economic Framework and Transatlantic Trade and Technology Council. All three administrations sought to build coalitions of countries with common rules or standards to collectively rival China’s scale. Despite their theoretical merits, however, all these efforts have either failed or scored only narrow gains. And now it is too late for such a vision: Chinese technologies have reached a tipping point of sorts, becoming ubiquitous in too many countries. The moment for massive, allied coordination to decouple drastically from China has passed. Selective collaboration on particular technology safeguards or supply chain diversification may be feasible, but most of the world has accepted a future with substantial Chinese economic presence in their countries. Even the United States’ closest traditional allies, Canada and the United Kingdom, seem to recognize this new reality and are approaching China with pragmatism. They are wary of China but consider enduring interdependence a fact of life, especially when the United States keeps changing its own approaches trade. Ottawa and London are embracing Chinese investment and exports, but with creative rules to better balance the costs and benefits. Canada, for example, has now abandoned huge tariffs on Chinese EVs in favor of import quotas with an eye to localizing production through carefully structured joint ventures with Canadian companies. Chinese firms are already localizing production in the EU, and a recent EU proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, would require limits on foreign ownership alongside supply chain localization and technology transfer requirements. These rules allow Chinese companies access to Canadian and EU markets but ensure that local production systems benefit. A similar strategy is possible in the United States. TIKTOK SUCCESS The United States does not need to choose between naive openness and blanket exclusion. Indeed, the Trump administration has on at least one occasion chosen a smarter path. ByteDance’s TikTok operation in the United States, which collects vast amounts of data on American users and uses an algorithm to push content, raised some legitimate national security concerns. Although the Trump administration’s process for handling these concerns was tumultuous, in the end, ByteDance agreed to sell its U.S. business to an American-controlled joint venture in which the Chinese company retained a minority share. Control over the TikTok software and its upgrades went to a U.S. team. All personal data must now be stored in the United States. These arrangements are subject to monitoring and reporting and prove that selective openness for Chinese direct investments is possible. Arrangements for securing robotic automation or safeguarding biomedical data would, of course, be more complex. And some Chinese investments should be refused. But the United States possesses the institutional capacity to craft serious protections. It can welcome investment in areas in which it strengthens American industry, while also imposing enforceable safeguards. The best outcome would be selective openness alongside a sustainable industrial policy strategy and, eventually, coordination with other large markets on governing risks transparently. The harder task is political: acknowledging that the United States is already behind in several vital industries and that the barriers Washington has built are costing the United States more than they are protecting it. item.title: Africa Can’t Afford to Squander Its Demographic Opportunity
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.75
For decades, observers have chalked up Africa’s slow economic growth to corruption, weak institutions, and poor leadership. But these explanations miss a deeper force at work. The single most powerful variable shaping the speed of economic growth, stability, and the chance of democracy taking root across African countries is the age structure of their populations. A country tends to be most productive when its fertility rate declines enough that working-age adults outnumber children and elderly people in need of care. When young adults make up a large share of the population—and they are educated, in good health, and able to find work—an economy can really take off. Societies whose populations are older also tend to be more democratic and less violent than those with younger ones. Africa’s fertility rate is still roughly double that of Latin America and South Asia, and the median age in sub-Saharan Africa today is 19.5 years, compared with 29.0 in South Asia, 34.0 in South America, and 43.0 in Europe. But in a few decades, the prime demographic window is expected to open in many African countries: as millions of African citizens mature into working age, the continent’s economic growth could accelerate sharply. Yet the same conditions that can unlock prosperity and democracy can also cause a country to combust if it is governed poorly. If there are not enough jobs to go around, young adults may rise up or be seduced by the promises of strongmen rulers. African countries must thus start preparing today for their moment of opportunity. ACT YOUR AGE In Africa, prospects for prosperity are still largely determined by demography. Currently, the continent is home to 22 low-income and 23 lower-middle-income countries. Because poor countries have limited domestic capital and attract little foreign investment, labor is the primary engine of economic growth. According to analysis using the Pardee Center’s International Futures forecasting platform, growth tends to accelerate when there are at least 1.7 working-age people for each child or elderly person. But today, the continental average is just 1.4 working-age people per dependent. As countries move into middle-income status, the availability of capital becomes more important than labor for driving manufacturing- and services-led growth. And as countries become even richer, technology and higher-value services, such as finance, steadily become the dominant factor driving economic expansion, overtaking both labor and capital. China, and what are known as the Asian “tiger economies”—Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea, and Taiwan—all followed a similar pattern: a large working-age population first drove rapid growth, then capital accumulation and technology transfers added fuel to the fire. Most African countries have not yet benefited from the demographic structure that launched these Asian countries. Africa’s transition was delayed by a uniquely heavy historical burden. The continent’s transition was first slowed relative to other regions because of the removal of working-age people through the slave trade; then, colonial rule left populations poorly educated and disconnected from the infrastructure and institutions needed to participate in the post–World War II surge in trade, industrialization, and technology diffusion. For centuries, Africa’s exceptionally high prevalence of deadly diseases, including malaria and sleeping sickness, also kept mortality higher and population growth slower than in temperate climates, even when women bore seven or more children over a lifetime. From the 1950s to around 1981, the ratio of working-age people to dependents in Africa was either stuck at low levels or declining, even as these ratios were already trending upward across much of Asia and Latin America. Over the past 45 years, the ratio has slowly started to increase, but it remains below 1.4 across much of the continent. The economic growth Africa achieved from the first years of the 2000s through the mid-2010s was driven to an unusual degree by the high price of oil, copper, and iron ore, itself stemming from China’s industrial expansion and rapid urbanization, not from a favorable age structure. But Africa’s young population is maturing. The number of African states with a median age above 30 is projected to roughly triple between 2025 and 2050. Fertility has been declining across most of the continent, while improvements in child survival and women’s education reinforce that trend. Forecasts using the International Futures platform indicate that Africa as a whole will reach the 1.7-to-one working-age threshold around 2053, with northern and southern Africa and several island states arriving much earlier. Our modeling also suggests that, with the right policies, governments could speed up the opening of the prime demographic window by a decade. The uneven transition means that opportunity will arise country by country, not all at once. If leaders prepare for it, even more African countries will count themselves among the fastest-growing economies in the world. THE YOUNG AND THE RESTLESS The same demographic structure that can unleash economic growth, however, can also be a source of political instability if mismanaged. Youthful societies place immense strain on schools, health clinics, and labor markets, which in turn erodes public trust in governments that cannot keep pace with demand for services. And when young adults—who are generally better educated, more willing to take risks, and more likely to mobilize politically than their older counterparts—make up a large share of the population, and when the economy offers them few ways to advance, the risk of unrest rises sharply. Such a dynamic was at play during the Arab Spring uprisings that began in 2010, and it recurs across today’s most volatile African states: the Central African Republic, Chad, Mali, Niger, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, and Uganda. According to research by scholars such as Jack Goldstone and Richard Cincotta, the predictive power of median age is remarkably consistent. The risk of internal conflict and revolutionary upheaval remains elevated for as long as a country’s median age stays below roughly 25.5 years. Crossing that threshold is one of the best predictors of declining conflict risk. Political turbulence falls further, and substantially, once median age passes 30.0—even before a society reaches full demographic maturity at 35.5. As of 2025, only a handful of African states had a median age above 30.0. To be sure, whether youthful grievances escalate into turmoil also depends on the government’s capacity to contain dissent. States with abundant resources and weak institutions, such as Algeria, can pour money into policing and surveillance to suppress unrest in the short term. But without accountable institutions, investments in security lead to corruption and elite capture rather than long-term stability. Consider, for example, Angola, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, South Sudan, and Sudan, where wealth from natural resources temporarily shores up regimes without political legitimacy. The risks from resource dependence and a young population compound each other: both independently raise the likelihood of civil conflict, and where they coincide, the risk is greater still. Recent African history bears this out. Data from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project, a political violence research nonprofit headquartered in Wisconsin, show a marked rise in riots and nonviolent protests alike across the continent since the 2010 Arab Spring. These incidents generally take place in urban areas and are driven by a combustible mix of rising education levels, limited job opportunities, rapid urbanization, and the spread of social media. Kenya’s tax-related protests since 2023, Mozambique’s post-election unrest in 2024–25, and youth-led demonstrations over public services and spending priorities in Moroccan cities in 2025 all fit this template: better-educated, connected young populations mobilizing against elites who control resources and offices they cannot access through ordinary political channels. AN OLD MAN’S GAME Societies whose populations are young are not just more prone to unrest but are also poor candidates for stable democracy. Research by Goldstone, Cincotta, and other scholars such as Jennifer Sciubba has shown that societies with very low median ages and high fertility, such as Egypt, are generally governed by authoritarian regimes. That is in part because rapid population growth typically outpaces the maturation of the civic institutions that democracies depend on to function, including independent media, legal advocacy organizations, and labor unions. In young societies, these bodies rarely have time to develop the depth and independence needed to check executive power. In the absence of inclusive growth and widespread civic engagement, frustrated young people will sometimes support strongman rulers who promise order and jobs, as they have in Ethiopia and Rwanda. Societies whose populations are older tend toward stable democracy. Mauritius, with a median age of 35.5, is the only African country whose demographics are auspicious in this regard. Research has shown that liberal democracies throughout the twentieth century have tended to consolidate once median age rises into the mid-30s, typically alongside the emergence of a larger middle class and a more diversified economy. (There are, of course, exceptions. Belarus, China, Cuba, Russia, and several Gulf states remain politically stable and autocratic, despite having older populations.) Intermediate societies, with median ages around 30, often produce mixed regimes—neither fully autocratic nor fully democratic—in which elections coexist with executive dominance, weak checks and balances, or contested rules of political competition. Algeria and Morocco fit this profile. This is not to say that ordinary people in societies whose populations are young should accept the rule of despots or that autocracy is likely to give rise to an effective development strategy. For every example of economic progress under an autocracy, there is one of decline. But once a baseline of order and development is achieved from the working-age population expanding faster than the number of dependents, incremental democratic reform becomes far more sustainable. In other words, Africa’s demographic transition could also come with stability and a democratic transition. A TALE OF TWO COUNTRIES A comparison between Ghana and South Korea illustrates how a government can both influence and take advantage of age structure. In the late 1950s, both countries were newly independent, had a similar median age—about 18 years—and similar levels of income. South Korea moved earlier on agricultural reform, mass basic education, family planning, and public health, driving fertility below the replacement level by 1984. By 1999, there were 2.6 working-age people for each dependent—among the highest such ratios ever recorded, matched only by China and the Asian tiger economies. Crucially, South Korea also quickly urbanized. By 1982, 60 percent of South Koreans lived in cities, so that people and firms were concentrated in ways that raised productivity and deepened labor markets. Ghana’s demographic transition unfolded on a different timeline. Fertility remained near seven births per woman through the 1960s and has fallen to about 3.4 today. Ghana is not expected to enter its own prime demographic window of opportunity until around 2033—half a century behind South Korea, although still earlier than most of its West African neighbors. Urbanization, too, arrived later: Ghana only recently became 60 percent urban. Ghana’s high proportion of dependents kept household savings low, limited the tax base, and prevented the labor market from expanding in ways that would otherwise have supported faster industrial growth. South Korea was well placed to influence its age structure because it received large amounts of foreign aid and was governed by an elite focused on industrialization and rapid growth. Between 1960 and 1980, the United States and other countries, such as Japan, sent South Korea $39 billion in aid (in constant 2021 values). Ghana, over the same period, received $6 billion. Both countries were ruled by corrupt militaries for a time, but South Korean leaders tended to invest their ill-gotten gains domestically while Ghanaians invested theirs in London and Paris. (Today, much of that money is parked in Abu Dhabi.) South Korea embarked on a vital agricultural transformation that increased productivity. Today, 94 percent of land in South Korea is privately owned and is therefore governed by secure, enforceable rights that incentivize investment and allow for land reallocation. Meanwhile, 80 percent of land in Ghana is held communally, and many farmers work merely to subsist. Societies whose populations are older tend toward stable democracy. But soon, the same forces that lifted South Korea into the ranks of advanced economies will be felt across much of Africa, albeit unevenly. It is up to African governments to make sure the prime demographic window of opportunity opens and to make the most of it when it does. Their starting point should be reducing infant and maternal mortality by expanding access to health care for children and pregnant women. When more children survive to adulthood, families do not feel the need to have many children as insurance against loss, and fertility begins to fall. In addition, voluntary access to modern contraception and sex education gives women and their families the option to have fewer children. Educating girls is the single most powerful way to reduce fertility rates, but the effects of doing so take more time to realize. The longer girls remain in school, the later they tend to marry and begin childbearing, which both lowers fertility directly and raises women’s future productivity and earning potential—reinforcing the link between demographic change and economic growth. Investments in water, sanitation, and basic health infrastructure are also helpful because they help prevent diseases that drive high mortality and, in turn, high fertility. Influencing fertility rates is not just a matter of service delivery; shifts in gender norms, attitudes toward child marriage, and reproductive autonomy also matter. Although these shifts tend to unfold gradually, politicians, media campaigns, and civil society engagement can nudge people toward wanting smaller families. Ultimately, a demographic dividend translates into growth only if the resulting cohort of working-age adults can find productive work. African governments must prepare by linking vocational and technical training to actual labor demand—for example, by offering employer-designed apprenticeships in construction, agricultural processing, logistics, renewable energy, and digital services. Governments can also widen opportunity by making it easier to start small businesses, expanding credit guarantees and digital finance, and improving transportation links and energy provision. Removing legal barriers and collateral requirements that disproportionately prevent women from obtaining credit and holding assets, while enforcing equal access to jobs and promotion, would also help. Civic institutions need time to mature alongside the population. Governments can improve the odds of a democratic transition by protecting independent media and courts, strengthening election management and legislative oversight, enforcing term limits, and creating opportunities for young people to participate in political parties and local government. Involving the youth in civil society can also improve intergenerational understanding between aging elites and the people they govern. THE AGE OF AGE Africa’s demographic profile is set to look markedly different by midcentury. Its labor force will continue to expand as those in China, Europe, and other aging economies contract. If African countries can make even modest productivity gains, their growth rates should outpace the economies of the now graying societies that drove global growth for the past half century. Yet Africa can’t become the world’s bright spot unless the region’s governments take action today. The stakes are considerable. Modeling from the African Futures program suggests that if African countries add roughly two percentage points to average annual economic growth—through faster fertility decline, better-managed urbanization, stronger ability to generate jobs for a growing workforce, more integrated trade, and higher agricultural productivity—the continent’s economy in 2050 would be 50 percent larger than under a business-as-usual scenario. Its population would be about 166 million smaller as prosperity further reduces fertility, and income per capita would rise from roughly 28 percent of the global average to 36 percent. If governments squander the opportunity through weak governance, underinvestment in health and education, or the inability to absorb a growing workforce, the same demographic momentum that could deliver growth will instead become a source of instability—just as the rest of the world ages and shrinks. item.title: Why We Are Living Through ‘Hyperpolitics’
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.27
Why We Are Living Through ‘Hyperpolitics’ Anton Jager explains why record voter turnout isn’t leading to systemic change. There’s a strange paradox in the world today. Citizens in countries around the world seem angrier and are voting more—but they seem unable to effect structural changes. The political scientist Anton Jager calls this “hyperpolitics,” in which political activity increases but membership of unions and political parties is declining. Jager’s new book, Hyperpolitics: Extreme Politicization Without Political Consequences, has become something of a cult favorite among Europe’s political and intellectual elites. But is hyperpolitics necessarily bad? Does it apply only to certain Western countries—Jager’s focus—or can it capture a broader global trend? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Jager about his thesis, whether movements such as the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) could capture the broader Democratic Party, and also how societies should try to deepen political engagement. The full video of our discussion can be accessed in the video box atop this page. There is also a free podcast version available on Apple, Spotify, YouTube, and other major platforms. What follows here is an edited and condensed transcript of our discussion. There’s a strange paradox in the world today. Citizens in countries around the world seem angrier and are voting more—but they seem unable to effect structural changes. The political scientist Anton Jager calls this “hyperpolitics,” in which political activity increases but membership of unions and political parties is declining. Jager’s new book, Hyperpolitics: Extreme Politicization Without Political Consequences, has become something of a cult favorite among Europe’s political and intellectual elites. But is hyperpolitics necessarily bad? Does it apply only to certain Western countries—Jager’s focus—or can it capture a broader global trend? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Jager about his thesis, whether movements such as the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) could capture the broader Democratic Party, and also how societies should try to deepen political engagement. The full video of our discussion can be accessed in the video box atop this page. There is also a free podcast version available on Apple, Spotify, YouTube, and other major platforms. What follows here is an edited and condensed transcript of our discussion. Ravi Agrawal: So I want to start with a basic definition. What is hyperpolitics? Anton Jager: The short answer is a three-word definition: Hyperpolitics is “re-politicization without re-institutionalization.” That is slightly academic and abstruse, so if you want to make it more concrete, hyperpolitics denotes a change in political culture in the West in which we see an increase in political activity on all kinds of fronts, whether it’s voter turnout, protest activity, or even political violence. That increase in activity, however, has not gone hand in hand with an increase in institutional membership. As you see the politicization curve going up, you see another curve declining: membership rates for political parties, unions, and civil society organizations, both on the left and the right. This new K-shaped or X-shaped development—high politicization but low institutionalization—is a combination that doesn’t really have precedence in the 20th century. The term hyperpolitics tries to describe this new state of affairs, and it does so in contrast with two preceding other modes of political engagement: the mass politics of the 20th century, which could be very high on politicization but usually was also very institutionalized, and then the “post-politics” of the 1990s and the 2000s in the aftermath of the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, which was both low on political involvement and on institutional density and strength. Hyperpolitics is a product specifically of the 2010s and the long decade that came after the 2008 credit crash, and it really tries to explain this new situation through a hypothetical tentative term. RA: Just to use a concrete example here, in the United States, voter turnout has been higher than ever before in the last two presidential elections. And yet union membership is much lower than it had been for most of the 20th century. And I think that kind of encapsulates the point you’re making of more politics but less investment, as it were, in terms of institutions. What is your sense of how we got here, and is it necessarily a bad thing? Because at some level, you could say that individuals feel empowered in the ability to be able to turn out to vote more, but without feeling that they have to be part of a doctrine of either the left or the right, or part of a party or a union. AJ: As to whether hyper-politicization is a good or a bad thing, I hope the book doesn’t come across as rendering a negative judgment on the hyperpolitical era, despite its limitations and some of its contradictions, because I do think the fact that people are again politically involved, and that there’s an increase in turnout, is something that every democrat should be enthusiastic about. For example, in Germany, we now see a doubling of turnout in the upcoming election in Saxony. In 2006, it was 44 percent; now, it’s going over 80 percent. That is not a crisis of democracy—you can talk about the economic crisis in Germany, but to talk of a crisis of democracy is empirically unsustainable. The question is, why does so much of this contemporary political activity not translate easily into concrete policy results, or why does it not so easily affect the existing power balance in society? Even as there has been an increase in turnout for U.S. elections, particularly presidential elections, it’s not very clear, for example, in U.S. inequality figures or on some of the large issues—whether it’s healthcare or certain issues of government provision—that the United States has actually made it easier for citizens to translate their preferences into policy results. There’s one spectacular example of this: There is now a long-standing majority in polling for public healthcare in the United States, but there’s actually a negative correlation between those preferences and the chances of it getting implemented. That encapsulates the hyperpolitical paradox. RA: For people who haven’t yet read the book, let’s take a couple of examples of movements that took off in various parts of the world but weren’t able to sustain themselves. Do you want to name a few? I know, for example, Black Lives Matter (BLM) gets talked about a fair bit. What kinds of examples do you think best encapsulate your thesis? AJ: There are a number of examples. Some of them are more chemically pure as hyperpolitical instances than the others. The BLM protests in the summer of 2020 are quite a striking example, because there are some numbers that indicate that one out of 10 American adults might have participated in them. They were the largest protests in U.S. history in purely numerical terms. You could also talk of the “yellow vest” protests from 2018 to 2020 in France, in which a group of French citizens angry at recent tax hikes—which they saw as unequally applied to parts of the working and middle class—took to the streets without an official leadership organization, but were simply recognizable through the yellow vest that every car driver in France gets with their vehicle. Once again, that was already a bit of an ideologically ambiguous movement, so it was difficult to place on the left-right spectrum. There are also movements on the right that qualify for this criterion. Jan. 6, 2021, for example, the riot that invaded the U.S. Capitol, is a great example of right-wing hyperpolitics, and it shows once again that it’s not exclusive to the left. It was an enormously energetic and aggressive campaign, mainly organized through WhatsApp groups and then mobilized through the Twitter feed of the then-president. But at the same time, a couple of weeks later, it was very clear that none of these people had joined the same organizations, they weren’t affiliated to the same civil society groups, and they dispersed. These are a range of particularly American, but also European, instances of hyperpolitics that show that this is a phenomenon that’s now recurring. And once again, it’s not something that can be easily placed on one side of the political spectrum. It’s in the center, the left, and the right. RA: I’m wondering, given the examples you cited, if you can make the case that the right has been more successful at the act of hyperpolitics, and having its way, than the left. Is there any truth to that thesis? AJ: Absolutely, and the book does investigate this striking asymmetry between the left and the right in the race for hyperpolitics, and why the right seems to have done better in the hyperpolitical era than the left. I would be cautious to say that all of the movements we mentioned have a track record of really striking success. When it comes to defunding the police, or deconstructing the large carceral system—one of the largest in the world—that the United States has, the aftermath of BLM was quite ambiguous in that most of those police departments regained their funding a year later. When it comes to U.S. police violence numbers, it’s not as if there has been a marked improvement in some of those. And, of course, with Jan. 6, [Joe] Biden was sworn in as president, and later [Donald] Trump won again. It’s not entirely clear what the organizational legacy of that movement was. But it is absolutely true that the right does seem to have done better. I think there are two simple explanations for this asymmetry. The first is that the right has access to sources of private funding when it comes to stimulating or supporting some of these hyperpolitical mobilizations, which the left simply does not. RA: Can I challenge you there, because the right would say the left has George Soros. And the left has all these other organizations that are actually quite well-funded. AJ: Absolutely. If you talk about the NGO [nongovernmental organization] complex or large parts of these civil society organizations that are funded by a source foundation, you could say that there is a left that has access to private funding. But I don’t see Jean-Luc Mélenchon or Jeremy Corbyn easily appealing to that kind of funding. There’s now a striking scandal in the United Kingdom with Nigel Farage, who is the leader of Reform UK—one of the new extreme-right parties that is challenging the authority of the Conservatives—who resigned from his parliamentary seat over a large sum of money he purportedly, or would have, received from a crypto-millionaire, and he stood for a new election and then won it again. It is very hard to find an equivalent of that kind of donation from a very wealthy millionaire on the left. There are cases of the left also receiving this kind of private funding; it’s just more easily available on the right. The second point that explains asymmetry is that the left faces a steeper climb than the right in contemporary societies, and many of the issues it seeks to address want to reverse certain power relations that are much more entrenched, and much more difficult to dislodge, than the ones the right attacks. You can see this very clearly in the left-wing Syriza party in Greece. It won elections on an anti-austerity platform in 2015 and then went into a confrontation with European authorities, sought to reverse the European Union’s austerity directives, and then held a referendum which was won on a no—so the Greek people rejected the continuation of austerity and they had to continue it nonetheless. Fratelli d’Italia [Brothers of Italy], the right-wing party in Italy, initially had a highly Euroskeptic position and sought to reform the eurozone, or maybe even have Italy exit the eurozone. Now that they’ve gone into government, they’ve completely shed this ambition. When it comes to their anti-migrant promises, it’s not entirely clear that they have been able to follow up on their most ambitious ideas of, for example, deportation. That indicates that the bar is higher on the left than it is on the right, and it also means that the left is more severely punished for its failure to fulfill its promises than the right is. RA: We’ve mostly been rooting our examples in the West. You’re very upfront in the book about how the West is what you know best, and therefore that’s what you draw on the most. But were I to ask you to stretch a little bit, I’m curious whether you think the idea of hyperpolitics applies to a country like India, for example, or even a country like China. China has the Communist Party (CCP), which has many millions of members. India has the BJP [Bharatiya Janata Party], which is the political wing of a group called the RSS [Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh], which has tens of millions of members and is deeply rooted in society. Do you see them as very different to the parties you’re imagining in the West? And therefore, do you think the two most populous countries in the world experience hyperpolitics as you’re describing it, or are they exceptions? AJ: This is a very important question. I just want to highlight that the reason that my book restricts itself to the West, as you indicated, is a product of ignorance or my limited knowledge of some of these non-Western spheres. It’s not as if I don’t pay attention to them, but I wouldn’t feel comfortable extrapolating or making grand pronouncements about them. RA: And you’re very humble about that. I really appreciate it. I wish more thinkers were that way. AJ: The developments the book describes really begin in 2008 and 2009 with the credit crash, which has its ground zero in the United States and then quickly spirals out into Europe. But 2008 was a global event. The crash had global repercussions. You saw that already with the Arab Spring. The decade of protest didn’t open in the West. It mainly takes part in North Africa. If you look at, for example, Brazil, India, or Indonesia, you can find many examples of these really energetic and very impressive protest movements that also find their place outside of the West. I think the Indian and the Chinese cases are, to put it bluntly, exceptions that prove the rule. The BJP in India is a real mass party, I’d say, in a classical 20th-century sense. As you say, it’s very closely connected to the RSS, and it differs from some of its extreme-right equivalents in Europe in that it has a very solid and large institutional infrastructure and a really deep civil society, which has been built up over several decades and has replaced the Congress party as the dominant party. Congress itself had become such a top-heavy party. The BJP has really replaced it as a cross-class formation. It is the largest party in the world; it has the most members in purely numerical terms. And it indicates that it is an outlier to many of the trends I describe. If you look at some of the protest movements in India in the last 10 to 15 years, you can see some of these hyperpolitical trends show up. Even the recent Cockroach movement, for example, which led to the resignation of an Indian minister, indicates that some of these trends, despite the BJP being a mass party, also affect other parts of Indian society. It is now a dominant way in which modes of opposition or protest movements also take part in a society that still has some of these mass parties. The Chinese case is even more fascinating because the CCP is also an outlier in that it has managed to reinvent itself as some kind of mass party, particularly after COVID. The pandemic really served as an occasion for the CCP to reinsert itself, particularly in the lower levels of society, also through surveillance, of course. But the CCP is also a cross-class party; it really has a cohesive function in the Chinese elite itself. The Chinese business elite and party elite are pushed much closer together. If you’re wealthy in China, it’s very likely that your biography is still very closely tied to the CCP. And that also explains why the kind of hyperpolitics we’ve seen in the West and the type of populism we’ve seen in the last 10 to 15 years hasn’t manifested in China in the same way. One explanation is obviously just repression. The Chinese state is more effective at quelling dissent. I don’t think that explains everything. There are spectacular growth rates that buy you consent. There is repression. But there is also the CCP as this mediator between the lower ranks of Chinese society and the higher parts of the Chinese business class. That probably explains why hyperpolitics, as it exists and manifests in the West, isn’t as visible in China as it used to be, even if there were anti-lockdown protests or protests against zero-COVID in China. When it comes to labor unrest, the official numbers actually don’t show the extent of what’s going on. But I do think it kind of proves the trend. The CCP has managed to reinvent itself as this mediating party and thereby indicates that it is the absence of these kinds of structures in the West that probably explains why hyperpolitics is more prevalent. RA: Fascinating. I have one last question for you. How do you develop an environment of compromise and civility? What systems, apart from just voting, can people and parties build to deliver the political consequences they so clearly want? AJ: Well, if this is a question about political violence specifically, I’ll just indicate that part of the hyperpolitical thesis does apply to the dynamics of political violence: There have been more attempts on Trump’s life than any previous presidential election. We can also see that someone like Luigi Mangione decided to take action into his own hands, instead of collective action or a campaign of Medicare for All. I do think that a decrease in political violence, which some people in the United States now desire, is only going to come if there are actual policy results. As I said, there is a large majority in the United States for something like public healthcare. There is a negative correlation between that public preference and the chances of it getting implemented as a policy. If Washington becomes more responsive to those preferences, I think you’ll probably see a decrease in some of these types of political violence. RA: But that’s very chicken and egg. AJ: Probably, but I do think the reason that American citizens are looking more toward political violence is because it does seem to be the last avenue they have available. They are voting more, they’re protesting more, but it’s not very clear that that is translating into a different gradient of social and political power. And if that gradient is not being affected, they will look to more individualized, desperate solutions. And I think Mangione and even other types of right-wing violence certainly fall into that category. RA: Hyperpolitics obviously is a trend. Do you think it has peaked? Will it peak soon? In other words, I’m just trying to get us toward, if a clear solution isn’t available, is there at least an end to the trend line? AJ: The problem here is that predicting something in social science is very difficult. I’m very uncomfortable with these astrological claims that say “hyperpolitics will be over next year or will only last for five years.” I just want to insist that the structural drivers of hyperpolitics that this book identifies are very deep-seated, quite old, and I don’t see them going away anytime soon. The real question is: Will someone find an institutional formula that moves us beyond hyperpolitics in the next five to 10 years? I don’t think that’s impossible. You can already see attempts on the left and the right—whether it’s DSA or the second Trump term, which is very different from the first Trump term, much more institutionalized, much more organized, such as the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 or the way ICE [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement] has been mobilized. So there are attempts at making that political activity more institutional. Whether that will mean hyperpolitics will be history next year or in five years or in 10 years—I’m not able to say. That is an open question, and people make their own decisions. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. Subscribe Subscribe Already a subscriber? . item.title: A Land Without the Troubles?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.68
A Land Without the Troubles? Northern Ireland’s most outlandish plan comes to fruition in Jan Carson’s new novel. In 1998, the Irish Republican Army (IRA) killed 29 people in the Omagh bombing, only four months after the Good Friday Agreement purported to put an end to the three-decade-long sectarian conflict known as the Troubles. It was the deadliest terrorist attack in Northern Ireland’s history. During the Troubles, Protestant unionists and Catholic nationalists clashed over whether Northern Ireland should remain in the United Kingdom or become part of a united Ireland. The conflict still permeates social and political life in the country, where efforts to confront its legacy are ongoing. In 2024, Northern Ireland established an independent inquiry to determine whether British state authorities could have prevented the carnage of the Omagh bombing. Two years later, the inquiry drags on, impeded by the difficulty of collecting evidence that is over a quarter of a century old, and the pain of dredging up historical grievances. In 1998, the Irish Republican Army (IRA) killed 29 people in the Omagh bombing, only four months after the Good Friday Agreement purported to put an end to the three-decade-long sectarian conflict known as the Troubles. It was the deadliest terrorist attack in Northern Ireland’s history. During the Troubles, Protestant unionists and Catholic nationalists clashed over whether Northern Ireland should remain in the United Kingdom or become part of a united Ireland. The conflict still permeates social and political life in the country, where efforts to confront its legacy are ongoing. In 2024, Northern Ireland established an independent inquiry to determine whether British state authorities could have prevented the carnage of the Omagh bombing. Two years later, the inquiry drags on, impeded by the difficulty of collecting evidence that is over a quarter of a century old, and the pain of dredging up historical grievances. In Northern Irish author Jan Carson’s new novel, Few and Far Between, a young anthropologist named Alex sets out on another mission to examine a messy past when she visits the place where her mixed-religion parents raised her: a fictional island archipelago that once sheltered a utopian community from the Troubles. Through chapters from Alex’s ethnography and the narration of the book’s central characters, Carson explores the dynamics of memory, reconciliation, and accountability that continue to haunt Northern Ireland. As in her previous work, Carson laces the novel with dark humor and magical realism, wielding absurdity to broach the lingering repercussions of the Troubles alongside the existential threats of our time. Balancing cynicism with charming earnestness, the book grapples with the dangers of melancholy and nostalgia in both personal and political life, prompting readers to consider what we lose when we paper over the past—and what further damage is possible when we drag that past back up again. Few and Far Between imagines an alternate history in which an outlandish idea proposed in 1958 by Northern Irish leader Terence O’Neill to drain Lough Neagh, the largest lake in the British isles, came partly to fruition. (In reality, the scheme was quickly deemed unworkable.) “For those readers calling themselves Northern Irish, Neagh’s the hole in the doughnut of your country,” Alex writes. “For those readers who are Irish, living both north and south of the six-county line, Lough Neagh’s the cyclops eye peering out of your country’s head.” O’Neill had a vision of a new town springing up in the center of the former lake where Protestants and Catholics could work alongside one another—a proposal “more laughable than the concept of emptying out an enormous lake,” Alex writes. The scheme was only half-delivered, resulting in a receded waterline and the emergence of an archipelago known as the “Ark.” When the Troubles began in the late 1960s, the Ark offered “asylum,” quickly becoming populated by people in mixed Catholic/Protestant marriages or who otherwise faced discrimination on the mainland. A small utopian community sprang up, “[f]ueled by some kind of heady optimism,” and it actively integrated “without a thought for the traditional sectarian divide currently devastating the North.” Fascinated by the Ark as “both a victim of the ongoing conflict and an act of embodied protest,” famed anthropologist RJ Connolly brought his wife and three children to set up their home on one of the islands, where he began to study the community. The novel bounces between timelines: the 1970s, when RJ’s children—Marion, Robert-John, and Rosemary—are kids; and 2017, when Alex visits the islands to find Marion and Robert-John still living there as the Ark’s caretakers, even though both of their parents are dead, and the vast majority of the Ark’s inhabitants left after the Good Friday Agreement. Yet despite the peace process, Carson makes it clear that the North “remains traumatized.” No formal truth and reconciliation process followed the Troubles, and without a real outlet to address trauma, the state left society-wide wounds to fester with an almost willful blindness. Although Marion concedes that children, or “weans,” as she calls them, “deserve a future unsullied by the past,” liberation from that past is almost impossible to come by for those who lived through it. This culture of silence has shaped Northern Ireland’s political and social landscape, functioning as a deliberate strategy to facilitate the transition of suspected former IRA members from paramilitaries to legitimate political actors, and enable negotiations with the British government. It also had deadly consequences. IRA members often justified their violence by rationalizing it as a way to reach their end goal of a united Ireland. When IRA leadership abandoned that goal in exchange for peace, many of its members felt left behind. That resentment contributed to the continuation of extremist violence during peacetime, as exhibited by the Omagh bombing. In Carson’s timeline, just as in ours, jurisdictional and cultural frictions were resurfaced by the 2016 Brexit referendum, making peace “wobblier with each passing year.” Brexit threatened, among other things, the stability of the Irish border, where no physical checkpoints have existed since the Good Friday Agreement, and European Union market rules allowed the free flow of goods. Over 10 years after the referendum (in which a majority of Northern Irish voted to stay in the EU), British leaders still have not fully solved the messy task of regulating trade on the border without imposing security checks reminiscent of the Troubles. Carson symbolizes these tensions through the functions and magical properties of the Ark’s islands, which, over time, became “a repository for all the shite that was meant to get sorted but never did.” After the exodus of the Ark’s residents, the island called Eglish Flat becomes a dumping ground for illegal or unwanted items, including the weapons of ex-paramilitaries. The Good Friday Agreement required all paramilitary groups in Northern Ireland to fully disarm within two years; as a result, “you could’ve paved the road to Dublin with all the firearms that found their way to Eglish Flat.” But while “[a] buried gun’s not killing anybody,” as one ex-combatant claims in an interview cited by Alex, the state’s failure to address deeper, more systemic issues manifested in other ways. As of 2017, nearly 4,000 people had died by suicide in Northern Ireland since the Good Friday Agreement—more than were killed during the entire duration of the Troubles. Tom’s Hard, another island in the Ark, is a popular destination for those attempting suicide. Church Flat, meanwhile, is occupied by “Almost-Deads,” spirits of people in limbo between life and death. The Almost-Deads appeared on Church Flat in great numbers toward the end of the Troubles, an “apt metaphor for the liminal state in which the North currently finds itself,” Alex writes; an “island caught in a temporary stasis between the present and what is yet to come.” Finally, Middle Flat houses “traumatized comatose individuals” known as “Sleepers.” They are almost exclusively women, a fact that one fictional official finds unsurprising given that “women bore the brunt of the Troubles,” caring for and protecting their communities during the worst of the conflict. Nearly two decades after the first Sleeper arrived, the rehabilitation rate remains close to zero. Fewer people seemed to be afflicted by the phenomenon for a time, until “Brexit reared its ugly head, dredging up old hurts and fears.” The novel’s post-referendum plot is driven by an existential threat to the islands. A result of global warming, toxic algae “troubles the water,” blooming up throughout the lake and slowly destroying the Ark’s landscape. The government proposes a plan to flood the Ark. It’s a standard policy: Cover everything up and hope it goes away. But a flood would only postpone the environmental impacts of the algae bloom. It would also displace Marion and Robert-John and force them to relocate to the mainland. When Alex arrives, Marion and Robert-John see her as a potential savior. Hoping her future book will convince the devolved government in Stormont not to proceed with its plan to flood the islands, they attempt to paint the Ark in a positive light for Alex, concealing its uglier aspects and their own painful pasts—which include abuse from their otherwise-revered anthropologist father—to the best of their abilities. But in Few and Far Between, what goes down must come up. The islands seem to know what’s in store. They fight their destruction. The Sleepers get restless. Buried things start to reappear. When Marion discovers one particularly shocking truth, her version of reality is rent apart. But though this nearly destroys her at first, it eventually drags her out of a dangerous melancholy. Revelation can be painful, Carson suggests. It can also be liberatory. Although political violence between Catholics and Protestants is rare in Northern Ireland today, the country’s lingering divisions aren’t far from view. Belfast, for example, is still full of towering “peace walls” separating the two communities, street art staking claims to identity, and Palestinian and Israeli flags projecting local tensions onto global conflicts. “When they scratch the surface—which they frequently do, mostly with words but sometimes with fists—there is still a deep divide running through the heart of the place,” Marion notes of those living in Northern Ireland. That divide has also manifested in rising anti-immigrant sentiment today, especially among Protestant loyalists. Few and Far Between pushes readers to face these tensions head-on, and to consider how grievances might be addressed. Is it better to reopen old wounds, or let bygones be bygones? Though that question does not project neatly onto Northern Ireland’s fractured present, it’s clear that attempts to simply cover things up never turn out the way we’d like to imagine. In the novel’s epilogue, set in 2018, onlookers and news crews observe as lost items and souls bubble up from the depths of the lake, including ghosts of those who died by suicide on Tom’s Flat. “Sad-faced, cloudy-looking creatures … hung like mist on the water’s surface, eyeing the heavens jealously. They clapped their cold eyes on the camera and did not flinch or look away, as if to say, Do not ignore us. Don’t pretend we’re not here.” Maxine Davey is an editorial fellow at Foreign Policy. item.title: The Clock Is Ticking Down on Another U.S.-Canada Trade War
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.27
The Clock Is Ticking Down on Another U.S.-Canada Trade War Senior Canadian officials are looking to make a deal to avoid new 50 percent U.S. tariffs. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at last-minute U.S.-Canada trade talks, Ukraine’s depleted arsenal, and Taiwan’s record-breaking defense spending proposal. Time Is Running Out Less than 30 hours remain for Canada and the United States to negotiate trade terms to avoid another round of sweeping U.S. duties. With senior officials from both sides convening in Washington on Thursday to discuss a potential deal, experts are waiting to see if Ottawa will cave to the White House’s demands or choose to bear the brunt of another tariff war. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at last-minute U.S.-Canada trade talks, Ukraine’s depleted arsenal, and Taiwan’s record-breaking defense spending proposal. Time Is Running Out Less than 30 hours remain for Canada and the United States to negotiate trade terms to avoid another round of sweeping U.S. duties. With senior officials from both sides convening in Washington on Thursday to discuss a potential deal, experts are waiting to see if Ottawa will cave to the White House’s demands or choose to bear the brunt of another tariff war. On Wednesday, the United States was scheduled to impose 50 percent levies on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, from dairy products to electronics to hockey sticks. However, less than two hours before they were set to go into effect, U.S. President Donald Trump abruptly postponed the tariffs for a 72-hour period, citing progress in ongoing trade talks. A third of that window has come and gone, though, and few details have emerged about what terms are on the table. According to a White House proclamation posted on Tuesday, Canada has expressed willingness to remove certain tariffs on U.S. goods—such as alcohol, dairy, and automobiles—that Trump has previously called discriminatory. The U.S. president also hinted on Tuesday that any deal could include resurrecting talks over the Keystone XL oil pipeline, which the Biden administration scrapped in 2021 to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and prioritize green energy. Ottawa has yet to confirm these commitments. But Canada isn’t the only one looking poised to make concessions. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Washington appears likely to lower U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum from 50 percent to 25 percent and on Canadian automobiles from 25 percent to 15 percent. Efforts to reduce U.S. duties on lumber and impose a potential credit system for Canadian auto parts are also reportedly under consideration. “Canada entered these discussions with the best overall trade terms,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X on Wednesday. “We are now moving towards an agreement that reinforces that Canadian advantage, including by securing the best terms in each of Canada’s most important strategic sectors and providing greater certainty about our future trading relationship.” On Wednesday, a White House official stressed that a deal is still “being finalized” and that any reported details “should be regarded as speculation” until there is an official announcement. However, that same day, Trump told reporters that “we may bring some of the tariffs down to the level where other countries are” because “Canada was paying a higher tariff.” Thursday’s talks included U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer; Dominic LeBlanc, Canada’s trade minister focused on U.S. relations; and chief Canadian negotiator Janice Charette. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio separately met with Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand at the White House. Today’s Most Read - The Top 10 Ways Trump Has Made America Weaker by Stephen M. Walt - Colby’s ‘Flexible Realism’ Won’t Work in the Indo-Pacific by Derek Grossman - Vance Pitches a New Objective for the Iran War by Keith Johnson What We’re Following Deadly airstrikes. Russian forces launched a massive missile and drone strike on Kyiv on Thursday, killing at least 15 people and wounding dozens more. “This Russian strike was one of the most cynical, calculated, and large-scale” since the war began, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on X. Local officials reported ballistic and hypersonic missiles as well as more than 160 drones, damaging around 30 residential buildings as well as a children’s hospital, a school, and a kindergarten. The assault cast light on Ukraine’s depleted missile defense arsenal and Kyiv’s repeated efforts to acquire more weapons from foreign allies. “The greatest threat is ballistic missiles,” Zelensky wrote. “And this is something that depends entirely on the supply of Patriot missiles to Ukraine and therefore depends on our country’s partners.” The U.S.-made Patriots are the only systems that Ukraine has with the ability to effectively intercept ballistic missiles. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stressed on Thursday that the European Union is working to support Ukraine’s anti-ballistic capabilities. Yet the bloc is finding its attention divided, as overnight Russian attacks also bled into Romanian and Moldovan territory. In response, von der Leyen pledged on Thursday to scale up military defense production for member states to counter what she called Moscow’s “hybrid war.” Prioritizing defense. Taiwan proposed increasing its annual defense spending on Thursday by 18 percent, bringing its total defense budget for 2027 to a whopping $35 billion. This would mark the first time that Taiwan’s proposal exceeds the symbolic 1 trillion Taiwanese dollar threshold. It signals Taipei’s growing determination to prepare for a potential Chinese invasion without having to rely on foreign allies, specifically the United States, which has repeatedly called on Taiwan to spend more on its own defense. The proposed budget, which would increase defense spending to nearly 4 percent of Taiwan’s 2025 GDP, would focus on modernizing the coast guard, providing pensions, and buying more arms from Washington. In December, the Trump administration unveiled its largest-ever weapons package for Taiwan, totaling $11.1 billion. Then, earlier this year, the White House floated another arms deal—this one worth $14 billion—to Taiwan, but Trump ultimately held up its approval to use it as a “very good negotiating chip” with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Thursday’s proposal must now be confirmed by Taiwanese lawmakers before it can take effect. This will likely prove challenging for Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, whose government holds a minority in parliament. Only on Friday did Taiwan’s legislature finally approve a budget for 2026 after a record delay. Evergrande’s downfall. A Chinese court sentenced Evergrande founder Hui Ka Yan to life in prison on Thursday after he pleaded guilty in April to charges related to large-scale financial fraud—including embezzlement, bribery, and inflated disclosures—between 2016 and 2021. Hui was also ordered to forfeit all of his personal assets, and his companies were fined a total of $2.35 billion. Evergrande was once China’s fastest-growing property developer. However, its prospects soured in 2021, when the company collapsed under more than $300 billion worth of debt (or roughly 2 percent of China’s GDP at the time). The default triggered one of China’s biggest property crises in history and led to lasting economic effects that are still felt today. “The amount involved in the crime is exceptionally large, the circumstances are particularly heinous, exceptionally heavy economic losses have been caused, and the harm to society is extremely grave,” Chinese state media outlet Xinhua wrote on Thursday. Although the ruling marks a dramatic end for Asia’s once second-richest man, it does not end the legal battles surrounding Evergrande, which now faces liquidation. Odds and Ends Six years after Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, left London for the sunny beaches of California, the estranged royals are heading back to the United Kingdom. The Associated Press reported on Wednesday that the couple plans to move into a private home outside of London by the end of this month and will send their children to British schools come September. Their return is expected to bring old hurts back into the limelight, as the two stepped down from official royal duties in March 2020, citing “toxic” press scrutiny, insensitivity toward Meghan’s mental health, and at least one instance of alleged racism. However, in recent months, Harry has expressed interest in reconciling with his family to spend more time with his father, King Charles III, who is battling an undisclosed type of cancer. item.title: What in the World?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.72
What in the World? Test yourself on the week of Aug. 15: Trump praises Kim Jong Un, the U.S. and Iran miss a deadline, and the U.K. shrugs off Russian threats. Fresh off summer vacation? Find out if you kept up with this week’s headlines with our international news quiz! Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts. Fresh off summer vacation? Find out if you kept up with this week’s headlines with our international news quiz! 1. U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday expressed displeasure at U.S.-South Korea military drills set to begin this week. In a social media post, how did Trump describe North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un? 2. The United States and Iran missed their 60-day deadline on Monday to reach a deal to do what? As the war drags on, the White House is continuing to adjust its war aims. The administration’s latest proposal, from Vice President J.D. Vance, is simply to lower oil and gas prices for U.S. consumers, FP’s Keith Johnson writes. 3. The United Kingdom vowed on Tuesday to continue aiding Ukraine in its war against Russia, one day after the Russian Embassy in London threatened the country for supplying Kyiv with what? 4. Where did Pakistan’s Supreme Court order imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan be sent in a decision issued on Tuesday? 5. Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday said Latin American countries should demonstrate “autonomy” during a meeting with which Latin American leader? 6. Following President Hakainde Hichilema’s election victory in Zambia last week, the United Nations human rights chief said on Wednesday that he was concerned about what happening in the country? The outcome will allow Hichilema, who has faced backlash for tightening press freedoms, to continue his plan for electricity expansion and critical minerals mining, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief. 7. News reports on Wednesday indicated that the Trump administration plans to send $206 million to Gaza for what purpose? 8. A Chinese court sentenced Evergrande founder Hui Ka Yan to life in prison on Thursday after he pleaded guilty in April to charges related to what? 9. Lithuania hosted its fifth annual corgi race on Saturday, which for the first time included a canine from which country? 10. Which global music superstar pledged on Monday to help rebuild 10 schools and a damaged university in Colombia, following a devastating earthquake in that country last week? Alongside the Howard G. Buffett foundation, Shakira’s Fundación Pies Descalzos will work to rebuild the schools, while the singer said she would focus her “personal efforts” on reconstructing the damaged university, The Associated Press reports. You scored It’s a big world out there! Brush up on global goings-on by subscribing to World Brief, Foreign Policy’s flagship daily newsletter. Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts. Drew Gorman is a deputy copy editor at Foreign Policy. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Tops’ New Silent Hero 4 Tanto Quietly Hits the Tactical EDC Knife Apex
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.57
For all the belly-aching about the sequelization of Hollywood, it’s worth noting that the product world got there much faster. Yet while movies generally get worse as the numbers go up (here’s looking at you, Zoolander 2), products often actually improve with updates. The knife and EDC world is no stranger to this phenomenon, as we can see right now with the Tops Silent Hero “franchise.” That latest generation, the Silent Hero 4 Tanto, is arguably the most stunning yet, even if its intended purpose isn’t for everyone. A history of Silents For the record, the original Silent Hero was a much different animal. Designed by Anton du Plessis for use in dangerous southern Africa anti-poaching efforts (see: Silent Heroes Foundation), the OG was a wilderness-ready beast boasting a drop-point blade measuring 6.38 inches.

item.title: SPECS Are Augmented Reality Glasses Built for the Real World
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.22
The idea behind most augmented reality experiences is escape: put on a headset, leave the room, and explore another world. SPECS take the opposite approach. Billed as augmented reality glasses designed for real life, SPECS use see-through lenses to overlay digital information onto the world in front of you: directions, translations, notifications, or a workspace, instead of replacing that world with another one. The goal is to create a computer you can wear, walk around in, and live with, all while staying engaged with the people and places around you.
