A personal big screen The centerpiece of SPECS is the display. Each lens provides a see-through waveguide built with billions of nanostructures, producing a 51-degree field of view, which is the equivalent of a 115-inch cinema screen placed about ten feet away. The display anchors digital content in physical space, so a virtual monitor, an interactive recipe, or a spatial timer stays put in the room as you move. For streaming, the virtual screen renders 16 million colors. For work, SPECS can cast a phone, laptop, or gaming device to a large private second screen via a wired connection. Six microphones capture audio while custom stereo speakers built into the temples provide open-ear sound only the wearer can hear. A standalone spatial computer, no phone required Unlike tethered headsets, Snap positions SPECS as a true standalone spatial computer. There’s no external puck and no wires, and the glasses work independently without a phone nearby. Onboard spatial intelligence maps the wearer’s surroundings and can understand the context of the environment to anchor information where it’s useful. Control is touch-free: hand and finger tracking means interactions happen through simple gestures and voice cues, with no screens or controllers. Bluetooth notifications from iPhone and Android are supported, and battery life is rated at up to 4 hours of mixed use, with the included charging case providing four additional charges for up to 20 total hours of mixed use. What you can actually do with them The real pitch for SPECS is how they slot into an ordinary day. In the kitchen, you can pull up a recipe on a floating screen above the counter and set spatial timers that stay anchored in the room whether you’re stirring a pot or washing your hands. Out on a run or a bike ride, turn-by-turn directions appear in your line of sight without requiring you to break stride and check your phone. Traveling abroad, real-time translation overlays text from signs or menus directly in your field of view. At your desk, SPECS can expand your workspace by casting a laptop or phone to a large private second screen — useful if you’re working from a cramped café table or a hotel room. For downtime, streaming content on a virtual 115-inch screen makes a long flight or a plain living-room wall feel considerably more cinematic. And because the display is see-through and the audio is open-ear, all of it happens while you remain aware of the room around you. Lightweight fit, visible privacy SPECS come in two sizes, a 47mm Narrow Fit and a 52mm Wide Fit, with adjustable nose pads for comfortable all-day wear. Plus the company says the design is now 40 percent lighter. Privacy is handled clearly: an LED light glows when someone is recording, the system asks before accessing sensitive information, and processing is prioritized on-device. Users control what gets stored, synced, shared, or deleted.

item.title: Timex’s Dive-Ready Automatic Field Watch Is Even More Affordable in Steel
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.11
The Expedition Pioneer sub-collection contains some of Timex’s most capable watches and generous bargains. While it is technically a field watch category, the GMT and time-and-date models both boast 200m water resistance and classic diver looks. The new Expedition Pioneer Automatic blends design elements from both of its predecessors in a stainless steel case that makes the bargain even sweeter. Timex’s new GADA watch features the same 41mm faceted case with squared-off lugs as its predecessors, but presented in brushed stainless steel. From there, it blends the GMT’s triangle-dot-dash hour track with the diver’s three-hand set. Interestingly, the new seconds hand is colored the same yellow as the existing GMT hand. Like the time-and-date titanium model, it features a date window at 3:00, but Timex swapped the Seiko Caliber NH35 for a Miyota Caliber 8215. Both Japanese wholesale movements beat at 3Hz and offer a 40-hour power reserve.

item.title: This Kentucky Bourbon Spent Its Last Three Years in Scotch Barrels
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.97
Since Angel’s Envy debuted its Port Wine Barrel Finished Bourbon in 2011, cask finishing has been a popular way to experiment with the traditional craft of whiskeymaking, especially since it doesn’t rock the boat too much and can even provide variety for your bar cart. One brand that’s known for its exceptional experimentation is Bardstown Bourbon Co. The Kentucky producer has finished its whiskeys in everything from pineapple-aged rum barrels to Indian single malt whiskey casks. However, its latest release is perhaps the first time it’s dabbled with single malt Scotch. Cask me no questions Bardstown’s new Lochs of Jura Barrel Finish is one of its most interesting releases to date. The liquid begins with a blend of 12-year Kentucky bourbon (21%), 11-year Indiana bourbon (30%) and 10-year Indiana rye (49%). A full mashbill breakdown of each component can be found on the whiskey’s product page.

item.title: Sennheiser Just Gave Hi-Fi Fans a New Genuine AirPod Rival
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.60
This week, there’s been a lot of news about Apple’s AirPods. Particularly, AirPods with built-in cameras. As shown in a leaked video, these new AirPods use Visual Intelligence and Siri to capture images you want to save for later. No need to take out your iPhone. But Bloomberg‘s Mark Gurman put the kibosh on the initial hoopla, reporting that, despite definitely being in the works, AirPods with built-in cameras won’t launch before 2027. So, we’re like still a year (or more) away. If you’re in the market for a new set of high-end wireless earbuds and want to set yourself apart from the AirPods-wearing masses, Sennheiser just introduced a new flagship pair. Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 The Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 (or Momentum 5, for short) are the company’s latest pair of high-end wireless earbuds with active noise cancellation. They’re essentially the next evolution of Sennheiser’s Momentum True Wireless 4, released in early 2024, and they bring key improvements. For those familiar with Sennheiser’s wireless earbuds, the biggest difference in these fifth-generation models may be the shape of the earbuds. The company says they have a new aerodynamic silhouette with a fin-less design that helps them achieve a “barely there” fit.

item.title: Costco Is Selling One of Bose’s New Affordable Speakers for Way Less
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.53
The Bose SoundLink Home is one of the company’s newer portable Bluetooth speakers. And it’s quite different from the rest of its SoundLink family. Released in late 2024, the SoundLink Home is a portable Bluetooth speaker that’s meant to be used around the home. It has a retro-inspired design, is made of fabric and metal and doesn’t have an IP rating. Basically, it’s designed to look good, but not to be brought to the beach. Also, unlike many portable Bluetooth speakers today, the SoundLink Home is really straightforward to use. You turn it on, use the pairing button to connect it to your smartphone and, boom, you’re in business. There’s no companion app to deal with. When Bose released the SoundLink Home, it offered it in two different colored finishes: gray or light silver. However, the company has since introduced a third option: warm wood.

item.title: 8 New Whiskeys You May Have Missed This Past Week
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.52
If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more The world of whiskey is rooted in tradition yet, simultaneously, always changing. Whether it’s new bottles from iconic distilleries or up-and-coming brands hoping to be the next bar cart staple, this guide should provide you with a few new options to consider. This time, a few releases stood out from the rest. Redemption’s Single Barrel Bonded Bourbon made a case for the bonded category’s staying power, and with single-barrel selection. Chattanooga Whiskey went further out on a limb with its Moldovan Ice Wine Cask Finished expression. Also, Jim Beam revives a decades-old collectors item. Plus, a couple of bottles from Scotland and Ireland that might have you running to Total Wine. Jameson Distiller’s Batch 2026 Jameson’s Distiller’s Batch marks the brand’s first US release from its higher-end Reserve Series, and it arrives with serious credentials. Master distiller Kevin O’Gorman crafted this single pot still whiskey at the Midleton distillery in County Cork, aging it across five cask types: American ex-bourbon, European Oloroso sherry, and virgin American, European and Irish oak. The result layers toasted oak, honeycomb and salted caramel with dark chocolate, cinnamon and orange peel. It has earned gold medals at both the San Francisco World Spirits Competition and the International Spirits Challenge. The Dalmore’s second Distillery Select release is a 14-year-old Highland single malt built for collectors who want something off the well-worn path. Distilled into American white oak ex-Bourbon barrels, it then spent one year and nine months in semisecco Marsala casks — a medium-sweet Sicilian fortified wine that layers in candied citrus, honeyed fruit, roasted nuts and gentle spice. Bottled at 53.7% ABV, only 1,110 bottles exist, available from 31 August at The Dalmore boutiques and its Cromarty Firth brand home. Copperworks American Single Malt Urban Family Barley Wine Cask Seattle’s Copperworks Distilling Co. and Urban Family Brewing Co. pulled off a clever cask exchange for this limited release: Urban Family aged its Treehouse in the City barleywine in a Copperworks whiskey cask, then returned it so Copperworks could finish its three-and-a-half-year-old 5 Malt signature whiskey there for 10 more months. The result, bottled at 50% ABV, layers sweet malt, tobacco, black walnut and ripe blackberry, and is available exclusively to Whiskey Club members. Jim Beam Ten Pin Bottle 10-Year-Old Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey Jim Beam revives one of its most iconic collector items — the bowling pin-shaped decanter — with a 10-year-old Kentucky Straight Bourbon bottled at 100 proof. The silhouette traces back to decanters Jim Beam gifted to friends and associates from the 1940s onward, making it as much a piece of brand history as a whiskey. At a decade of age and full proof, the liquid promises more oak concentration and a longer finish than its lower-proof predecessor. About the Author: Ethan Brehm is an associate editor at Gear Patrol writing about footwear, watches, spirits, EDC and more. When he’s not shopping for his next G-Shock, he spends his time watching movies and planning a future road trip with his family. He firmly believes CDs sound better than vinyl. Want to stay up to date on the latest product news and releases? Add Gear Patrol as a preferred source to ensure our independent journalism makes it to the top of your Google search results.

item.title: Vero Engineering Evolves Its Acclaimed, Affordable Avid EDC Knife with a Strong New Blade
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.51
In 2025, Vero Engineering took home a major accolade from Blade Show Atlanta: Imported Folding Knife of the Year. The knife that brought the award home was the Avid 1. Now, a year later, that same knife is in its third iteration. Better still, the Vero Engineering Avid 3 marks a new frontier, adding a new blade shape to one of the brand’s most approachable and affordable silhouettes. Avid engineering Those familiar with Vero Engineering likely won’t be surprised to hear about Avid’s pedigree. After all, the Joseph Vero-helmed brand has consistently produced exceptional EDC knives and fixed blades since its inception in 2018, earning a well-deserved cult following. What Vero has not been known for, however, is affordability. Unfortunately, the brand’s penchant for high-end engineering and materials means most of its offerings come at a premium.

item.title: Today in Gear: Smith Gives Its ’90s Eyewear Icon a Celebratory Japanese Uplift
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.35
In celebration of Beams’ 50th birthday, this limited-edition sunglass revisits a decades-old collaboration between the Tokyo-based brand and Portland, Oregon’s Smith, now updated with modern tech and looks. The revival retains Smith’s patented Slider innovation, the industry’s first dual-lens interchangeable system from 1995, while adding ChromaPop performance lenses. (The installed Photochromic one can be swapped for included Low-Light Copper and Black options.) Meanwhile, the black frame gets accented with BEAMS’ signature clear orange on the inner frame and under-rim, with a bespoke special-edition pouch rounding out the package. Mattel’s Brick Shop pays tribute to gaming history with a 1:1 scale, fully buildable replica of the original Xbox console and its iconic Duke controller. Once it’s built, you can open the console lid to trigger the original Xbox startup sequence, then use the controller’s working buttons to cycle through four light and sound sequences tied to three included dioramas — one each for Halo, Psychonauts and The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind. Each diorama slots directly into the console and features 1-inch NanoWorld figures of iconic characters, making this a display piece as much as a hobby build. J. Press x Original Madras Trading Company Indigo Handloomed Chore Jacket There’s something to be said for producing a basic garment to the highest possible standard, as J.Press and OMTC did with the humble chore coat. It’s built with pure cotton canvas handloomed in India, and dyed with genuine plant-based indigo. Hemmed cuffs, three patch pockets and a spread collar fit the standard blueprint. Just be careful during the first few wears and washes, as natural indigo will bleed. Knoll updates Eero Saarinen’s classic Executive Side Chair by adding a wood veneer back. This gives the normally fully upholstered 1950 design more of a mid-century modern look and provides more versatility when adding it to new spaces. The chair is available with three veneer finishes: light oak, light walnut and ebonized walnut, all of which are matched to the chair’s bent wood legs. Outerknown The Beachcomber Relaxed Jean – Washed Black Originally designed for men, the Beachcomber quickly crossed over into a popular unisex staple. Now, Outerknown’s Beachcomber Relaxed Jean makes its debut in Washed Black, a vintage-leaning colorway that adds to its low-slung, baggy appeal. Built with 13 ounce organic cotton woven at Italy’s Candiani Mills, the relaxed silhouette features chainstitch embroidery, copper rivets and dull nickel hardware to round out its considered style. Size up for an oversized, skater-influenced drape; stay true for a cleaner, higher-rise line. Goruck built the Achilles specifically for a broader, masculine frame — a distinction that matters when you’re logging serious miles under load. The vest’s 420D Robic exterior pairs with a nylon-spandex double-weave interior, and its specialty-coated steel pellets resist corrosion and odor through the sweatiest sessions. Dual-density shoulder straps and quick-release cummerbund handles keep it dialed in for rucking, running, Murph prep and everyday conditioning. It backs all of it with Goruck’s Scars Lifetime Guarantee. Range Rover’s From Sea to Sea curations are a limited-edition, SV Bespoke collection of three distinct Range Rover variants available in Desert Ember, Summit Frost and Ocean Crest. Each draws design inspiration from a defining American landscape in celebration of the 250th anniversary of the United States. All three share the same 4.4-liter twin-turbocharged V8 producing 523 horsepower and 553 lb-ft of torque. Just 250 examples will be built in total.

item.title: Ford’s Toughest Ranger Reaffirms Its Utility with an Emergency-Grade Uplift
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.28
Ford’s Ranger Super Duty remains off-limits to American buyers, but that hasn’t stopped the Blue Oval from finding ways to make its forbidden fruit even more appealing. Just a few months ago, FoMoCo Australia updated the pickup with a refined XLT version. Together with the truck’s rugged capabilities, it presented a tempting vision of what could be. Now Ford has revealed a built-up Ranger Super Duty it’s calling Project FireTrak. Beyond demonstrating the truck’s potential chops as a fire-response unit, I’d argue it continues to tease the pickup’s overlanding potential. The Ranger earns the assignment The Ranger Super Duty before you is the product of a collaboration between Ford Australia, Deakin University and specialized upfitters XL Service Bodies and Zeliox Australia. It’s envisioned as an alternative to larger rigs and ladder trucks, more easily maneuvered in urban zones to arrive on the scene in eight minutes or less.

item.title: Nike’s Viral $95 Mule Gets a Tactical, Army-Green Makeover
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.16
Sneakers are Nike’s bread and butter. But the brand’s biggest hit of 2026 almost doesn’t qualify. The unorthodox Mind 001 is a slip-on mule that sells out every time it restocks, including a seven-colorway drop on August 20 that evaporated in less than a day. Thankfully, Nike is already previewing the next batch of Mind 001 variants. The collection is headlined by a colorway called “Tarp Green” that sees the mule take on a tactical, mil-spec aesthetic with its interplay of olive and tan on the outsole. Mind games Of course, looks are only half the story. The real draw of the Mind 001 is the promise of what they do. The design features almost two-dozen foam nodes on the bottom, each of which moves independently to transmit sensory feedback from the body to the brain.

item.title: Ugg Goes Full Western with Its Cow-Print Clog
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.06
Cowboy style has been going strong in fashion circles for the past two seasons, and the cowboy-approved trend isn’t showing signs of slowing down. The latest example of its staying power comes in an unexpected package. Ugg took its Otzo clog, already one of the more versatile new slides in its lineup, and covered it in cow print. The result is the Otzo Western Clog, a limited-run riff on the brand’s elevated everyday silhouette that commits fully to the western trend without tipping into costume territory. Goin’ country While most everyone recognizes Ugg’s iconic Tasman slip-on, the Otzo is a sleeper hit; an IYKYK clog, if you will. The sleek design features a contoured EVA foam footbed, streamlined leather upper and slim outsole.

item.title: Sony Is Getting Back Into Desktop Hi-Fi in a Weirdly Cool Way
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.02
These days, Sony is a juggernaut in the audio world. It makes some of the best noise-canceling headphones and earbuds you can buy. Its portable Bluetooth speakers are incredibly popular. It’s also at the bleeding edge of innovation for home theater soundbars and home theater speaker systems. And that’s just the tip of Sony’s audio empire. That said, one area where Sony has been lacking lately is in desktop audio … it currently doesn’t sell any desktop speakers. Well, that is now officially changing. Sony Pulse Elevate Last September, Sony announced the Pulse Elevate, a set of wireless desktop speakers that, well, sort of resemble miniature versions of the company’s PS5. Each speaker is the same color and has a similar shape (not size) to the console. The speakers are compatible with Mac and PC, as well as the PS5 (so, presumably, they can be used as TV speakers, though that hasn’t been specified yet) and Sony’s handheld remote player, the PlayStation Portal.

item.title: This $650 Automatic Dive Watch Has a Sapphire Dial That Adds Intense Visual Depth
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.90
Sector’s Design Lab is the Los Angeles watchmaker’s experimental division, providing a playground for collaborators to create fascinating iterations of the brand’s core collection. It allowed Holme & Hadfield, a brand known for its handcrafted display cases, to add a fascinating sapphire dial to the Sector II Dive. The result is a printed hour track that appears to float, suspended on its own plane halfway between the handset and dial plate. In a way, all watches are display cases, with the dial protected by a transparent sapphire, mineral or acrylic crystal. This collaboration takes it a step further by leveraging that transparency to create a fun visual trick. At arm’s length, the H&H Edition appears to be a pared-down version of the Sector II Dive, with the titular sector dial replaced by a flat, matte black surface. The dial is simplified with only a white hour track, minute track and a pair of brand logos. The date complication is deleted (one of my favorite adjustments), and the only touch of color is a green seconds hand. The foundation of this special-edition Sector II Dive remains unchanged, with a 40mm brushed stainless-steel case placed on a stainless-steel three-link bracelet featuring a proprietary NEM micro-adjustment clasp.

item.title: Kawasaki’s Pint-Sized Ninja Four-Pot Just Got a New Reason to Be Worried
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.82
If you’ve ever shopped for a bike on the smaller side (like 600cc or less), you’ve probably noticed your choices are pretty limited when it comes to engine configurations. Singles and twins are generally far more economical than more complex triples and fours. However, China’s motorcycle boom is proving that small displacement doesn’t have to mean simple. From CFMoto and Kove to QJMotor and Voge, there’s a raft of new names touting big bike value at prices that undercut established competitors by thousands. Another is ZXMoto, an outfit my colleague Steve Mazzucchi highlighted for its retro-styled 500F. The brand has already proven its Honda-duping abilities with that bike, and now it’s made it clear that it’ll be aiming for Team Green as well. A new challenger approaches That’s because ZXMoto’s 500RR is rapidly growing its market presence. After debuting the bike at CIMAMotor 2024 and reaching its first delivery milestone the following year, ZXMoto has now confirmed not only the bike’s EU Whole Type approval but also its UK launch in September.

item.title: Long-Term Travel and the Accounts That Stop Recognizing You
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.89
Four months into a trip through South America, a long-term traveler can suddenly find their bank has flagged them as fraud. There may be no warning. The card is declined at the counter, the app refuses to open, and the only option is a phone number that does not accept calls from outside the account's country. Long-term travelers often encounter this problem, which is rarely triggered by the transaction alone. The connection also has a part. Banks and payment processors review factors like location, network reputation, and connection type when assessing a login. A ProxyWing ISP proxy provider uses IP addresses registered to internet service providers rather than data-center IPs, which helps explain why different connections may be classified differently. Why Unfamiliar Connections Can Trigger Account Lockouts What Actually Trips the Alarm It is seldom the amount you spent. It is the shape of the session. - Speed of movement matters. A login from Peru eleven hours after one from Colombia is fine, but eleven minutes is not. - The reputation of the network matters. Hundreds of people share hostel and cafe Wi-Fi, and if any have done something suspicious, the address carries that history. - Connection type. Traffic that looks like it comes from a data center rather than a home or a phone gets scored much more harshly, which is why certain VPNs make things worse rather than better. - Doing something unusual at the same time. Changing an address or adding a payee from an unfamiliar country is what turns a flag into a lock. The Two-Factor Problem Nobody Plans For Losing a phone at home is inconvenient. Losing it in month five of a trip can lock you out of everything at once because the phone is usually the second factor for the bank, the email that lets you reset the bank, and the authenticator app that protects the email. The chain matters. If your recovery codes are stored in the email account that needs the authenticator on the lost phone, you have a loop with no way in. This is the most common way travelers get genuinely stuck rather than merely inconvenienced, and it takes about fifteen minutes to prevent. - Print the recovery codes for your email plus primary bank on paper, carried separately from the phone. - Add a second authenticator device if any of your accounts allow it. An old phone without a SIM works fine and can be kept at the bottom of the bag. - Check whether your bank's two-factor works over SMS only. If it does, a local SIM will break it, so you need to know before you swap the card rather than after. What To Do Before You Leave The single most useful thing is boring. Set up a second account at a different bank, fund it, and carry the card separately. Everything else on this list is optional, but that one is not. - Register a travel notice if your bank still offers one. Many have quietly dropped them. - Make sure your phone number on the account is one you can actually receive calls on abroad, not just texts. - Download the offline recovery codes for anything that uses an authenticator app. - Take a photograph of the back of your cards, cropped so the number is not fully visible, and store it somewhere you can reach without your phone. - Tell one person at home which banks you use. If you end up needing someone to receive a letter or make a domestic call on your behalf, this saves a day. How Different Connections Get Treated | Connection you are using | How a bank tends to score it | Practical result | | Local SIM with mobile data | Low risk, looks like an ordinary phone | Usually fine | | HotelWi-Fii | Medium, shared but stable | Occasional extra verification | | Hostel or cafeWi-Fii | Higher, heavily shared | Verification, sometimes a lock | | Commercial VPN | High, recognized as a data center range | Frequently blocked outright | | Residential connection at home | Lowest | The baseline everything else is measured against | | AirportWi-Fii | High, transient and shared | Avoid logging into banking entirely | | Tethering from your own phone | Same as the phone itself | The best option on the road | The general pattern is similar across many banks: the closer a connection looks to an ordinary home line, the less friction a traveler is likely to encounter. The closer your connection looks to an ordinary home line, the less friction you get. This is also why the free VPN people install for privacy tends to be the thing that locks them out. Which Accounts Survive Travel Better Not all banks handle this equally; the difference is structural rather than customer service. Banks built around mobile apps cope better because their fraud models assume people move. Older institutions with branch-based verification cope worst because their recovery path assumes you can walk into a building. The pragmatic setup most long-term travelers use is one app-based account for daily spending, one traditional account holding most of the money and rarely touched, and a card from a third provider kept separate from the wallet. It sounds excessive until the first lockout. If You Are Already Locked Out Do not keep retrying. Repeated failed attempts push the account further into lockdown and make the eventual phone call longer. Find a dependable connection, ideally mobile data on a local SIM, and use the in-app message system if available. It is slower but works from anywhere. If you do have to call, use a voice-over-internet service that presents a number in your home country. Many bank fraud lines will not accept an international caller ID at all, and this is the difference between resolving it today and resolving it next week. FAQ Will telling my bank I am traveling prevent this? It helps for the first few weeks and then stops mattering. Most travel notices expire after thirty days, and many banks have removed them entirely in favor of automatic detection. Is a VPN a good idea for online banking abroad? Generally no. It protects the connection, but it makes you look less like yourself, and banks weigh that heavily. Use mobile data instead. Why does my card work in shops but the app will not open? Different systems score card payments and app logins. The card transaction has a physical terminal behind it, which is strong evidence you are there. The app login has only the connection. How long does a lock usually take to lift? If you can complete identity verification, minutes. If it needs a phone call to a domestic number, expect days. This is the main argument for the second card. Does using the same connection every day help? Yes, more than most people expect. Staying somewhere for a fortnight and using the same Wi-Fi builds a pattern the bank recognizes, which is why lockouts cluster in the weeks when you are moving fastest. This article was published in partnership with ProxyWing.

item.title: The Paperwork Nobody Warns You About: Certified Translations for Visas, Residency, and Life Abroad
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.43
Nobody starts planning a year abroad by thinking about their birth certificate. You think about flights, routes, maybe travel insurance if you're responsible. Then one day you're in a consulate waiting room in Santiago or Seoul with your working-holiday application, and the officer slides your documents back. "This needs to be translated. Officially." Just like that, your start date moves by three weeks. I've seen this scene play out more times than I can count, and it almost always catches people off guard. The travel itself is the easy part now. Border runs, SIM cards, finding an apartment through a Facebook group at 2 am-we've all figured that out. The paperwork behind long stays is where trips stall. So here's the unglamorous guide I wish someone had handed me years ago. When a Stamp in Your Passport Isn't Enough Short tourist visits rarely require any of this. The trouble starts the moment you want to stay somewhere: a working-holiday visa in Australia or Japan, a digital-nomad visa in Spain or Croatia, a student enrollment in Germany, a residency application in Portugal. Each of these asks for supporting documents, and each authority wants those documents in a language its clerks can clearly read. The usual suspects: birth certificates, university diplomas and transcripts, police clearance certificates (also called criminal record checks), marriage certificates, and sometimes bank statements or proof of income for nomad visas. If your documents were issued in English and you're applying somewhere that accepts English, lucky you. Everyone else needs official translations, and "official" is the word that trips people up. A quick note on getting them done. Many travelers try a bilingual friend or a chatbot first, but immigration offices often reject these because there is no accountability. Travelers needing professional help can use a certified translation service like Protranslate.net, which offers document translation in more than 100 languages. Before ordering, confirm that the translation and certification will satisfy the authority receiving your application. "Certified" Means Different Things in Different Countries This part confuses almost everyone, so let's slow down. For applications submitted to USCIS in the United States, a certified translation generally means a complete English translation accompanied by a signed statement confirming that the translation is accurate and that the translator is competent to do the work. Other immigration offices, universities, and government agencies may apply similar rules, but you still need to check the requirements for your particular application. Several European countries use a more formal system involving sworn or officially authorized translators. Depending on the country and the office reviewing your documents, the translator may need to appear on an approved list, use an official stamp, or have the translation certified by a notary, lawyer, consulate, or another authorized body. Spain, for example, commonly requires foreign documents used in visa and residency applications to be translated into Spanish by a sworn or otherwise officially accepted translator. Portugal allows several routes for certifying translations, and some documents in English, French, or Spanish may not require translation at all. The rules can also change depending on the type of document and the authority receiving it. The practical takeaway: never order a translation before you know which system your destination and the specific office handling your application use. Check the exact wording on the authority's website or ask the office directly. Then send those requirements to the translation provider. Ten minutes of reading can save a hundred euros of redone work. The Apostille Is Not a Translation (And Vice Versa) Second biggest source of confusion. An apostille is a separate certificate issued under the Hague Apostille Convention. It authenticates the signature or seal on a public document and the official capacity of the person who signed it. It does not translate the document or verify that everything in it is true. Many residency processes require both a document bearing an apostille from the appropriate authority in its country of origin and a translation, sometimes with the apostille page translated as well. Before beginning, confirm whether the apostille must be obtained before translation and whether the apostille page itself must be translated. The sequence varies by authority. I've seen a couple in Lisbon lose a month because their marriage-certificate translation did not reflect the apostille added afterward. It's a good reminder to get the exact instructions before starting. And on marriage: a surprising number of backpackers end up staying. You meet someone in a hostel in Medellín, and two years later you're filing marriage paperwork in Colombia. Suddenly, you may need your birth certificate apostilled and translated into Spanish, in accordance with the local authority's rules, with your parents' names spelled exactly as they appear everywhere else-which brings us to the pitfalls. Where Applications Actually Fail Names that don't match the passport. Transliteration is the silent killer for anyone with a name that changes alphabets. If your passport says "Aleksandr" and the translator writes "Alexander," a strict clerk can reject the whole file. Always send translators a scan of your passport photo page and ask them to follow it exactly. Expired police checks. Many applications require police certificates issued within a recent window-often three or six months-but the exact rule depends on the destination and visa. People request the check, wait while gathering everything else, then find it expired before the appointment. Sequence your documents: slow-moving ones (apostilles, university records) first, short-validity ones last. DIY and machine translations. Tempting, cheap, and routinely rejected when submitted without the required certification. Even if the translation is accurate, the lack of a certification statement may make it unacceptable. Some countries also bar applicants from translating their own documents, even if qualified. Wrong document version. Universities may issue several transcript formats, while civil registries offer short-form, long-form, or certified copies of the same record. An immigration office may require a version that includes details omitted from the shorter copy. Confirm the precise document type before paying to translate the wrong one. Notarization mix-ups. A notarized translation and a certified one are not the same, and a notary stamp does not improve a bad translation. Some authorities require notarization in addition to certification, while others do not. Paying for it "just in case" may be unnecessary, so check the exact wording from the receiving office. A Little Prep Before You Fly Scan everything before you leave home: birth certificate, diploma, transcripts, and marriage certificate (if you have one), all at 300 dpi and stored in the cloud. Getting a fresh copy of a birth certificate from another continent is a special kind of misery, and most translation providers work happily from clean scans. Budget time, not just money. Some straightforward certified translations can be completed in 24 to 48 hours. A sworn translation in a country with few appointed translators for your language pair may take a week or two, especially around holidays. Consulate appointment slots in busy cities can also book out weeks ahead. Work backward from your appointment date and allow extra time for every step. Keep both physical and digital copies of every translated document after the process ends. Residency renewals, tax registrations, or even opening a bank account may require some of the same paperwork, and you'll be very glad you don't have to start over. None of this is fun, exactly. But there is real satisfaction the day you walk out of an immigration office with a residence card in your pocket, knowing the boring folder of stamped, sealed, correctly spelled papers got you there. Do the dull part properly once, and the interesting parts of living abroad get a lot smoother. This article was published in partnership with Protranslate.

item.title: Campervan Camping in the American West: Rules and Hiking Basecamps
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.15
The pitch for hiking out of a campervan is simple. Your bed, your kitchen, and your gear are all parked where you want to walk, so you can be on the trail at first light instead of driving in from a motel 40 minutes up the highway. The reality is that it takes more planning because the American West is a patchwork of land agencies, each having its own rules about where you can legally sleep. Get that part right, and a van is the best hiking basecamp there is. Get it wrong, and you'll spend your evenings circling gravel lots looking for somewhere you won't get a knock on the window at 11 pm. Here's what actually matters. You Usually Can't Sleep at the Trailhead Start here, because it undoes the assumption most people arrive with. Inside national parks, sleeping overnight in a vehicle is almost always limited to designated campgrounds. Capitol Reef states it flatly: camping or sleeping in your vehicle overnight is not allowed anywhere except a designated campground. Grand Teton says the same and adds that overnight parking at trailheads is only permitted with a backcountry permit. Yellowstone, Glacier, and Yosemite take the same line. Overnight sleeping or camping in pullouts, picnic areas, and trailhead lots is generally prohibited after dark, whether you're in a tent, a sedan, or a fully self-contained Class C. National forest land is looser, but not as people assume. The Forest Service defines camping as spending the night on its land in any non-permanent structure, including sleeping in your vehicle. So a "No Camping" sign at a Forest Service trailhead applies even if you never open the door. BLM land is the most permissive of the three, and it's where most legal free camping in the West actually happens. Campground or Dispersed: Choose Based on the Hike, Not the Price Developed campgrounds buy you certainty, a water spigot, and a legal place to be at 2 am. Many popular national park campgrounds accept reservations up to six months in advance, but booking windows vary, so check the current listing on Recreation.gov. A few numbers worth knowing before you book a vehicle: - Watchman, Zion. 164 sites, all reservable, including 95 with electric hookups, plus a dump station and potable water. Generators are prohibited at Watchman; South and Lava Point allow them during limited hours (8 am - 10 am and 6 pm - 8 pm). - Devils Garden, Arches. 51 sites; reservation only from March 1 to October 31; first-come, first-served the rest of the year: no hookups, no dump station, no showers. - Willow Flat, Canyonlands Island in the Sky. Twelve first-come sites at $15 a night, a 28-foot vehicle limit, and no water at all. It fills daily from late March through June and again in fall. - Fruita, Capitol Reef. 71 sites, reservable year-round six months out, no hookups. Dispersed camping on BLM and Forest Service land is often free and can put you closer to an early trail start, but rules vary by location. Stay on routes open to your vehicle, use previously disturbed campsites, and check with the local field office or national forest for stay limits, water setbacks, fire restrictions, and camping requirements. In Utah, BLM guidance limits stays to 14 days, prohibits camping near developed recreation sites like trailheads, and requires campsites to be at least 300 feet from corrals, gates, livestock water, and other range improvements. Review the BLM Utah dispersed-camping guidance and rules for the public land you plan to visit before camping. The wrinkle is that "dispersed" increasingly means "designated dispersed." The Alabama Hills below Mount Whitney is the clearest example. Camping outside a developed campground there is now restricted to marked sites, and you need a free BLM permit that doesn't reserve or guarantee a spot. Measure the Van Before You Plan the Route This one is new, and it's already catching people out. Since June 7, 2026, Zion National Park has banned vehicles longer than 35 feet 9 inches, wider than 7 feet 10 inches, taller than 11 feet 4 inches, or heavier than 50,000 pounds from the Zion-Mount Carmel Highway between Canyon Junction and the East Entrance. The old $15 tunnel escort permit is gone with no replacement. Measurements include mirrors, rooftop air conditioners, and bike racks. Exceeding any single limit disqualifies you. That's stricter than it sounds. Cruise America's C25, its most popular model, measures 24.93 feet long, 8.33 feet wide, and 12.20 feet tall. It fails on width and height. The height includes the rooftop air conditioner, which is standard on that unit. If you're in a mid-size Class C, the classic east-side run between Zion and Bryce isn't available. The signed detour goes east on SR-59 from Hurricane, then on Arizona SR-389 and US-89, roughly 80 miles, taking about an hour and a half to two hours. For Bryce, Highway 20 north of Cedar City adds about 63 miles. Do not let your phone reroute you onto Sheep Bridge Road or Smithsonian Butte Road; both are steep, dirt roads, and the park warns against them. Some converted Sprinters and Transits clear all four limits, but dimensions vary by model, conversion, and exterior accessories. A Class C generally does not. Dimensions are listed on every vehicle page on rental comparison sites like Campstar, so it takes about a minute to check at booking. That beats finding out at Canyon Junction with a ranger waving you back. Food Storage Is a Legal Requirement, Not a Suggestion In bear country, this is regulated, and "food" is defined more broadly than most expect. Yosemite counts drinks, trash, toiletries, sunscreen, soap, lip balm, and even empty coolers. The good news for van travelers is that hard-sided RVs and campervans count as adequate storage in Yosemite if everything is out of sight and windows, doors, and vents are closed when you're not at the site. Pop-up and soft-sided campers do not qualify. Neither does a regular car after dark, which is why you'll find food lockers in most Yosemite trailhead lots. Sequoia is stricter still and expects lockers to be available at all times. If you're choosing a rental, a canvas pop-top is a real trade-off in the Sierra. It's a lovely place to sleep, but a liability for storing food. Leave No Trace, Van Edition The standard seven principles all apply, but a few land differently when you're driving your accommodation around: - Water in, water out. Dump blackwater only at authorized dump stations. Greywater rules vary by agency and location, so assume it must be contained unless the local land manager says otherwise. Carry it to a dump station and factor that into how long you can stay out. - Use found sites, not made sites. Don't level ground, dig trenches, or build new fire rings. If there's an existing ring, use it. - Check fire restrictions the week you travel, not the month before. Seasonal orders in the West change quickly, and in many places, stoves and campfires are restricted. - Pack out everything, including pet waste. Most dispersed areas have no trash service. Four Regions Worth Building a Trip Around Eastern Sierra, California. Highway 395 from Lone Pine to Mammoth is arguably the best hiking corridor in the country for van travel, with trailheads climbing straight off the valley floor. Base at Tuttle Creek (83 first-come BLM sites, $10) or Inyo National Forest's Lone Pine Campground, and treat the Alabama Hills as a designated-site option rather than a free-for-all. Moab, Utah. Arches does not require timed-entry reservations in 2026, so visitors may enter during operating hours with a valid park pass. Parking remains the main constraint: once congestion builds and lots fill, the park may temporarily delay additional vehicles from entering. These restrictions can last three to five hours. During the busy season, arrive before 8 am or after 4 pm, and have an alternative plan in case entry is restricted. Check the park's current traffic and travel guidance before visiting. Zion and Bryce, Utah. Spectacular, heavily managed, and now size-dependent. Book Watchman early, size your vehicle to the highway limits, and build the detour into your drive times if you can't. Consider these additional hikes for a road trip to Zion National Park as you plan your route. Rocky Mountain, Colorado. Timed entry runs from May 22 into mid-October 2026, with two permit types. Bear Lake Road access is controlled from 5 am to 6 pm, and the rest of the park from 9 am to 2 pm. Reservations cost $2 on Recreation.gov, with a small extra release at 7 pm the night before. If you want an alpine start, entering before the window opens is a legitimate strategy. A Planning Order That Works - Book the hardest campground first and build the rest of the trip around it as soon as its booking window opens (for example as six months to the day). - Check whether your parks require timed entry for the dates you want, and set an alarm for the release. - Measure the vehicle against the routes you've drawn, not just the campground limits. - Line up a dispersed backup for every in-park night you didn't get, and confirm it's on a designated route. - Download offline maps and your reservation confirmations. Cell service at Devils Garden, the Needles, and most of the Eastern Sierra is somewhere between poor and nonexistent. None of this is complicated once you've done it once. The rules exist because these places are loved to the edge of their capacity, and the small amount of homework buys you the thing you came for: waking up already there, boots by the door, with the trail starting 40 feet from where you slept. This article was published in partnership with Campstar.

item.title: The Post-Travel Blues: Why Coming Home Can Feel Harder Than Leaving
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.05
The suitcase is still open on the floor. There is laundry to wash, food to buy, and an inbox that seems louder than it did before the trip. Instead of feeling refreshed, you feel flat, restless, or tearful. People often call this the post-travel blues, while online it may be described as post-vacation depression. The phrase captures a real emotional slump but is not a formal diagnosis. Earlier studies found vacation-related well-being improvements could fade after people returned home and resumed work. However, a 2025 meta-analysis suggests those benefits may last longer than previously thought.1, 2 The useful distinction is whether the mood begins to ease as ordinary life settles, or remains persistent and disruptive across daily life. Understanding the difference between sadness and depression can add context without turning a difficult homecoming into a self-diagnosis. Why Re-Entry Can Feel So Abrupt Travel changes the structure of a day. There may be more novelty, movement, shared time, or freedom from routine duties. Even a difficult trip creates momentum: catch the train, find the hostel, reach the trail. Home replaces that motion with familiar rooms and unfinished chores. The return also brings practical pressures. Laundry, groceries, expenses, work messages, and family needs may arrive while sleep is still off. Jet lag or late nights leave you tired and less focused, making the contrast sharper. Sometimes the sadness is simply about an experience ending. That does not make you ungrateful, and it does not prove that life at home is wrong. How the Slump May Show Up A return-home low varies, but people often describe: - Feeling flat, irritable, restless, or unusually tearful - Low energy or trouble concentrating - Sleep timing that remains out of step - Strong nostalgia and little interest in normal plans - Dread about work, chores, or familiar responsibilities None of these signs identifies a disorder on its own. They can occur with travel fatigue, disrupted sleep, stress, ordinary sadness, or a mental health condition. The pattern matters more than a single symptom, especially whether it eases and how much it affects daily life. A Measured Return, Not an Instant Reset A re-entry plan is not treatment or a test of resilience. Its purpose is to reduce avoidable friction while you observe what happens next. - Familiar time cues help. Returning to usual meal and sleep times, where practical, gives the day structure while jet lag settles. - A smaller landing list. Urgent tasks can be separated from those that can wait. One grocery run and one work priority create a more realistic first pass. - Create a place for the trip. Printing a photo, cooking a meal you discovered, or recording a few memories lets the experience remain part of your life. - Choose one local point of interest. A walk, favorite lunch, or connection through peer support puts something concrete on the calendar without demanding another major adventure. Online replay can add another layer. Experimental research found that exposure to certain forms of social comparison on Instagram can reduce momentary well-being.3 A separate randomized trial found that taking a one-week break from social media boosted well-being and reduced symptoms of depression and anxiety.4 Neither study focused specifically on people returning from travel, so the findings do not prove that scrolling causes post-travel blues. Still, when revisiting idealized trips intensifies comparison or worsens your mood, taking a temporary break may be reasonable. The goal is a workable landing, not a perfect first day. When the Low Mood Deserves More Attention Depression is not simply a stronger form of disappointment. Clinicians consider the combination, persistence, and impact of symptoms. Reasons to seek assessment include: - Low mood or loss of interest on most days, without signs of easing - Marked changes in sleep, appetite, concentration, or energy - Work, relationships, or basic self-care becoming difficult to maintain - Persistent hopelessness, worthlessness, or a sense that you cannot cope - Thoughts of self-harm, suicide, or not wanting to be alive These signs do not confirm a diagnosis. A primary care clinician or licensed mental health professional can consider travel disruption alongside your health history, previous mood patterns, and current pressures, then discuss suitable support. You do not need the right label before starting that conversation. Safety concerns change the priority. Set this article aside and use immediate support rather than waiting for the mood to pass. Making Room for the Landing An emotional dip after travel can coexist alongside appreciation for the trip. The balanced response is neither to dramatize nor dismiss it. Reduce immediate friction, restore familiar rhythms, and watch your mood's direction. Persistent or disruptive symptoms deserve support. Homecoming is part of travel too, and sometimes it needs a landing period. Safety Disclaimer If low mood becomes severe or you have thoughts of self-harm or suicide, seek immediate support. In the United States, call or text 988 or visit 988lifeline.org. Outside the United States, contact your local crisis service or emergency number. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services now. Sources 1. Ryan S. Grant, Beth E. Buchanan, and Kristen M. Shockley. (2025). I Need a Vacation: A Meta-Analysis of Vacation and Employee Well-Being. Journal of Applied Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/apl0001262 2. Jessica de Bloom, Sabine Geurts, and Michiel Kompier. (2012). Effects of Short Vacations, Vacation Activities and Experiences on Employee Health and Well-Being. Stress and Health. https://doi.org/10.1002/smi.1434 3. Phillip Ozimek, Gabriel Brandenberg, Elke Rohmann, and Hans-Werner Bierhoff. (2023). The Impact of Social Comparisons More Related to Ability vs. More Related to Opinion on Well-Being: An Instagram Study. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs13100850 4. Jeffrey Lambert, George Barnstable, Eleanor Minter, Jemima Cooper, and Desmond McEwan. (2022). Taking a One-Week Break from Social Media Improves Well-Being, Depression, and Anxiety: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking. https://doi.org/10.1089/cyber.2021.0324 This story is provided in partnership with Modern Recovery Services.

item.title: How to Recognize When Your Customers Want You to Act
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 6.89
Summary. Customer-listening systems have become adept at identifying what customers want and how they feel, but they often miss a third critical signal: when customers expect action. By combining AI with During the past decade, companies have invested heavily in becoming customer centric. Digital platforms now generate continuous streams of reviews, feature requests, support conversations, and community discussions that firms use to identify new ideas, prioritize product changes, and guide the timing of innovation. AI-powered analytics and translation tools allow companies to process feedback from customers around the world at unprecedented scale. Most customer-listening systems today focus on two familiar signals—what customers want, and how they feel—but they often miss a third signal: when customers expect the company to act. That signal, which we call temporal urgency, is most commonly embedded in subtle cues that have to be picked up during customer communications.

item.title: Can an AI-Powered Scribe Curb Physician Burnout?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 6.04
Share Podcast Can an AI-Powered Scribe Curb Physician Burnout? The use of automated note-taking tools during patient visits holds promise in reducing physicans’ administrative load–but the tradeoffs are complicated. In 2024, Mass General Brigham, the largest health system in Massachusetts, piloted an AI-powered ambient note-taking program among a subset of clinicians to address increasing rates of staff burnout and turnover–largely driven by the administrative burden of clinical documentation in the electronic health records (EHR). The pilot program aimed to test AI tools which used natural language processing to record, transcribe, and summarize physician-patient encounters, reducing time spent on documentation and allowing physicians to focus more on patient care. Early results showed promising reductions in clinician burnout, intention to leave, and increased physician efficiency. But concerns about the technology, including the generation of inaccurate notes with errors or hallucinations, made physicians resistant to learn and adopt it into their workflows. Harvard Business School Associate Professor Susanna Gallani and host Brian Kenny discuss the challenges leadership at the health care organization anticipated as they considered scaling the AI technology responsibly in the case: The AI Scribe: Enhancing Physician Presence and Curbing Burnout at Mass General Brigham. BRIAN KENNY: Welcome to Cold Call, the podcast where we dive deep into the groundbreaking ideas in Harvard Business School case studies with the faculty who wrote them. In healthcare, some of the most important innovations aren’t new drugs or breakthrough devices. They’re new ways of giving clinicians back the one resource they can never make more of, time. As artificial intelligence rapidly finds its way into hospitals and medical practices, leaders face a difficult balancing act. Can technology reduce administrative burdens without creating new risks? Will it strengthen the relationship between physicians and patients or subtly change it? And how should organizations measure success when the benefits extend beyond efficiency to include trust, wellbeing and the quality of care? Today’s case explores a real-world effort to answer those questions inside one of the nation’s leading academic health systems. We’ll examine the organizational challenges that accompany technological change and the difficult trade-offs involved in evaluating investments whose returns are both financial and deeply human. My guest today is Professor Susanna Gallani, and we’ll discuss her case, “The AI Scribe: Enhancing Physician Presence and Curbing Burnout at Mass General Brigham.” I’m your host, Brian Kenny, and you’re listening to Cold Call on the HBR Podcast Network. Susanna Gallani studies performance management systems and explores the interplay between monetary and non-monetary incentives, and you probably study much more than that too, Susanna. Welcome back to Cold Call. SUSANNA GALLANI: Thank you. Thank you for having me. It’s good to be back. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, it’s been a little while, so we’re happy to have you back on the show, and we were just chatting before we rolled tape here, and every conversation these days seems to turn to AI. It’s just top of mind for everybody, to the point maybe of AI fatigue, but there are some real-world implications for the case that you wrote and for how Mass General is trying to use AI to help physicians. So, thanks for writing it. Thanks for being here to talk about it. SUSANNA GALLANI: Sure. My pleasure. BRIAN KENNY: Maybe we just get started by asking you, how did you hear about this? Why did you think this would be an interesting case to write? SUSANNA GALLANI: So there’s a combination of things that are happening in this space. First of all, the case is written with Rob Huckman and Suraj Srinivasan and also an external co-author, Asaf Bitton, who is at Ariadne Labs, and of course the conversation about AI in healthcare is everywhere. Everybody talks about AI in healthcare and what we can do or cannot do with that, and we were looking for our course, “Transforming Healthcare Delivery,” which is a second-year course here in the MBA program. We were looking to introduce more of this AI content in our course, because as you can imagine, the evolution of AI in healthcare is a big transformational drive, and we still don’t know exactly what it’s going to do, but we want to be up with it as it evolves, and so Rob had heard about this implementation, and I had known about that system. MGB, which is the organization that we study in the case, is not the only one that is implementing this technique and this technology. It’s pretty much everywhere right now, but MGB was doing it at a large scale, and of course, it’s a leading academic medical center. So it was interesting for us from a number of perspectives, because it layers up, in addition to the delivery of healthcare, there’s also the training and the research part, and so all of these aspects kind of converge into the problems that we address in the case. BRIAN KENNY: MGB being Mass General Brigham, just for our listeners who aren’t from the Boston area, it’s an enormous enterprise. I don’t know how many physicians they have on there. SUSANNA GALLANI: About 12,000. BRIAN KENNY: Okay. So just enormous. So this is an effort to scale something up in a very significant way, and I think oftentimes, when we think about AI in healthcare, we’re thinking about how it could accelerate cures or treatments of some kind. This, I found to be very interesting, because it was really about how they’re doing their work and how they can do their work more efficiently. Can you talk maybe a little bit about some of the challenges that clinicians face? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. So in a way, I have heard this described as the first innovation in healthcare that is improving care without asking the physicians to do more, and I want to extend this. This is not just physicians, it’s clinicians in general, because there’s nurses and there’s advanced practice providers as well. So this is not just a solution for physicians, narrowly defined, but this is the first time that we’re trying to do more and better in healthcare while taking work off the physician’s plate, the clinician’s plate, which is important, because we know we have a burnout problem. We have a wellbeing problem in healthcare. We have a turnover problem. If you listen to the first Friday of the month job report, healthcare jobs are always at the top of the list in terms of job creation, because there’s so much churn, and in addition, the needs for healthcare are increasing. Populations are aging. During COVID, we’re still experiencing the tail end of the COVID effect where people didn’t take as good care of themselves as they should have or they would have in other times. So there’s a lot of demand of physician’s time. In addition to that, we see that physicians don’t want to be physicians anymore, because it’s becoming a job that is away from their calling and it doesn’t let them really engage with the patients in the way that they would want, which is where this technology comes in, because it’s a way for them to really free themselves up from the monitor or the computer while they are sitting with the patient and really focus on the conversation like you and I are doing with each other. Imagine that as I’m saying these things, you were typing up things on your computer. It would feel very unnatural to me to be talking to you, and the same thing is in the office visit, and think about the experience of a patient. I always say healthcare is one of the most human experience we can have, and having the physician look into your eyes or listening, actively listening to what you’re saying and engaging in your conversation instead of doing a lot of what we do in the classroom, which is absorb what you just said and just transfer it to another medium helps a lot in the relationship with the patient. BRIAN KENNY: I hadn’t really thought about it until I read the case, but it occurred to me that my doctor does take a lot of notes while we’re having meetings, and that seems to me like a fairly recent thing, and I think it’s part of the administrative tasks of doctors have increased exponentially. We’ve got all these systems, the information needs to be in there. They’re trying to get better at sharing information across platforms so that your dermatologist can see what your primary care physician is doing and so on, but it reminds me a little bit of education. In elementary education, my wife is a teacher and the amount of administrative work that she has to do has increased quite a bit over the years. So it just sort of sparked that for me. Maybe you can describe what AI Scribe is and how it works. SUSANNA GALLANI: Yeah. It’s actually very simple as a concept. Obviously very complicated to implement it or to develop it, but basically this is how it works. When you see the doctor, they will probably ask for your permission to record your conversation with them, and it will be through an app on their phone. There’s nothing magical. There’s no invasive technology of any kind. BRIAN KENNY: They just put the phone on the table. SUSANNA GALLANI: Just put the phone on the table, and if you agree to that, that conversation will be recorded, and the recording will be decoded by an AI engine behind the scenes, and it will automatically populate the notes that the doctor would otherwise take during the visit. That’s all it is in a nutshell. Now, this unlocks a number of other things. First of all, there’s billing attached to that. So as the AI decodes what was said in the interaction, they also understand that the AI understands or identifies services that are being provided and can attach a billing code to it. So there’s a revenue generation aspect to it, which, by the way, the doctor would have to do anyway. So it’s not that we’re increasing the billing, not necessarily at least, and this is still a task that the doctor would have to do, and oftentimes, they end up doing after hours, the so-called “pajama time,” which is so dreadful, and it takes physicians away from their family time. BRIAN KENNY: So is it agentic in the sense that it just does it automatically? It takes agency? SUSANNA GALLANI: So the agentic part is what happens after with the data. At the moment, the core of this technology is just simply recording, transcribing, and interpreting in a way, in a way that you can create billing codes. The other thing is prescriptions. So if there is a drug that is being discussed in the interaction, the AI identifies that drug and puts it as a possibility for the prescription that the doctor might want to sign off. Now importantly, none of this is set in stone until the doctor actually signs the notes. So there’s still a requirement for the physician to go through the note and make sure that everything has been done correctly and approve it, otherwise the process is not complete. Shortly after, one of the main safety measures of this technology is that the recording is completely deleted. BRIAN KENNY: Okay, but the notes exist. The notes remain. SUSANNA GALLANI: The notes remain in the EHR of the organization that implements… BRIAN KENNY: Who was it at Mass General Brigham that decided they should try to do this? Were they trying to solve a particular problem or were they just aware? Was it the burnout that you mentioned? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. Predominantly that was the driving force. In fact, they actually stated very clearly in one of our interviews that that was exactly the reason. The main reason why they wanted to try this technology was to reduce the burnout among their clinicians. BRIAN KENNY: What were the sort of organizational challenges that they had as they tried to implement this? How was it received by the physicians? SUSANNA GALLANI: Variation as you can imagine. So initially they piloted with about 800 people that were self-selected, and so that went quite well. Although it did spark some controversy and some concerns. There are concerns on all sides. The physician, for example, sometimes is uncomfortable because they have to actually say more things out loud. BRIAN KENNY: Interesting. SUSANNA GALLANI: Because the AI will not transcribe something that it doesn’t hear. So it’s important that the physician kind of verbalizes their thinking, the drugs that we just mentioned. So if I don’t say, “I’m thinking about prescribing you whatever milligrams of this particular drug,” the AI has no idea that you’re thinking that. So in order for it to do the work for you, you have to actually verbalize actively during the visit, which is very different. BRIAN KENNY: Could be better for the patient, though, because you’re hearing a lot more than you might otherwise hear. SUSANNA GALLANI: It could, to the extent that the physician uses accessible language, and that’s one of the barriers that now the patient might actually be sitting next to somebody who’s speaking gibberish from what they can understand, because they are using technical terms and classification of stages of disease and things that might be obscure or maybe somewhat terrifying for the patient that doesn’t understand what’s being said. The other pushback was, “Well, when I read this note, this is not how I would write the note.” So there’s a level of comfort and acceptance and identity that is kind of missing when the note is automatically generated by a machine, and these notes are there to be read later on, and so if the physician doesn’t recognize their code, for lack of a better term, they resist to that. Say, “Well, this is not the information I would want to have in the note. Of course, you can imagine some physicians said there’s too much information, because the fact that Mrs. Jones recently lost her husband and feels lonely might be very significant for the primary care physician or for somebody in behavioral health, but maybe for the surgeon that is doing their appendectomy, is not important. So how do we tailor the amount of additional information that is non-clinical in nature? There’s variation in how much people desire to have in the note. So there’s a number of those additional challenges, and plus there’s change. There’s change and there’s trust that needs to happen. So the physician also doesn’t know what this information is going to do, and so there’s a little bit of resistance upfront. From the patient’s perspective, the most prominent type of challenge is accepting that that conversation is being recorded. So where is my data going? What is this data going to be used for? Is it still my data? Do I feel comfortable speaking to you naturally when I know it’s being recorded? BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, yeah, and I could see, with all the rules and regulations that we have in place to protect people’s information and identity, I could certainly understand that being a concern. There also might be the cynics out there who say that the hospitals are only doing this because it’s in their best self-interest from a legal perspective or a productivity perspective. Were there certain things that Mass General was sort of measuring as they went through this process? Sort of key metrics that they had in mind? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. They measured productivity for sure. That was one, but mostly what they were most interested in was their burnout measures, and during this pilot program, they actually noticed a significant drop in burnout. BRIAN KENNY: Really? SUSANNA GALLANI: People that had embraced this technology felt that they had more time for themselves, that they didn’t feel they had to be on their electronic medical records the whole time during the visit, that they could engage with the patient, but also their family time was freer and more under their control. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. SUSANNA GALLANI: So they definitely noticed an improvement there. BRIAN KENNY: Okay, and are they also using it…? A lot of people are doing telehealth visits now. That’s a way that people are seeing their doctors without having to go in person. Do they still use the technology even in a telehealth type? SUSANNA GALLANI: That was not in the case, but it would be very difficult for me to imagine that that doesn’t happen, because it’s even easier. We have recordings of our Zoom meetings, so why wouldn’t we use this in a telehealth situation? BRIAN KENNY: Were the physicians at all… And this may not have come up in the case either, but it makes me wonder if physicians were concerned that it would be used for review purposes or my performance is being gauged by what’s coming out in these notes. SUSANNA GALLANI: So the notes are not technically part of the performance evaluations. They are for the trainees, which is another important piece of the case, but the concern that the physicians voiced with us was, “You are now giving me back time. What are you going to ask me to do with that time?” BRIAN KENNY: Right. There’s the cynical piece I was trying to get out before. SUSANNA GALLANI: That was the cynical piece, exactly, and that is a valid concern, because in the case, we describe one physician remembered when they were given human scribes, but this human scribe had a cost, and so they had to produce more, so see more patients, in order to pay for the human scribe to be assigned to them, and so the same type of concern was underlying this implementation saying, “Yeah, that’s great. Now you’re giving me back time, but how are you going to take that time back in other ways?”, and so if we end up doing this, obviously the purpose of reducing burnout will just go out the window. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. You want to try and create some more life balance for these people who are working crazy hours all the time. You mentioned there were some early adopters, the people who sort of signed up for it voluntarily. What happened when they tried to do a more general rollout of it? Were there people who were refusing to use it? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. First of all, it was voluntary. So nobody is compelled to use it, but there is some sort of an expectation, because the second order effect, one of the second order effects of this technology is that it generates better data, and so imagine anything you want to do with clinical data, whether it’s research, whether it’s improving care, you want to have enough adoption, enough mass, to have that mass of data so that it’s consistent across an organization. That would make sense. Well, when they open it up for a larger group, which they still haven’t rolled it out to everyone, but they’re progressively getting there, one of the largest groups, which is the group that historically has the highest level of burnout is primary care. Once they opened it up to that group, it was opt-in, but for those people that chose to use the license, many of them, a significant amount did not pursue it. So they had the license, they just didn’t do it, and in fact, there was a rule that if you didn’t use it for three months, they would ask you why and potentially take it away, because it has a cost. There is a monthly fee for this license, which is person by person. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. I mean, we’re finding that the human side of AI, the getting people to adopt the tools and to use them, is highly variable. Some people are comfortable doing it. They think, “Oh, this is great. This is going to make my life easier.” Other people are thinking, “This is something new I have to do. I have to learn how to use this and what if it breaks or what if I don’t do it right?” What would you say to people who are listening, who are maybe going through the same kind of a process in their own organization? What are the sorts of things that you have to be thoughtful about as you’re trying to scale up this kind of platform? SUSANNA GALLANI: The first thing is trust. We talked about it. It’s really difficult for people to just embrace this. When this technology changes daily, it is, from a user’s perspective, an enormous black box. You put things into it, and you don’t really know what happens to those things. Things being information, sometimes sensitive, sometimes personal, and so having this expectation that everybody will jump at the opportunity to use it is probably misguided. BRIAN KENNY: Yes. SUSANNA GALLANI: So understanding what do you need to do to make it so that people trust what you’re going to do with that technology. Generally speaking, security of that technology, it is a black box for the leadership too. It’s not that we understand this infinitely well. BRIAN KENNY: We’re all learning. Yeah. SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes, and it’s changing so much that we tend to understand less and less instead of more and more in certain ways of what it does and what it’s capable of doing. So the first thing would be trust. The second thing would be use it to bring up the humanity of the workers and not to replace them, because there’s a huge fear. Now, this is less prominent in healthcare, I will say, than other industries, but we all are thinking about, “Is this thing going to take my job?”. So understanding that that is a concern that people have, even if it is buried in the back of your psychology, but especially if you’re bringing this technology in to help people—make it help people instead of making them afraid of it. BRIAN KENNY: We’ve done a couple of other cases that are similar in nature to this one. One was Pernod, the spirit company, and they were rolling out a platform, an AI platform, to their sales organization, and the benefit that they touted was essentially the same thing, which is, “You don’t need to worry about what’s going on underneath the hood with your customers. We’re giving you an opportunity to really develop a relationship with your customer. We’re giving you information that’s going to be helpful to them and help your relationship with them,” and this is reminding me of that, but even at that, there were a lot of salespeople who felt like it was going to cramp their style and people were going to be understanding their customers better than they were and then they wouldn’t need the salesperson anymore. It sounds like Mass General is really just trying to help these clinicians free them up of some of the tasks that they’ve had to do that are not patient focused, and really give them an opportunity to focus on the patient, which sounds like a win-win. SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. It’s exactly that. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. As we think about this particular case, which is sort of at the intersection of technology operations and management control, are there lessons that you can think of that this could offer more broadly outside of a healthcare setting, let’s say, like we were just talking about, who are considering AI for sort of thought intensive work, knowledge intensive work? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yeah, for sure. The fact that this is happening in healthcare is just the context. It is, as you were mentioning, happening in many other industries. So it’s not specific to healthcare. Obviously in healthcare, there is maybe a specific type of risk because we’re talking about healthcare data or healthcare information, which is a little bit different than maybe your purchasing information, which it still has to be treated with respect and the appropriate safety precautions, but I think healthcare is one level deeper than that. So in terms of generalizable lessons, well, one thing that is clear to me is that we don’t have to jump into this all at once, and especially when we’re not ready. This technology is changing way too fast to make it profitable or valuable if we jump in when we’re not ready, because by the time we get the organization to be ready, then that technology will be obsolete. So one of the things that they are pondering at Mass General Brigham, but I’m sure in other organizations too, is when is the right time to introduce this technology, and for whom? I mentioned the trainees before. So this, again, it’s a problem that we see in other industries as well. I actually had a recent conversation with a legal firm in England that is thinking about introducing AI for their work, but the problem they share with Mass General Brigham is, what are you going to do with the trainees? When you have a junior partner or an associate in a law firm, as well as a resident at Mass General, are you going to teach them to use AI or are you going to be AI independent, should that technology go away or not work? Or what are the opportunities that we’re missing in not training our trainees to use AI, but at the same time, what opportunities are we missing if we train them just to use AI?
