So either way, you have to consider the pros and cons of either choice. BRIAN KENNY: Right, and we know that one of the ways that AI learns is by consuming mass amounts of information. So it almost seems like when you scale this up, you really do need to get a high percentage of adoption, or you’re not going to get the full benefit of what the AI is capable of doing. It’s not going to learn as much as it could, and not as fast. So it’s pretty complicated to think about all the implications of that. This has been a great conversation, always is when you’re on the show. So thank you for being here. Just one last question would be, if you think about maybe one thing that our listeners should take away from this case, what would it be? SUSANNA GALLANI: I go back to the point I made earlier, which is think about the human that is using the technology, and use the technology to solve a problem that the human has before thinking that it’s just going to be great. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. SUSANNA GALLANI: We have to really be specific of what problem we’re trying to solve, and I think that Mass General Brigham did a great job in really pinpointing what was the purpose of that implementation. It was not just about… Certainly, they’re not unhappy to improve productivity, but the purpose, the driver of the decision was we have to reduce burnout, and that was their priority. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, that’s great. Susanna, thank you for joining me on Cold Call. SUSANNA GALLANI: Thank you. Thank you for having me. BRIAN KENNY: If you enjoy Cold Call, you might like our other podcasts: Climate Rising, Coaching Real Leaders, IdeaCast, Managing the Future of Work, Skydeck, and Think Big, Buy Small. Find them wherever you get your podcasts. If you have any suggestions or just want to say hello, we want to hear from you. Email us at coldcall@hbs.edu. Thanks again for joining us. I’m your host BRIAN KENNY, and you’ve been listening to Cold Call, an official podcast of Harvard Business School and part of the HBR Podcast Network.

item.title: 4 Steps to Transform the “Middle Office” with AI
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.49
Summary. Companies are spending heavily on AI, but many are still struggling to turn that investment into measurable business results. One reason is that they’re overlooking the middle office, where Recent evidence on AI adoption has revealed a sobering paradox. Economists who linked large-scale adoption surveys to administrative payroll records found that although most employers had rolled out AI tools in areas where AI should have the highest probability of impact, the effect on earnings and hours two years on was statistically indistinguishable from zero. Despite capable technology and workers reporting productivity gains, the promised benefits failed to materialize on the bottom line.

item.title: 3 Warning Signs Your Supplier Is in Distress
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.48
Summary. Suppliers to multinational corporations are under growing pressure from tariffs, logistics disruptions, compliance demands, and repeated global shocks, yet many buyers still rely on conventional Suppliers to multinational corporations are under growing strain. Tariffs, logistics disruptions, rising compliance demands, and repeated global shocks have raised the cost of serving large corporate buyers. Recent studies suggest that many large buyers pass at least part of these additional costs down to suppliers rather than sharing the burden. For many suppliers—especially smaller firms and those in developing economies—the problem is not simply that costs are rising. It is that they are often expected to absorb those costs while continuing to meet the same standards for quality, delivery, auditing, and compliance.

item.title: What Does AI Talent Look for in an Employer?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.20
Summary. The competition for AI talent remains strong—and expensive. How can companies possibly compete for skilled AI talent when Silicon Valley behemoths are offering salaries and signing packages The tech hiring landscape is in a state of flux. On one hand, companies like Meta have laid off thousands of employees, fueling concerns that artificial intelligence will eliminate many technical jobs. At the same time, many of the world’s largest technology firms are engaged in an intense scramble for AI talent. Despite the recent layoffs, Meta continues to aggressively pursue AI researchers and engineers with compensation packages reportedly worth millions of dollars; Elon Musk is creating an “elite unit” to recruit top AI engineers that reports directly to him; and Amazon recently announced plans to hire thousands of engineering employees and interns in 2026 (including, possibly some of the recently laid off Meta employees). As one AI company department head noted, “If I’m going to spend a billion dollars to build a model, $10 million for an engineer is a relatively low investment.”

item.title: Research: The Innovation Problems AI Can’t Solve
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.82
Summary. Generative AI can accelerate innovation, but the article argues that its default use often reinforces the human bottlenecks it is meant to solve. In ideation, models steer teams toward familiar Every innovation team now has the same tools: the same foundation models, similar prompt libraries. Yet the results are wildly uneven. Some teams report a creative renaissance while others report a flood of homogenized, forgettable ideas that all sound like they came from the same person. The reason isn’t which model you’re using. It’s that generative AI acts on the human bottlenecks buried inside that process. These bottlenecks respond to AI in different—sometimes opposite—ways.

item.title: The Innovation Strategy Most Companies Miss
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.60
Share Podcast The Innovation Strategy Most Companies Miss A conversation with Dartmouth’s Vijay Govindarajan and MIT’s Amos Winter on why designing for emerging markets before developed ones can yield benefits. Companies often build products for wealthy markets first and then try to adapt them for the rest of the world. But according to Dartmouth Tuck professor Vijay Govindarajan and MIT professor Amos Winter, designing for the toughest constraints first—whether that’s affordability, portability, or limited infrastructure—can lead to products that perform better everywhere. They explain how leaders can identify high-impact opportunities, uncover customer needs through deep field research, and design solutions that balance performance with cost. They also discuss why organizational mindset—not technology—is often the biggest obstacle to global innovation, and where AI can (and can’t) accelerate the design process. Together they wrote the book Global by Design: How to Create Innovations That Scale, Travel, and Transform. ALISON BEARD: I’m Alison Beard. ADI IGNATIUS: And I’m Adi Ignatius, and this is the HBR IdeaCast. ALISON BEARD: Adi, today we’re focusing on how to create products and services with widespread global appeal. But let me start with a question for you. If you wanted to make something that would be popular around the world, where would you start? ADI IGNATIUS: Well, I guess the obvious example is look for products and services that are successful in one market and try to adapt them to other ones. ALISON BEARD: Like Coca-Cola and different sizes and levels of sweetness or Nike running shoes with lighter mesh or a more basic iPhone? ADI IGNATIUS: Yeah, I mean they all seem to be doing pretty well. ALISON BEARD: Yes, they are. But our guests today say that a lot of companies actually fail when they try to adapt goods in this way, and there might be more value in taking a different approach. Amos Winter, professor at MIT, and Vijay Govindarajan, professor at Dartmouth’s Tuck School of Business, argue that there’s an advantage to tackling international markets first, using innovation to solve the toughest problems most efficiently there, versus starting with offerings for wealthy markets and then watering them down. Winter and Govindarajan, who goes by Vijay, are authors of the book Global by Design: How to Create Innovations That Scale, Travel, and Transform. Here’s our conversation ALISON BEARD: Why should leaders today take a global perspective on innovation from the very beginning? AMOS WINTER: Well, I think you can look at it from a number of opportunity standpoints. One, business. The greatest economic growth in the world right now is in emerging markets. And so that, in addition to the large populations, creates amazing business opportunities. But I think the other opportunity is from a social perspective. All the most compelling issues facing humanity really present most compellingly in low resource settings; you can make that positive humanitarian impact and make a viable business at the same time. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. VG, you and a few coauthors introduced the idea of reverse innovation about 15 years ago now, I think. How does this work build on that? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I would call it reverse innovation 2.0, because the reverse innovation that I pioneered 15 years ago, it was really looking at it from a business strategy point of view. When I accidentally met Amos, I realized reverse innovation has actually two sides. There is a business strategy side, but then there is an engineering side. And I said, wouldn’t it be nice to bring these two perspectives together? That’s what led to global by design. ALISON BEARD: And you hear the phrase global by design. And the first thought or challenge that comes to my mind is that if you’re trying to design for everyone, for the world, you’re not really designing for anyone. So, how do you address that worry? AMOS WINTER: Well, a big part of making globally attractive solutions is figuring out what core values are shared across many different markets. So, I suspect people don’t worry about iPhones selling everywhere or Coca-Cola selling everywhere. There’s commonalities between different user groups that you can utilize. And then there’s modifications to products that are relatively small that you can make so they best align with different markets to maybe change price point or change feature set. But that core value that’s universally appreciated still persists between markets. ALISON BEARD: And do you think that companies still try to target primarily wealthy markets first and then are unsuccessful in adapting to less developed countries? AMOS WINTER: Yeah, very much so. Part of that is historical in that really all product design for the last 200 or so years has been focused on U.S.-European type markets. Part of that I think is still because of a bit of a stigma in that companies can look at poor countries and think like, “Oh, those are poor people. They can’t afford to buy products,” which isn’t true at all. They’re also consumers. But I would say more and more multinationals are realizing that the big economic gains in the world are happening in emerging markets. But even if you see that opportunity, actually realizing it is challenging because now you’re designing for different population sets than we’ve historically designed for. So, if you’re say an American engineer sitting in Wisconsin, how do you get into the mindset of a mother of five in India? That’s a totally different demographic. And so, a lot of this book also is about expanding the perspective of innovators so you can see these new opportunities and see the requirements they present. And so, you can design effectively for them because you’re better informed about the differences in the markets and what they demand for solutions. VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: If you really look back, innovation always started in rich countries and the reason is rich countries have resources and rich countries have consumers who can afford to buy those innovative products which are premium priced. The reason this is important is there is a dominant logic that develops inside the organization. So, the biggest barrier to reverse innovation is not technology. It’s not that people don’t understand emerging markets are important. It is the dominant logic. Companies are so entrenched in terms of the systems, the structures, the processes, the incentives, the capabilities. It is extremely difficult. It’s like moving the Titanic 180 degrees. That is the real problem. It’s a mindset issue. It’s not a technology issue. ALISON BEARD: And so, while there have been innovators in these emerging markets that have developed solutions for those markets, you’d like to see more cross-pollination? AMOS WINTER: Well, coming back to why this is reverse innovation 2.0 is that emerging markets present new challenges than what we’ve designed for in wealthy markets. And the situation I’m constantly in as an innovator, and I think many multinationals are facing in emerging markets, is that consumers there still demand a certain level of performance in the products that they buy. Nobody wants semi-clean water, nobody wants a semi-functional toilet. There’s baseline performance. But those consumers may not be able to afford to pay for the existing solutions at the price point that’s already in wealthy markets. And so, you’re faced with this conundrum of how do we provide that high performance at a low cost to engage emerging markets? And what’s powerful about this in the reverse part of this is that if you can actively focus on emerging markets first and figure out that high performance, low cost solution, you end up creating something very valuable. Valuable enough to be adopted in emerging markets, but also valuable enough to potentially disrupt wealthy markets by providing just as good or better performance at a much lower price. VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: And I would say there are three forces that are coming together. That’s why it’s also a place for entrepreneurs. The three forces that are coming together is the rich country, the growth has slowed down. The second is in the emerging markets, as you rightly said, there are smart companies which are innovating and they could potentially disrupt multinationals in their own home market. So, the second threat these companies are facing is, hey, we cannot ignore emerging markets because those giants from emerging markets can come and disrupt us. And the third is affordability. Affordability crisis has hit even in a rich country like the U.S. People can’t afford to buy healthcare. They can’t afford to get good education. They can’t afford to buy grocery. So, we need affordable solutions in the U.S. And where best to find them is in poor countries. ALISON BEARD: So, let’s dig into some practical advice. First, how do you recognize global by design opportunities? AMOS WINTER: So, we talk about in the book three merits that you really need to check yourself whether you’re satisfying before you launch into a new initiative. And so, the first of those is what we call problem merit. And that’s a gut check on understanding, are you solving a problem that’s going to impact ideally a large number of people in a meaningful way? And ideally with a business opportunity behind it. So, if you’re successful in making that impact, there’s a viable business to scale and sustain a solution. And that problem merit identification goes beyond just saying, “Oh, people need clean water.” It’s really distilling what are the metrics of performance that must be satisfied for a successful solution. So, it may be volume of water or what contaminants you have to get out or the price point people are willing to pay. Then the second area of merit we have to evaluate is what we call innovation merit. And that’s a gut check on is innovation actually required to solve this problem? Because there’s many problems where you can just give money through philanthropy or maybe just adapt something in a slight way for it to work in a new market. So, you have to convince yourself, does actually something new have to be created to solve this problem? And then the third area of merit we talk about that you have to satisfy is what’s called value merit. And that’s all about aligning value propositions. So, one, people are going to support your work, creating a solution. And two, people are going to support the dissemination of your solution, which typically means people are going to make money by using your product or at least derive value from it and people are going to make money by producing and selling it. We represent it in a Venn diagram. When you look at that Venn diagram and you say, “Hey, I have a compelling problem. It needs innovation. And boy, if I’m successful, it’s going to deliver a lot of value.” That not only shows you have a compelling opportunity in a resource constrained market, but also that you likely have a reverse innovation that’s going to deliver value globally because it creates high performance at low cost. ALISON BEARD: And if you’ve identified a problem that is large and could be tackled in any market where innovation is required and you might be able to create value, how do you then narrow it so that you can focus on something specific enough to design around? AMOS WINTER: There’s a very important concept that we talk about called being a tempered dreamer. And that is all about recognizing your own limitations as an innovator and figuring out the niche where you can make the largest impact. And so, I’ll give you an example. The most inspiring professional meeting I’ve ever had in my life was with a mission director for Gaza and West Bank. I met him in Israel and he said, “Look, we need solutions for farmers to grow better crops, to have water, to have energy. We need that now in order to prevent extremism.” Because if people have these more promising livelihoods by being like a farmer, they’re less likely to join a terrorist group. And this resonated with me very powerfully from a patriotic standpoint. I care about global stability and insecurity in the U.S. I’m not a policymaker, but I do create irrigation technology, desalination technology. And I realized that I can play my part by creating those technologies to help global stability, even though I’m not a government employee. And so, I think innovators have to figure out what skills do they have, what resources do they have, what is tractable to realize in a reasonable amount of time in order to still be creative and ambitious, but narrow down where can I make an impact? ALISON BEARD: VG, do you have an example from the corporate world where you’ve seen leaders or executives identify those three things that we’re talking about, the problem merit, innovation, merit, value merit, but then narrow down the problem in a way that it’s something they can tackle? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: When I went to work for GE Healthcare, I was sent to India. And what we quickly realized was there was almost 60% of Indians who did not have access to healthcare devices that we have in the U.S. So, we found a very huge problem that can be solved, which is how do you give access to high quality medical imaging products to these 60% of Indians? Then we said, “That’s like boiling the washer. That’s so big.” So, we said, “Let us focus on one small s egment within this, which is EKG, the electrocardiogram,” because as it turns out, the bulk of the people who die in India, they’re because of heart attack. So, EKG is a very important thing that is missing. So, we said, how do we create an EKG machine which has got the features of the $20,000 EKG machine we have in the US, but at a price point Indians can afford, which is $400. So, now we have come to a very specific problem which requires innovation to close the gap. We went from big to something that we can actually solve. ALISON BEARD: So, let’s talk about that process of innovation. You talk about three parts, elucidating requirements, designing a solution, and then scaling locally and globally. But there are steps within these phases, so I want to pull them apart and sort of tackle each one at a time. When it comes to elucidating requirements, how should innovators work to understand all of the stakeholders’ needs and goals? So, Amos, in your example, it’s those farmers in Gaza. Vijay, in your example, it’s the doctors trying to do medical testing, heart testing in India. AMOS WINTER: So, it’s always valuable to map out who are all the stakeholders that are going to play a role in the dissemination of your eventual product and understand the power that they have on your success or failure. So, you can usually just do that as a mental exercise and map it out like, oh, the government’s going to subsidize this or there’s a retailer who’s going to do this. And once you map those out, nothing beats going to talk to them. If you can travel and go interact with them and talk with them and build rapport and understand their needs and desires and requirements, you get a much clear insight about what value propositions are going to resonate with them and promote them to adopt your solution. And the big thing about elucidating requirements is figuring out what problem are you actually trying to solve and intentionally putting yourself in a necessity as a mother of invention situation. We talk about this idea of primary and secondary requirements. So, a lot of innovation is very much driven by primary requirements and a lot of academic research is driven by primary requirements as well. So, you want to make the lighter or faster or more efficient gizmo. And a lot of that innovation work forgets that, well, if the gizmo is adopted, it has to be cheap enough and people have to like how it looks and it has to last long enough. So, if you intentionally, as you’re elucidating requirements, try to form as comprehensive a set as possible of the primary and secondary, you put yourself in the best position for success and not missing some of those critical, but maybe hidden secondary requirements too late in the game. VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I think once we decided we wanted to create a value product, what we did was a small portion of our innovation team went and lived in rural India for two months. The mandate I gave the team was don’t focus on the solution. Focus on the problem. Independent of the solution. And when they lived there, they observed the villagers. They talked to the villagers. They did deep ethnographic research and came out with four important requirements. One is affordability. The machine can’t cost more than $400. That’s all they could afford. Second, it has to be portable because there was no hospital, no imaging center in these places. You got to carry the device. Third, it has to work not out of house electricity because most of these villagers didn’t have electricity. And fourth, it should be easy to repair because these villagers didn’t have places where you could go repair them, easy to operate and easy to repair. So, they just came back with those requirements. It is by actually living in rural India. ALISON BEARD: And how long do you spend on this elucidating requirements phase before moving on to actually prototyping and testing solutions? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I think corporations want to move fast, but the same time, do it right. Fast and fail is no good. So, I think this EKG project took us 18 months from beginning to end until we came up with the solution, which was hugely commercially successful. So, the design requirements took us three months. But as Amos said, it’s not a black and white, it’s about we got to get this right because this is the foundation on which everything relies. So, get the requirements right. ALISON BEARD: Okay. So, now to that design phase, could one of you just briefly walk me through an effective structured design process? AMOS WINTER: Yeah. So, your very general design process is first understand the problem you’re trying to solve and generate a list of requirements, then generate multiple ideas for viable solutions. People tend to kind of lock themselves into favorite ideas oftentimes and just think of one really cool one. If you think of a cool idea, force yourself to take a step back and say, “What are some other ways I could solve this?” Then you have to evaluate those ideas and down select to what the most compelling concept is. Then you go into a detailed design phase where usually a concept has multiple parts to it. So, if you’re designing a consumer product, there may be the product, there may be the packaging, there may be marketing. And so, you work out all of those different parts and then you integrate them together into a fully integrated final solution. And so, a lot of times you want to take a mock-up or it might be kind of a kludgy prototype, but it actually works correctly. Take that back to stakeholders. Get a gut check. Is it working before you really polish a product? So, you want to do some testing to know you’re on the right track and then go into a deeper validation where you may do a field pilot or a randomized control trial before you actually go to market. ALISON BEARD: How is AI helping with all of this? AMOS WINTER: I think it’s an incredibly powerful tool in terms of aggregating a lot of information really quickly. I’m finding it amazing as a designer so I can get a whole background on a field of work very, very quickly and understand the lay of the land. What AI is not equipped well-to-do right now is directly solve the type of problems we’re talking about in this book. Because one, a lot of these problems deal with information that’s not formally recorded. And so, you’re dealing with people’s emotions and also math and physics and economics, and you have to integrate those together in an interesting way. Second is I work in physical technologies and AI still has a lot of knowledge gaps around the physical world in nuances around weather or friction or all these little things that we as people perceive. AI doesn’t have the feel of touch and insight in the same way as people do. And then the third is that so much of the work I do personally and that we talk about in this book depends on building rapport and talking face-to-face with stakeholders. And so, when you get to know stakeholders, that can influence how you actually design things because you get insights in how they’re thinking. That relationship building is still so important in the type of design that I do in design for really global products. ALISON BEARD: We’ve been talking a lot about products, but does this global by design process work for services, business models, internal practices as well? AMOS WINTER: Good design is good design no matter the field. So, one example we put in the book is about how McDonald’s figured out how to make hamburgers really quickly and cheaply. And so, before they designed a building and installed the kitchen, they mocked up the layout of the building on a tennis court. And they got a bunch of high school kids who would be their future employees to act out all the actions of filling drinks and flipping burgers. And they were able to figure out the flow of the process without any physical infrastructure. And the same goes with policy. You need to figure out your design requirements before you implement a policy. So, that’s something we really try to bring out is that the principals in the book are relevant across fields. ALISON BEARD: Let’s now talk about scaling. How has the fact that you’ve followed this global by design process made it more likely that you will be successful in adapting your initial product to deliver around the world? Is the idea that if you follow these steps, that shift to scaling locally and globally will be inherently easier? AMOS WINTER: I think it comes down to reducing uncertainty and actively always trying to put yourself in that necessity is the mother of invention situation. Too much innovation is a game of playing darts blindfolded. And I think academia is guilty of this, is that you throw a lot of darts, you hit some bullseyes. But if you take that time and care and effort to aim, you may not hit a bullseye, but you’re much more likely to hit it. And so, that time and care and effort goes into the define your requirements. If you know what problem you’re trying to solve, you’re more likely to solve it. Designing a solution, well, if you go through a diligent process to create something you’re confident in, rather than just conjuring something willy-nilly, it’s more likely to be successful. And if you test it with actual people who would adopt it, then you get good feedback. Going both local and globally, there’s some strategy you can really identify to understand what features are going to be demanded in different markets. What is the core value that translates across markets? How do I correctly segment my products so I’m not cannibalizing? So, that’s foresight, which again is aiming those darts so you don’t fall into an unknown that’s a trap that ends up killing your product. ALISON BEARD: VG, what’s the biggest challenge that you see companies run into when they try to scale? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I think the biggest and the most problematic ones for multinationals is they’re afraid these high performance, low cost solutions will disrupt their premium priced products in the US. Because if you’re going to bring a $400 ECG machine into the US where you are currently selling $20,000 ECG machine, if the $400 start replacing the $20,000, your profit margin disappears. So, this is the biggest worry companies have. The way to overcome this is not to see this as substituting the $20,000 ECG machine, but it is about transforming the whole industry. And you will continue to have market for $20,000 ECG machine. Maybe the market may decline slightly, but the overall industry will expand phenomenally because of this. So, you have to think of this as transforming the space as compared to one-to-one substitution. This is the biggest mindset issue. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. More generally, how should leaders find the most innovative people in their companies to tackle these kinds of projects? AMOS WINTER: I think it comes down to equipping people and giving them the opportunities to think about problems from their own vantage point and creating a culture of asking about that and valuing their input. Because a forklift operator in a warehouse is going to really understand the problems of moving stuff around a warehouse. So, if you create a culture of saying, “Hey Joe, what’s causing you a lot of time and agony? Or do you have an insight of how we could speed things up?” That person’s going to give a lot of great feedback. And so, I see this happen a lot actually in companies around the world in that they try to isolate innovation to a certain group of people. And what can be most toxic is if the innovation has to come top down because you’ll get the business leaders who are amazing, wonderful, smart people, but they’re lacking a lot of context and perspective about problems like on the ground or on the shop floor. So, if you can bring together those perspectives, it makes you much more powerful as an innovator. And I say this in every class I teach too. The most powerful tool a designer has is perspective. ALISON BEARD: How do you do this at an under-resourced company? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I say resources are the biggest impediment to global by design because then you have resources. You substitute resources for thinking. So, you throw money at the problem. In fact, I would say to the CEOs that I work with, give your innovation team less resources. When you give people less money, they actually do out of the box thinking. I would also say it is always very good to put in the innovation team at least a few people. Of course, you want domain experts and so on and so forth, at least a few people who are mavericks. And my definition of mavericks, they satisfy two criteria. One, they always talk about crazy things. Second, they’re an organizational nightmare to manage. Put them on the team because they are more likely to come up with totally out of the box ideas. ALISON BEARD: What would you two like executives to go out and do today, this week, to start thinking in a more global by design way? AMOS WINTER: You know what I love, Alison, is I meet companies all the time that have a sense of opportunity. They see that there’s new markets they could grow into, often emerging markets. They want to do it. And many of these companies want to make a positive social impact too, and they’re just unsure of how to approach that opportunity. So, I guess the advice to executives is I would say dream big about where your business can grow and how you can really harness the collective purchasing power of these massive, rapidly growing markets around the world. And I think maybe the humanitarian side of me would say too, can you do it while making a positive impact in the world? And my answer would be, yeah, absolutely. ALISON BEARD: You’re anticipating my last question, which is in what areas of business or society do you most want to see this thinking applied? You talk about wicked problems and the fact that we have a lot of them. So, what’s your ambition for where we should all be looking? VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: I say there are three sectors which are absolutely craving for the ideas that we have in the book. Education, healthcare, and energy. These are three foundational sectors on which economies get built, and we need affordable, high quality solutions in all the three. ALISON BEARD: All right, listeners, get started. Amos, Vijay, thank you so much for talking with me today. I’ve learned a lot. AMOS WINTER: Thank you, Alison. VIJAY GOVINDARAJAN: Thank you so much. ALISON BEARD: That’s MIT professor Amos Winter and Dartmouth Tuck Professor Vijay Govindarajan. They’re co-authors of the book, Global by Design: How to Create Innovations That Scale, Travel, and Transform. Vijay also has a LinkedIn weekly column on innovation. Next week, Adi will dig into how to build a sustainable long-term career in today’s uncertain world. If you found this episode helpful, please share it with a colleague and be sure to subscribe and rate IdeaCast in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, consider subscribing to Harvard Business Review. You’ll get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive insider newsletter, and unlimited access to HBR online. Just head to hbr.org/subscribe. Thanks to our team, senior producer Mary Dooe, and senior production editor, Kristin Murphy Romano. And thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. We’ll be back with a new episode on Tuesday. I’m Alison Beard.

item.title: Living and Working in the Age of Longevity
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.50
Share Podcast Living and Working in the Age of Longevity A conversation with London Business School professor Lynda Gratton on the new rules for long-term career planning. People are living longer, healthier lives than ever before. But many of our assumptions about executive careers—from climbing the corporate ladder to retiring at 65—haven’t caught up. London Business School professor Lynda Gratton says we need a new way of thinking about work and life, and argues that traditional career paths are giving way to more flexible, multi-stage journeys that require greater personal agency, continuous learning, and a long-term perspective. She explains why leaders should think of their lives less as a ladder and more as a fabric they actively weave over time, and offers up practical advice for balancing productivity and personal well-being, preparing for career pivots before they’re necessary, and developing the skills that will matter most in an AI-powered future. Gratton is the author of the upcoming book Living the 100-Year Life: How to build a career that lasts and a life you love. ADI IGNATIUS: I’m Adi Ignatius. ALISON BEARD: I’m Alison Beard, and this is the HBR IdeaCast. ADI IGNATIUS: So, Alison, as you know, my father passed away recently at the age of 104. He stayed sharp pretty much up to the end and that is relevant to our conversation today. ALISON BEARD: Yes, I am so sorry about his passing. He was such an amazing man. Not only a father to you and several highly accomplished siblings, but secretary of the Navy in the 1960s and then a successful businessman. ADI IGNATIUS: Well, thank you, I appreciate that. But my point in mentioning that is that a lifespan like his is becoming less and less rare. We’re living longer, we’re living healthier, there are many more centenarians, and that has profound implications for work and for our careers. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. I don’t know if I personally want to work until I’m 100, but I do think that old notions about retiring at the age of 60 or 65 don’t really make sense anymore. Many of us can be very productive and lead valuable work lives for much longer. ADI IGNATIUS: Yeah, exactly. And I think management has to adapt to this, individuals do, too. And our guest today, Lynda Gratton, has excellent advice on how people should think about their career options over a relatively long time span. Gratton is a professor of management practice at London Business School and is author of the new book Living the 100-Year Life, which builds on her earlier book co-written with Andrew Scott called The 100-Year Life. She has a lot to share about how we can plan our careers differently in light of our longevity and what organizations need to do to keep up. Here’s our conversation. LYNDA GRATTON: Thank you very much for having me. ADI IGNATIUS: So for our audience, I want to talk mostly about the implications of this on work and career. But before that, at a high altitude, how should we think about all of our very possibly centenarian lives, about the pace, the expectations, about the pursuit of happiness? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, I would say that we’ve always wanted to have more years. Anyone, if you ask anyone, “What would you like, would you like more years?” Everybody’s going to say, “Yes, of course I’d love more years.” And actually, right now we have that opportunity. We have the opportunity to do what our parents and grandparents didn’t do, which is to live a great deal longer. But of course, that’s complex for us in many ways because some of the ways that our institutions are formed, the assumptions we have about our lives, all of those are based on the idea of a three-stage life. You are educated, you work and you retire at 60 or 65, and then you live maybe for 10 years. But now I’m saying you could live to 100, everything else has to be remade. And this generation of people, whatever age you are right now, all of us are learning how to do that, whether we’re 70, 50 or 30. We’re actually learning what does it take when you live a 100-year life? I’m incredibly optimistic about it. I think it’s a wonderful thing. But it does mean that we have to change the way we think about our lives. ADI IGNATIUS: So I tend to be somebody who lives to work as opposed to works to live. How should somebody like me think about my working identity in this era, in this new world? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, the economics of a 100-year life is that you need to make money in some form or another probably into your 70s or even your 80s unless you’ve saved 20% of your income from the time that you started work, or maybe 15%, and very few of us have done that. And so- ADI IGNATIUS: I have not. LYNDA GRATTON: You haven’t. No, neither did I. So it’s a sort of a financial reality, but I don’t think it’s really that that makes it important. I think what really makes it important is the idea that work can be such a wonderful thing for humans. It brings so much things. It develops our skills, it allows us to meet new people. Especially of different generations, which I think is really important as you age. It allows us to have new experiences. So I am all for working into our 70s and even possibly our 80s. But then of course, to do that, you’ve got to think about, well, how are you going to do that and what sort of work do I do? And that I think is the question that lots of people are asking right now. ADI IGNATIUS: Well, and is the career ladder - I mean, the blueprint of the working life now for younger people is very different from when I entered the workforce, where you worked for one company or maybe a couple for long stretches. Is the career ladder obsolete? Is that not the way to think about work and career now? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, if you think about a ladder, you can imagine yourself climbing up that ladder. And what does it require? Well, it requires a lot of energy, but not really a lot of agency because all you have to do is put one hand on the next rung. What I think is happening now is that we have to use our personal agency and that’s something that’s entirely different from what we’ve had to do in the past. And there’s lots of ways of thinking about, lots of metaphors to think about your life. The one that I use is the idea of weaving your life, where you’re the weaver and you’re weaving your life. And every day, you’re weaving a life that creates both productivity for you, but also nurture. And those two elements to your life are so important because you need both of them, but the reality is that they’re hard to deliver at every point in our time. ADI IGNATIUS: So I think many of us are relatively passive, have exercised relatively little agency in our careers because we’ve been headhunted, somebody has come out. Or we need a job and we apply to 10 places and one says yeah. There’s a passivity to that. You’re really urging us to have that kind of agency and that’s important if you’re going to live until you’re 70 or live until you’re 100. But why are we so bad at that and how do we get better at that? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, I think fundamental to the career ladder was this idea that the transaction between you and the organization is that you were a child and the organization was an adult. It was sort of an adult-child thing where the organization said, “Don’t worry, I’ll look after you,” and you as a child said, “Okay, I’ll do the best I can. I’ll put one hand above the other on the ladder.” We’ve actually moved to something which is much more adult to adult. The adult in the sense of what organizations require of you and what they say they want in the deal they describe, but also adult in terms of how we as individuals make commitments, understand ourselves, decide in a reflective way what we want. And I think we’ve been moving … I wrote a book years ago called The Democratic Enterprise, which described the beginnings of that shift and I think that shift is now really, really on its way. And being an adult means you have to be proactive and that’s something that I talk about a lot in the book. How do you gather your proactivity? ADI IGNATIUS: So you write that we should all try to weave our 100-year life into our 20s, into our 30s, into our 40s and 50s. What do you mean exactly by that? LYNDA GRATTON: What I love about the metaphor of weaving a life is that when you think about your life as a loom, there’s a past, all the stuff you’ve woven already. There’s where you are right now with the choices you and I are making right this moment in our lives. And then we have the future, which of course is hard for us to imagine, but we do have a sense of what our future self is. And I think that’s a really profoundly human idea. And across that loom, there are threads that help us to be productive. Threads like mastery or knowing, cooperating or amplifying, which is the way we work with AI. And they’re really important, but if you just have that then you burn out. So the threads of nurture are also really important. Threads which are about our relationships, intimacy, friendship. But also, how we manage energy, both in terms of calming ourselves and indeed, in terms of creating adventure. And those eight threads are there in our lives at all times and it’s we who choose which to strengthen and which to leave fragile. Now often, we don’t make that choice consciously and sometimes we’ll regret those choices, but each one of us has got to that stage at any point in time in our life. ADI IGNATIUS: So we’ve been talking mostly about how individuals should think about their lives and their careers. But I want to move it into the institutional level now because I don’t think our laws, or our protocols or our practices are in step with everything you’re writing about. That we, our institutions do basically shuffle people off when they’re 60 or 65 because they’re too old, or they’re too highly paid or don’t know the new technologies. That, it seems to me that needs to be resolved, that that’s a fundamental conflict in this era where we are living, not only living longer, but we’re healthy and we can be productive. We need to be productive. And workplace laws that are probably 100-years-old. LYNDA GRATTON: Yeah, absolutely. We just haven’t yet designed institutions for longevity, we really haven’t. We’re beginning to design them for technology, but we still haven’t designed them for longevity. And that’s going to be difficult because it means letting go of a whole lot of assumptions that came with a career ladder about promotion being the only way up, about people staying a long period of time and never coming back again, or not coming in at the age of 30, but every step, every step is a step that you take. You can’t take sabbaticals, you can’t work flexibly. So there’s a whole bunch of stuff that has to change. And when you see change happening at the level of a society, individuals are always the first thing to change and then institutions eventually catch up. And I think we’re in that stage right now. I have colleagues who are working into their 80s, other companies have. I’ve got friends who are taking sabbaticals at different times in their life. There’s fathers who are doing parental leave in a way that they never did before. So the world of freelancers. You remember the HBR article that Diane Gherson and I wrote about the huge increase in freelancers. So we’re already seeing a lot of those early signs that actually organizations, perhaps not realizing that that’s what they’re doing, they are becoming more flexible about the way they employ people. And that really helps anyone who wants a portfolio life or a multi-stage life. ADI IGNATIUS: Can many of us afford the portfolio life or is that … The portfolio life sounds great to me at my stage, at this stage in my career. A portfolio life, my kids, young people I know, there’s no health insurance, there’s no … The portfolio life is a constant hustle. Is that what we need to adapt to? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, it could be. There’s lots of different ways of running a life and my thinking is that there might be times when you just want to stay with a company. There might be times when you want multi-stages and a multi-stage means that you stay with a company and then perhaps you start your own business, perhaps you do something else. So the variety is in the sequence, but the variety can also be horizontal, like in a portfolio, where you try and do all these things at the same time. And as you rightly say, Adi, that’s hard to pull off. And we think about people in their 60s and 70s being able to pull it off. But interestingly, when I asked my MBA students, “How many of you anticipate having some sort of portfolio life,” a load of them put up their hands. And then I said, “Well, what age do you think this is going to happen?” And they said, “Right now.” I thought, “Wow, that’s really interesting. They’re seeing it as a life choice from the beginning, not something that you build up.” Now, why are they thinking that? Well, I think that that HBR article that Diane and I wrote about freelancers gives you a little bit of an understanding of that. Because actually, if you build skills, if you work as a freelancer, if you start your own business, you actually can begin to build a portfolio much earlier than we had imagined would be possible. Now, that’s not to say that lots of people are going to build portfolios, or it’ll be the majority, but I think what we are going to see is a lot more variety about the fabric of our life. When you say it’s a ladder that everybody’s climbing, everybody’s climbing the ladder together and they’re all going up in the same way. When you say it’s a fabric that we’re weaving, actually your pattern could be so different from my pattern. And that’s what I think we’re going to see, a lot more choice, a lot more variety. But of course, that brings the question of personal agency right to the center again. ADI IGNATIUS: So that, that sounds great in terms of personal development. Why should managers care about this? Why, as we as individuals weave our lives and our work lives, do leaders need to change their mindset to appreciate that and absorb that? Or how should leaders respond to this and in what way is this in the interest of managers who are trying to run a business? LYNDA GRATTON: Yeah. Well, I just ran a pilot program this year with three very large companies, with the executives from three large companies. It was a 10-week program and the question was how do we think about supporting longer lives? And actually, the results of that program were really fascinating because what it showed … Well, the first thing it showed is that there is real burnout going out in 40-year-olds. In fact, I wrote an hbr.org piece about this, the pivotal 40s. So if you’re a manager and you’re worried about burnout in your 40s, you need to be worried about longevity. Because what’s happening is people are getting to their 40s and going, “Really, is this it? Is this another 20 years of this? I’m out.” Either physically or metaphorically out. And you don’t want that. So I think that it’s in your best interest. The second reason why managers should care about this is that in a time of AI where AI knows so much, wisdom, networks, judgment are really important and that develops with experience, with age. And I think thirdly, we know there’s so many advantages for multi-generational teams to work together. So there’s all sorts of good reasons why you should think about, openly about employing people at whatever age they’re at and not really thinking too much or worrying too much about are they over 50, are they over 60, are they over 70. And if you’ve got a really good performance management system, you can do that. So at London Business School, for example, we have a couple of faculty who teach into their 80s. Why are they there? Well, in part because we have a feedback system with our students where every student has to rate every professor at the end of the semester and that’s made public to all of the other professors. And let me tell you, if you’re not really on your game, you don’t need anyone to tell you that. And so as long as you have really good performance management, people know whether they’re still performing. You don’t need to use age as a proxy. ADI IGNATIUS: Right. You probably also have tenure though, that is part of the explanation. LYNDA GRATTON: Yeah, we do have tenure and that is part of the explanation. But actually, I think that pride is even, well, not always in every case, but often pride beats tenure. ADI IGNATIUS: So you mentioned AI. And I’m sure a lot of listeners are thinking about, “Wait, wait, wait, wait, wait. Maybe this all makes sense, but AI changes everything.” Our assumption has been AI wipes out entry level work. It wipes out a lot of other work. And the conversation shifts to, instead of this work ethic that you’ve talked about, that maybe we redefine the definition of happiness in life, which is not necessarily I derive happiness and satisfaction from work, but maybe there’s another measurement. And maybe I work less and have hobbies more because AI is doing all the work. How do you think about how AI changes, accelerates, decelerates the phenomenon you’re writing about? LYNDA GRATTON: When I was naming the eight threads, and certainly the four threads of productivity, I created the thread called amplification, which I certainly wouldn’t have had 10 years ago. And the amplification is the thread that connects us to AI, that actually brings us together. And what we know about AI right now, but of course this will change, is that if you’re experienced and have good judgment, it will increase your productivity by six-times. So one of the questions we have to ask, as you are saying now is, well, if I’m going to be six-times more productive, what do I do with all that time and how do I spend it? Do I just do more of the same or do I do different things? And the threads in a way, particularly the nurture threads like adventure and calm, are a real invitation to do things differently. I think the second thing about AI is that we can anticipate that a proportion of our jobs will be taken by AI every year. And so weaving the fabric is a lot better than running up a career ladder because when you’re weaving a fabric, you’re already transitioning, pivoting. You’ve already got self-awareness. You’re already thinking about, “What do I need? Who am I? Where am I? What are the promises I want to make to my future self?” So it’s a much more robust way of thinking about a life than thinking it simply as a career ladder. ADI IGNATIUS: So I want to ask you for really practical advice because we are HBR after all. Starting with individuals, what are some first steps people can take to start thinking about all of this in a healthy way? And when I say all of this, it is you are likely to live longer than you have imagined, you’re likely to be productive maybe longer than you had anticipated, and your future happiness and self-worth depends on getting this right. What are some of the first things people can do right now? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, I think the first thing they can do, as you suggest, is actually acknowledge that they could live to 100. That’s a big first step. Secondly, you can really ask yourself, “Where am I now?” One of the things that I did with the book is to build a diagnostic to help people work that out. You can go to the website, it’s freely available, and you can download your report. Because I do think knowing where you are now is really important. So for example, in my case when I started working on this, I realized that my thread of friendship was pretty fragile. I’d spent so much time working, building mastery and it really made me think, “Okay, if I want to live to 100 and have a great life, I know friendship’s really important.” And that leads to the third point, which is to say small actions and experiments. I don’t think anyone pivots … I couldn’t say today, “Okay, I’m going to have a great friend by tomorrow.” But what I could do is to say, “You know, I could talk to one of my friends this evening for eight minutes,” it turns out it’s only eight minutes you need, and I’ll promise myself to do that. Or else I could say, “I’m not feeling very calm at the moment, I’m going to go for a walk tomorrow morning.” So what I’m saying is that you actually commit to things that are going to be useful for you in the future. And those are things like friendship, calm, having an adventure, building a skill, these are all relatively small things that you can start. So I would say start now and choose something that’s going to help you, that lasts into the future. ADI IGNATIUS: Are you positing that there’s a trade-off maybe between working all out when you’re earlier in your career versus pacing yourself and planning for the long haul? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, I think one thing that I feel and this just comes from teaching students for almost 40 years now, I wouldn’t really judge what anyone does with their lives. Some people are going to just really go for it and some people won’t. But I think it comes back to this question about self-awareness, really. If you’re really working on your productivity threads, you’re building mastery, you’re working with loads of people, you’ve got your AI really working for you, you know a great deal, there’s four threads of productivity. If you’re really focusing all your effort on that, then you have to acknowledge that your other threads, the nurture threads about your friendship, your calm, they’re probably becoming fragile and you need to think about what you’re going to do about that. And so I think the wonder of a long life is we can all live it in our own ways and I’ve stopped making judgment calls about how other people live their lives. But I do think we need to, in terms of personal agency, take responsibility for how we’re living our life and the implications of that. What I’ve noticed in the diagnostics, lots of people have already completed it, that people in their 40s are saying, “The weakest thread I have is calm and what could I do to bring more reflection into my life?” And that’s a question we could ask at any stage in our life. ADI IGNATIUS: Yeah. Well, you write that people should revisit some of these questions repeatedly throughout their lives. LYNDA GRATTON: Yeah. ADI IGNATIUS: What are the signals that it’s time to revisit yourself and ask those questions again? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, for me, it just happened three years ago when I was walking actually in France and just feeling really down. I’m wondering to myself, “What the hell is going on here? Why am I walking and crying?” Walking and crying, we’ve all done that. And I think it could be a moment like that when you think, “I have no idea why I’m doing this.” I talked to someone earlier today and they said, “I just got on the Northern line,” which is one of the undergrounds in London, “and I’m thinking tor myself have I got to really do this for the next 20 years?” So I think your body tells you when it’s time to ask yourself those three questions, the three guiding questions in the book which are, “Who am I? Where am I now? And what actions can I take now and promises to my future self?” ADI IGNATIUS: So yeah, driving and crying is a red flag for me. LYNDA GRATTON: Oh, if you’re driving and crying … ADI IGNATIUS: Driving and crying, yeah. LYNDA GRATTON: I can’t drive and cry. If I cry, I’d better stop. ADI IGNATIUS: I’d recommend it. LYNDA GRATTON: Oh, no, no. Okay, driving and crying. Yes. ADI IGNATIUS: Think about it. Now, crying on an airplane doesn’t count because there are atmospheric things, yeah, yeah, that make us all … LYNDA GRATTON: Everybody cries. We all, everyone cries on … Yeah, I agree. We can’t count the aircraft crying, but we can certainly walk and cry or drive and cry. Yeah. ADI IGNATIUS: All right, so back to the practical advice. Again, from an executive level, from a leadership perspective, you feel like managers … First of all, there are tons of layoffs out there these days. A lot of the hiring I see is people trying to bring in starting level people who are AI conversant, who’ve grown up with it, who know what to do with it. It doesn’t necessarily, on the surface, order well for an older workforce that is trying to take agency in their career. What are ways that executives should think about everything you’re talking about in ways that benefit the company by engaging with people who have the potential to be productive in their 70s, 80s, 90s even? LYNDA GRATTON: First of all, Adi, I absolutely agree with you, that this is a very tough labor market. It’s tough for people who are young, it’s tough for the middle people and it’s tough for old ones. So I don’t want to be Pollyanna about any of this and say, “Look, there’s this magic bullet or magic pill that’s going to somehow make it right for everyone,” because it is really tough. I have kids in their 30s, I feel it. I think many of us do who are listening right now. It’s the adult to adult really point I would make, which is to say you got to take control of your working life. Nobody else is going to do it for you. The marvel about the parent-child is the parent took control for you, and they might not have done a great job of it and they probably didn’t. But at least they pretended to, but they’re not doing that anymore now. And I think you’ve got to decide what working life you want. And also, understand where the world is going and what skills you might need. For example, we know that AI is going to take 20% of the tasks you currently do so you got to think about, “Well, what tasks do I do that AI isn’t going to be able to do? How could I become more human?” And we know that being more human is about the relationships you build, the friendships you build, the judgment you have, the way you think about information, the way you think about knowledge, the adventures that you have, the stories that you have. AI I know does a marvelous job of telling stories, but we all know it isn’t a storyteller. It’s humans who are storytellers. So I think we are in an enormous transition. I’m in my 70s, we’ve been around a long time. I’ve talked about, written about work now for 50 years. This is a truly astonishing moment to be at work and it does require us to really reimagine what it is we want from work and what organizations are there to do. I ran a pilot with three companies, executives from three companies, it went over 10 weeks. We transcribed everything they said to each other and these are the three things that really came out in terms of the new way that they were thinking about their careers when they realized more about who they were and what was happening to the world. Number one, they really understood that you’ve got to prepare before you need to. There’s no point in letting yourself get burnt out. Prepare before you need to. Number two, commit to what lasts. For example, friendship is something that’s going to last, mastering a skill is going to be something that lasts. So think about your future self when you’re making commitments. And thirdly, protect time for judgment. If we’re saying personal agency is so important, you need time to be able to think. And all of those executives said, “We don’t have any time to think.” And the program actually gave them an opportunity to legitimately talk about themselves, and talk about their lives, and living a 100-year life and thinking about it. And that, for me, came out so clearly. People are yearning to have an opportunity to think and talk to each other about this incredibly important topic. ADI IGNATIUS: So I love this optimism, I love the agency. Again, I feel like institutions, laws, practices have to adapt because I think age bias, it’s not allowed, but it is or it happens. It’s evident, it’s in front of our face. It’s something companies do all the time, they shuffle out the older people and they find legal ways to get away with it. So I think something has to shift in addition to the inner sense we have that we want to live these productive lives. LYNDA GRATTON: Yeah. Well, and you know very well I’ve written extensively about what organizations should do. I wrote Redesigning Work, it was one of your covers a couple of years back. So it’s not that we haven’t told organizations what they should be doing. I don’t think any company is naïve about what they should be doing. The question is are they going to do any of those things? And so what I’ve decided to do with the next decade of my life is just to show what the benefits are when you encourage people to think about the fabric of their life to help people develop personal agency. And we’re launching, at London Business School, an institute for longevity, work and careers, and that also will do that. So I do feel as if there’s a sea change and it takes institutions an awfully long time to move. But there’s a lot of really positive signs. You see people working into their 60s and 70s and being great. You see freelancers building, you see dads taking paternity leave. All the things that you hadn’t seen before are now beginning to come and so it’s good news for everybody. It gives us more freedom, more variety. ADI IGNATIUS: All right, well, we’ll have to get you back in your 90s, maybe for your centennial, to give us a perspective. But, Lynda, thank you for the conversation. LYNDA GRATTON: Thank you so much, Adi. Thank you. ADI IGNATIUS: That was Lynda Gratton, professor of management practice at London Business School, founder of HSM Advisory, and author Living the 100-Year Life: How to Build a Career that Lasts and a Life You Love. Next week, Alison digs into how we can better leverage indirect influence in our organizations. If you found this episode helpful, share it with a colleague, and be sure to subscribe and rate IdeaCast in Apple Podcasts, Spotify or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, please consider subscribing to Harvard Business Review. You’ll get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive insider newsletter and unlimited access to HBR Online. Just head to hbr.org/subscribe. Thanks to Senior Producer Mary Dooe and to Senior Production Editor Kristin Murphy Romano. And thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. We’ll be back with a new episode on Tuesday. I’m Adi Ignatius.

item.title: What Separates AI Agents That Ship to Production from Those That Don’t
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.77
The enterprise AI conversation has quietly shifted. Two years ago, executives asked whether their organization could build an AI agent. Today they are asking whether their organization can trust an AI agent. The question of trust runs on two fronts: the agents they have built that now run in production and the coding agents their developers rely on daily to build software. Most organizations can’t trust their agents in either case. Working demos of AI agents are common, but agents customers depend on day after day that improve over time and hold up to real-world edge cases are rare. Closing the gap is not a modeling problem. It is a verification problem. Organizations can build software at agent speed, but they cannot yet verify software at agent speed. Traditional software testing is a solved problem: Engineers write unit tests, continuous integration blocks regressions, and deployments are gated. But AI agents break every assumption behind that playbook. They are nondeterministic. The same input can produce different outputs. Small changes to a system prompt or tool description can cascade into failures that only appear in multi-step workflows. A model upgrade meant to improve performance can introduce silent regressions no one notices until customers report them. Five Components of the Feedback Loop Many engineering teams still operate their agents the way they first tested them: manually, in a spreadsheet, iterating on prompts, and hoping a fix does not quietly break three other workflows. The business consequences add up quickly. Projects that reach a working demo stall for months, sometimes indefinitely, because the team cannot demonstrate the agent is safe to release at scale. Engineering time drains into whack-a-mole debugging. Release cycles slow down. Anticipated return on investment (ROI) does not materialize because the agent never reaches the customer-facing scale the business case required. Cost visibility becomes its own problem, as fleets of agents, including the coding agents that developers are running on their laptops all day, can quietly drive up spend that no finance team can attribute. The gap between organizations that have institutionalized this discipline and those still improvising compounds every week. The teams closing the gap treat AI agents like a software product, with a real feedback loop built on observability. Five components define the foundation: - Production traces flow continuously into an observability layer using open standards, so every agent decision, model call, tool invocation, retrieval, and response is inspectable. - Evaluation moves from brittle string matching to layered evaluators, including large language model (LLM) judges scoped narrowly to specific behavioral checks and deterministic code-based tests where they apply. - Real production traces, including failures, become the golden data sets teams evaluate against, not synthetic happy-path examples. - Experiments compare prompt, model, and configuration changes against those data sets before anything ships. - Continuous integration pipelines gate merges on evaluation pass rates. Because the underlying instrumentation follows OpenTelemetry-based open standards, the same discipline works across cloud-native runtimes without locking teams into any single vendor’s stack. What is new, and where the industry is heading, is that the loop itself is starting to run without humans driving every step. Long-running agents now surface what to investigate, propose fixes as pull requests, and grade their own work with engineers supervising and approving rather than executing every task. An Advanced Testing Framework One AI-native engineering team has spent more than two years building and operating a production agent that helps developers debug and improve other agents. The team’s earliest testing framework was a spreadsheet. What changed everything was the shift to treating real production traces, measured in trillions of spans and evaluated across tens of millions of evaluation runs, as the foundation of engineering. Today the team runs continuous evaluations in production, gates every prompt and tool change behind continuous integration (CI-integrated) evaluation suites, and increasingly uses long-running agents to triage, categorize, and prioritize the team’s own production failures. What used to take hours of engineer debugging now takes minutes. The team ships faster, catches regressions before customers do, and continues to improve the agent even as usage scales. The durable advantage in agentic AI will not come from the underlying model. Foundation models will keep getting better and cheaper for everyone. Code is being commoditized by coding agents. Models are being commoditized by the menu of foundation models available on every hyperscaler. What is left and what compounds is context: the observability, the evaluations, the release discipline, and the feedback loop that makes every deployment safer than the last. Enterprises accelerating agentic AI on AWS are increasingly relying on partners that have already built this discipline into their own platforms. To see how AWS and Arize are helping teams operationalize agentic AI in production (agents running in your applications and the coding agents building them), visit Arize on AWS Marketplace or explore the resources at arize.com/partners/aws.

item.title: I fed my Android apps fake location data to make myself harder to track
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 6.35
Part of owning a smartphone is knowing that apps track where I go more than I'd like to admit. That doesn't mean there's nothing you can do about it. I started spoofing my location on purpose: here's what happened, why it's worth trying, and what else you can layer on top of it. An introduction to location spoofing How Android lets you fake where you are Location spoofing is the practice of feeding your phone's operating system, and by extension every app that requests location data, coordinates that don't match where you physically are. On Android, this is built into the platform rather than being some obscure hack. Inside Developer options, there's a setting called "Select mock location app" that lets you designate a third-party app as the authoritative source for GPS data. Once that's set, any app on your phone that asks for location, whether that's a weather app, a social network, or a delivery service, receives whatever coordinates your mock location app is broadcasting instead of your real GPS position. If you're familiar with Android hacks, it's probably not the first time you've heard of this. Back in the day, this would be a common hack for games such as Pokémon Go, where you could change your location in order to catch Pokémon that weren't available in your area. I used a free app called Location Changer to test this, though there are several similar tools, each with slightly different features like route simulation or timed location changes. The setup took about five minutes: enable Developer options by tapping the build number seven times, find the mock location toggle, select the app, then drop a pin anywhere on the map within that app. From that point on, my phone insisted it was in Reykjavik while I sat in my living room. It's worth noting that this only fools apps relying on the phone's location services. It doesn't touch your IP address, so anything checking your network origin, like some fraud-detection systems or region-locked streaming services, will still see your real general location unless you pair it with a VPN. Spoofing GPS and masking your IP solve different problems, and conflating them is a common mistake people make when they first try this. Some apps go a step further and check the SIM card in your phone to see your region. But if all you need is to spoof the actual location an app would get if they were checking your GPS, this is gold. Why should you do it? The privacy case for lying to your apps Location spoofing sounds like something someone would do if they had a very specific reason to—if you're one of those people, perhaps seek a marriage counselor instead of reading this article. But there are legitimate reasons to consider it. The most immediate reason to spoof your location is that a huge number of apps request it without needing it for their core function. A note-taking app, a game, or a flashlight utility asking for precise location has no functional reason to know where you are, yet many do, and that data often gets bundled and sold to data brokers who build profiles used for targeted advertising, insurance risk modeling, or resale to other companies entirely. Feeding these apps fake coordinates breaks that pipeline at the source without requiring you to hunt down and deny every individual permission request. There's also a more personal angle. Location history can reveal patterns, like where you sleep, work, worship, or seek medical care, that most people would rather not have logged indefinitely by companies with imperfect security records. There's a reason why Google stopped storing Maps Timeline data on the cloud. Data breaches happen regularly, and location data pulled from a breached database is far more useful to a bad actor than most other personal information, since it can reveal routines in a way a leaked email address cannot. Price discrimination is another reason this matters. Some retailers and travel booking sites adjust pricing based on a user's inferred location or perceived affluence, and spoofing to a different region has, in various documented cases, changed prices shown for flights, hotels, and even food delivery. Of course, this is not good for everything—you probably have no business spoofing your location on a rideshare app if said app needs your exact location to pick you up. But you can score a neat $200 or so off your next vacation if you're smart enough with your spoofing. Finally, there's the simple matter of consent. Sharing location should be a deliberate choice tied to a specific need, like navigation, not a default state that dozens of apps quietly benefit from in the background. Other things you can do Pairing location spoofing with broader privacy habits Spoofing GPS coordinates is one piece of a larger privacy practice, and it works best alongside other adjustments. A reputable VPN handles the network side of the equation, masking your IP address so that services checking your connection origin don't see your real region either. Combined with mock GPS data, this gives a much more consistent false location across both location-service requests and network-level checks. Reviewing app permissions directly is still worth doing even if you spoof location, since some apps request access to contacts, microphone, or storage that have nothing to do with their function. Android's permission manager, found in Settings under Privacy, lets you audit every app that has ever asked for a sensitive permission and revoke access individually, or switch location access to "only while using the app" for tools that genuinely need it occasionally, like a maps app. Resetting your advertising ID periodically, also available in the privacy settings on most modern Android versions, disrupts the ad profile that's been built around your device over time, since that identifier is what ties your behavior together across different apps, even when personal information isn't directly shared. For anyone comfortable going further, disabling MAC address randomization exceptions and being deliberate about which Wi-Fi networks a phone auto-joins reduces another avenue of passive tracking, since Wi-Fi access points can be used to estimate location independent of GPS. None of these steps alone is a complete solution, but layered together, they meaningfully shrink the amount of consistent, accurate data companies can collect. Small setting, real control over your data Spoofing my location wasn't about hiding from anyone specific. It was about reclaiming a default that companies had quietly set in their own favor, one setting at a time.

item.title: Super Cruise costs $40 a month, but 60% of GM owners skip it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.86
GM has sold hands-free highway driving capability under the Super Cruise name since 2017, marketing it as one of the most capable systems on the road. New GM buyers get three years of Super Cruise with select vehicles, but once that trial ends, most don't pay to renew the feature each month. Only 30 to 40% choose to keep it, according to a company announcement GM made in April 2026. While Super Cruise has benefits when it comes to handling the tedious stretches of a long commute or road trip, whether it’s worth paying for after the free trial comes down to where and how often you drive. Super Cruise and its capabilities stay with the vehicle, so the hands-free highway driving feature transfers to the next owner with an active subscription. Those looking at a pre-owned GM vehicle can also use the information below to decide whether Super Cruise is worth paying for each month. How and where Super Cruise works Map coverage and price tag Super Cruise is now available on more than 20 models across Chevrolet, GMC, Cadillac, and Buick, along with GM's truck lineup. According to the automaker, customers have logged more than a billion hands-free miles on the system as of April 2026, with nearly 750,000 vehicles currently on the road with Super Cruise functionality. A hands-free highway driving system, Super Cruise can handle steering, acceleration, and braking on compatible highways, relying on LiDAR map data, real-time GPS, cameras, and radar sensors to keep the vehicle centered in its lane. For drivers, that means they can take their hands off the wheel on long highway stretches, reducing the fatigue of constant steering corrections during a commute or road trip. The LiDAR data comes from GM's dedicated mapping fleet, not the vehicle a customer drives. GM's Super Cruise documentation describes the system as using a “LiDAR-scanned map database," built in advance by a separate fleet of specially equipped vehicles that scan roads ahead of time and create the map, similar to how Google Street View cars work.
