Activate Low Power Mode One of your strongest weapons against battery drain is Low Power Mode. With it enabled, your phone only performs the most essential of tasks, so background activities like downloads, iCloud syncing, and mail fetching are disabled. Low Power Mode will automatically kick in when the battery falls below 20%, but you can also activate it manually to keep your phone going for longer. Head over to Settings > Battery and turn on Low Power Mode. You can also add Low Power Mode to the Control Center under Settings > Control Center. When activated, the battery icon in the top-right corner will turn yellow. 5. Adjust Screen Brightness The greatest hurdle in your fight for more battery life is your phone's own screen. Smartphone displays are bigger and brighter than ever, but they are also murder on your battery. You can't really get around this fact, but you can turn down the brightness. Manually adjust brightness levels in Settings > Display & Brightness by using the slider bar. A slider is also accessible via the Control Center; press lightly on the brightness icon and move the slider down. You should also turn off auto-brightness to ensure your changes stick. Open Accessibility > Display & Text Size and disable Auto-Brightness. Your phone will no longer try to adjust its brightness based on the current lighting situation, which will avoid situations where the screen becomes brighter than it really needs to be. 6. Manage When Your Phone Locks Since the screen is your battery's enemy, you should also think about managing when the phone's display turns off automatically. You can adjust this setting under Display & Brightness > Auto-Lock. If you tend to put your phone down without locking it, set this to something lower to give the battery a break. It may also be worth disabling Raise to Wake if you don't want the screen to turn on simply by picking it up. 7. Control the Always-On Display Exclusive to the Pro and Pro Max models for iPhone 14 and later is the Always-On display, which shows the time, widgets, notifications, and wallpaper while the device is locked. Apple has taken steps to ensure it doesn't consume too much power, but you can disable it from Display & Brightness > Always On. If you keep it on, it will turn off if the phone is face down, stored in your pocket or bag, when the Sleep focus is enabled, or at your set bedtime. 8. Turn Off Location Services Location services are helpful for apps like Google Maps or Yelp, but the GPS pings that occur in the background can drain a battery. You could turn off location services completely via Privacy & Security > Location Services, but this greatly affects the usability of your device. Instead, rein in individual apps by customizing how they use your location data: Never, Ask Next Time Or When I Share, While Using the App, or (in some cases) Always. For example, with Google Maps, it's best to set it to While Using the App so that it only pings your location when you actually need it. 9. Turn Off Background App Refresh When you close an iOS app, it can still check for updates and new content periodically—a process that can drain battery life. You can disable Background App Refresh completely or just for certain apps under Settings > General > Background App Refresh. Here, you can disable specific apps if you only want to cut off refresh-heavy programs, like email or social media platforms. Otherwise, select Background App Refresh and set it to Off (or Wi-Fi if you want to restrict it, but not outright disable it). Disabling it completely won't stop the apps from working, but it may take a moment for new information to appear when you return to them. 10. Cut Down on Notifications If your screen lights up with a preview of every notification you receive, it's consuming power with each text, breaking news alert, or social media follow. Cutting down on these interruptions can save your battery (and sanity). Open Settings > Notifications and choose which specific apps should be allowed to send notifications to your phone and where. Turn off Lock Screen or choose Notification Center so that alerts won't be sent to your lock screen. If you prefer not to make any permanent changes, Focus mode allows you to set restrictions for when notifications can come through. 11. Turn Off Wireless Services From Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and cellular data, your phone has many wireless features running in the background. It continuously searches for nearby Wi-Fi connections, which is why the list of available networks constantly changes when you're out and about. If you're in a real power jam, you can turn off cellular data, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and AirDrop from Control Center—or just enable Airplane Mode to disable all your phone's cellular features. 12. Slap on a MagSafe Power Bank This might sound like cheating, but a great way to ensure extended battery life is to use a power bank or wireless MagSafe charger from a third-party manufacturer, which allows you to charge the phone without needing to plug it into the wall. This way, you'll be able to top off the device right from anywhere—even your pocket. If you want something made by Apple, your options are limited. The company previously sold a MagSafe Battery Pack that connected to the back of the phone to charge wirelessly, but that was discontinued. If you bought the iPhone Air, a new battery pack was unveiled exclusively for Apple's ultrathin offering. It can technically be used on any iPhone 17 model, but you have to turn it sideways to make it fit. 13. Service or Replace the Battery No battery lasts forever, though, so if performance drops low enough, Apple has a few solutions. Your phone will notify you when it may be time to replace the power supply. If you pay for AppleCare+, it includes battery service if your phone falls below 80% of its original capacity. The company's Self Service Repair Store also sells replacement batteries you can install yourself at around $40 to $70 (after returning your old component for a credit). About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: Xerox C305ae Review: Busy Team? Flex Some Real Color Laser Muscle
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.86
The Xerox C305ae Color Multifunction Printer ($639) is a moderately fast all-in-one (AIO) color laser printer designed for small-to-midsize offices or workgroups. It features a large 50-sheet automatic document feeder (ADF), a 4.3-inch color touch screen with access to a wide range of settings, and the option to add one or two expansion trays. The C305ae has unusually high manufacturer’s ratings for both its peak daily duty cycle and recommended monthly page volume, so in theory you’ll be able to push it hard if your workload suddenly goes into overdrive. The C305ae's robust customization capabilities, via its touch screen and mobile app, make it especially well-suited for companies that like to fine-tune devices and closely track any scanned or printed documents. But the PC software doesn’t have the same impressive selection of device settings as the mobile app, so it may not be a good fit for companies that aren't mobile-first. Overall, though, it's a solid alternative to the Editors' Choice-award-winning Brother MFC-L3780CDW. At 17.7 by 16.2 by 15.8 inches (HWD), the Xerox C305ae is fairly typical in size for its speed and price. The Brother MFC-L3780CDW is almost 2 inches shorter but makes up for it by being 2 inches wider. The HP Color LaserJet Pro MFP 4301fdw is about 2.5 inches shorter, while being about 1 inch deeper than the C305ae. And the Canon Color imageClass MF753Cdw is about half an inch shorter and more than 2 inches deeper than the C305ae. Unless you plan to place your new AIO into a very tight space, the relative size of these models won’t make much difference. These models' weights have somewhat more variation. The C305ae weighs in at 44.6 pounds. For comparison, the Brother MFC-L3780CDW weighs slightly more at 47.8 pounds, while the Canon MF753Cdw comes in at an even heavier 48.5 pounds. And those models might seem light compared with the HP 4301fdw, which tips the scales at a hefty 51.6 pounds. On paper capacity, the C305ae offers no real surprises. It has a standard 250-sheet input tray, a single-sheet manual-feed slot, and a 50-sheet ADF. The Brother MFC-L3780CDW improves on that combination by replacing the single-sheet manual feed slot with a 30-sheet multipurpose tray. The Canon MF753Cdw and HP 4301fdw improve on that by increasing the size of the multipurpose tray from 30 sheets to 50 sheets. On the output side, the C305ae has only a 100-sheet output bin, while the Brother, Canon, and HP models have a roomier 150-sheet bin. If you often leave your printer unattended during large print jobs, you may appreciate having a large-capacity output bin. If you do need additional paper-input capacity, Xerox lets you add one or two 250-sheet trays to the bottom of the C305ae to bring the onboard capacity to 751 sheets. That edges out the Brother MFC-L3780CDW, which allows only a single 250-sheet expansion tray for a total capacity of 530 sheets. The Canon MF753Cdw also allows only a single expansion tray, though that tray’s 550-sheet capacity would bring the Canon’s total capacity up to 850 sheets. And the HP 4301fdw offers a similar upgrade path, with a single 550-sheet expansion tray that brings its total capacity to 850 sheets. Of course, these upgrades cost extra; a single 250-sheet expansion tray for the C305ae costs $149. Just how hard can you push the C305ae? Xerox rates this model with a peak daily duty cycle of 5,000 pages. For comparison, the Brother MFC-L3780CDW, Canon MF753Cdw, and HP 4301fdw are rated for a lower 4,000 pages. It’s a similar situation with the manufacturer’s recommended monthly page volume. The C305ae is rated for 75,000 pages, while the Brother, Canon, and HP models are rated for 50,000 pages. Clearly, the C305ae is the standout model within this group when it comes to dealing with heavy workloads. If that’s especially important for your work environment, you may want to strongly favor the C305ae. Any AIO in this price class should support USB, Ethernet, and Wi-Fi connectivity. All four of these models do that. All four also have a dedicated USB port that will allow you to print from or save scans to a thumb drive, which isn’t always the case. On the C305ae, that dedicated USB port is conveniently located on the front panel to the left of the touch screen. Within this group, only the Canon has an integrated NFC card reader for badge authentication. If that’s important to your organization, you may want to favor that model. As with the other wireless-capable models, you can access the printer over Wi-Fi using either a computer or a mobile device. The C305ae is compatible with Apple AirPrint, Mopria Print Service, Chromebook, and Wi-Fi Direct. And you can use the Easy Assist app to wirelessly print documents or photos from your phone or tablet. The C305ae is also competitive in terms of the size of its LCD-based control panel. It has a fairly large 4.3-inch color touch screen, which makes it relatively easy to adjust settings on the unit itself. That’s the same size as the color touch screen on the HP 4301fdw. And it’s noticeably larger than the 3.5-inch color touch screen on the Brother MFC-L3780CDW. Top-size honors here, though, go to the Canon MF753Cdw, which squeezes an even larger 5-inch color touch screen onto its front panel. Some unusual hardware add-ons for the C305ae are worth noting here. In addition to the previously mentioned 250-sheet expansion tray, you can purchase a 128GB Intelligent Storage Drive ($273.48), an adjustable printer stand ($329.45), a swivel cabinet ($223.30), and a Contact Card Reader ($139). One element of the design of the C305ae’s outer cabinet may come as a surprise. After unpacking the unit, I noticed that the right side of the front panel seemed to be bent outward. This seemed odd, as the shipping box showed no apparent damage. On closer inspection, I could see that the inner cabinet behind the bent panel was similarly curved, but in the opposite direction. It didn’t take long to realize that this is meant to be a customer-friendly feature. It’s not always clear how to open the front of a printer. Xerox has decided to show you just where to reach in to pull the front panel toward you to access the toner cartridges. Once you’ve unpacked the printer and turned it on, the touch panel will prompt you to use your mobile phone to complete the setup. You’ll be shown a QR code to facilitate downloading the Xerox Easy Assist app to your phone. And from there, you can email yourself a link to download the software and drivers for your computer. The software and drivers are compatible with Windows 10 and 11; Windows Servers 2016, 2019, 2022, and 2025; and macOS 14, 15, and 26. All of the C305ae’s features are supported on both Intel and AMD processors. During the software installation process, you’ll see a screen that offers the option to download "Xerox Start Smart - Driver Installer (Recommended)." That’s for the drivers only. For the PC software app, you’ll also want to click "Additional Software and Support." That’s where you can download the Xerox Print and Scan Experience app for your computer. You can use that app to check the toner level in each cartridge. You can also use it to (as the name suggests!) print and scan from your computer, and even alter the document parameters for the current scan or print. What it can’t do is change the printer's internal settings. To do that, you’ll need to use either the mobile app or the control panel. Both the Easy Assist mobile app and the onboard control panel are well-designed and easy to use. The Easy Assist home screen has five large text-labeled icons: Scan, Print, Supplies, Support, and Settings. They offer a strong complement of options and settings. For example, under the Scan heading, you’ll be able to give the resulting scan file a customized name, as opposed to the default time-and-date name. You can choose the file format for the scan (either PDF or JPG). And you can adjust the scan’s resolution from 75dpi to 600dpi. Other scan-related options include whether to automatically remove blank pages, which scan source to use (ADF, scanner glass, or automatically detect), and what size the scan’s target should be. Under the Settings heading, the app lets you set up a scan-to-email procedure so you can scan documents and share them as email attachments directly from the printer. You can set up a default name and phone number for any outgoing faxes. And you can change the printer's administrative password without accessing the printer itself. Also, under the Supplies heading, you can see how much toner remains in each of the four cartridges, detect which tray is currently empty, and order supplies directly from Xerox. On the C305ae’s touch screen, you’ll find even more options and settings. The home screen features eight large text-labeled icons: Print, Copy, Scan, Fax, Job Queue, Settings, Address Book, and Scan Center. From there, you can change the job accounting frequency (daily, weekly, or monthly), create customized maintenance configurations, assign login permissions, and set the file format for any thumb-drive-directed scans. There’s an option to allow remote control of the printer via an external VNC client. And you can set the default destinations for your scans (to a network folder, an email address, a printer, or a fax), as well as the scan’s default resolution, image quality, darkness, edge handling, image handling, and color handling. As with the Easy Assist app, the C305ae’s control panel offers an impressive range of configuration options. Those could be a real asset if you need to configure your printers to meet stringent corporate or federal standards, especially regarding document tracking, device maintenance, and multilayered security. Xerox rates the built-in scanner's speed at 48 pages per minute (ppm) for monochrome scans and 21ppm for color scans. The maximum scan area from the ADF is 8.5 by 14 inches, while the maximum scan area from the glass platen is slightly smaller, at 8.5 by 11.7 inches. Scans from the ADF are limited to a 600dpi-by-600dpi resolution. Unlike some other AIOs, such as the Brother MFC-L3780CDW, the C305ae doesn’t offer higher-resolution output when scanning from the platen rather than the ADF. Xerox rates the C305ae’s print speed at 32ppm when printing onto letter-size paper. That’s fairly typical for a mid-level all-in-one color laser. The Brother MFC-L3780CDW is rated slightly slower, at 31ppm, while the Canon Color imageClass MF753Cdw and HP Color LaserJet Pro MFP 4301fdw are rated a little higher, at 35ppm. To see if the C305ae could meet or exceed its ratings, I benchmarked it over an Ethernet connection with our standard Intel Core i5 desktop testbed. The C305ae comes out of the box configured to print two-sided (duplex) pages. For such printers, we clock both two-sided and one-sided (simplex) performance. When printing our 12-page Microsoft Word text document (excluding the first page), I clocked the Xerox at 31.2ppm in simplex mode and 16.6 images per minute (ipm, where each image is one side of a two-sided page) in duplex mode. That simplex result was a modest 0.8ppm below its rated speed. Unfortunately, that wasn’t quite fast enough to keep with the other three AIOs. The Brother MFC-L3780CDW edged out the C305ae by just a hair with its 32ppm simplex speed. The Canon MF753Cdw whisked past both of them with its solid result of 34.7ppm. And surpassing them all was the HP 4301fdw, with its impressive speed of 36ppm. Next, I timed the C305ae as it printed our standard collection of colorful and complex business documents: Adobe Acrobat PDFs, PowerPoint handouts, and Excel spreadsheets and graphs. When I combined those results with the scores from printing the 12-page Word document. I found it took a moderately fast 98 seconds to print the entire suite. While that was only fast enough for a third-place finish within this group, it was quite close to the second-place finisher, the Canon MF753Cdw. That model was just 3 seconds faster than the C305ae, at 95 seconds. First-place honors went to the HP 4301fdw and its very brisk 87 seconds. The laggard in this test, Brother's MFC-L3780CDW, took a more leisurely 110 seconds. And while no laser-class printer can match a dedicated photo printer for quality prints, I did time PCMag’s two standard 4-by-6-inch test snapshots with the C305ae to see how fast it might print photographic materials. It averaged about 9 seconds per image, which is relatively fast for a color laser printer. While the C305ae’s test scores for our black-and white text documents were about average, it did perform a bit better than that with our color business documents. If you tend to print a lot of color documents with photos, charts, or graphs, you can expect a small speed boost compared with the more typical monochrome text documents. With any laser-class printer, you should be able to produce near-typesetter-quality text that’s suitable for most business text documents. The C305ae easily meets that standard for those kinds of documents. I was able to read typical business fonts down to a very small 4-point size. Everything that I printed with the C305ae looked clean and professional. I saw no stray dots, unexpected vertical lines, or misplaced patterns. I also didn't experience any jammed or misaligned pages when printing, copying, or scanning. With printed charts and graphs, the colors were well-defined, with no bleed-in along the edges. The colors were precise and pleasing across the spectrum. Skin tones were accurate and well-rendered. Contrast and saturation levels were appropriately set to match the original content. The C305ae’s printed photos looked similar. Their colors, contrast, and saturation levels were always right where they should be. As with any laser-class printer, you won’t be able to print borderless pages as you can with an inkjet printer. That said, the C305ae’s photo print quality is more than adequate for brochures, newsletters, real estate flyers, or similar business documents. While the purchase price is important, a printer’s running costs matter more, especially if you plan to do a significant amount of printing with its service life. The C305ae should shine here because it offers three types of toner cartridges: Standard Yield, High Capacity, and Extra High Capacity. The Extra High Capacity cartridges will cost more, but they’ll provide you with the lowest cost per page. Those cartridges would help you lower the C305ae's running costs to about 2.7 cents for a monochrome page and about 16.6 cents for a color page. For comparison, the Brother L3780CDW would cost about 2.3 cents for monochrome and 12.3 cents for color. The HP 4301fdw would cost about 2.3 cents for monochrome and 14.1 cents for color. And the Canon MF753Cdw would cost about 2.4 cents for monochrome and 14.7 cents for color. Those are significantly lower than the C305ae’s costs for both monochrome and color. If you plan to print a lot of pages with your new AIO, especially color pages, be aware that the C305ae essentially adds a small surcharge to each page that you print. Whichever model you choose, try to purchase the highest-capacity cartridges to reduce per-page costs for your model. If you think that isn’t important, consider the consequences of buying Xerox’s three types of cartridges. If you buy the Standard Yield black cartridge, your monochrome cost per page will be 5.8 cents. With the High Capacity black cartridge, you could lower that to 3.3 cents. And with the Extra High Capacity black cartridge, you could lower it even further, to 2.7 cents. In this case, you would be paying more than twice as much per page in toner costs if you were to purchase the Standard Yield cartridge versus the Extra High Capacity cartridge. Final Thoughts Xerox C305ae Color Multifunction Printer - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Xerox C305ae Color Multifunction Printer is well-equipped to take on a heavy workload. The 50-page ADF, 4.3-inch color touch screen, and optional paper input trays help to make it fully competitive with similar AIOs. It has excellent print quality, especially with its color printouts. And its duty cycle and volume ratings are the best that we’ve seen for this class of color AIOs. Who should buy the Xerox C305ae? Given its otherwise strong credentials, it may come down to how you prefer to control your printer. While the computer software lets you alter many of the document parameters related to printing and scanning, it doesn’t let you change the device’s internal settings. Xerox makes up for that by providing extensive document and device settings on both its mobile app and the unit itself. For many corporate administrators, that would be an advantage, not a disadvantage. If that’s your situation, the C305ae might be just the model for you. Otherwise, you might prefer the Brother MFC-L3780CDW. It’s our Editors' Choice winner for budget color laser AIOs. That model’s software bundle includes several apps that let you adjust various settings related to its print, scan, and fax capabilities. It also has a lower purchase price than the C305ae, as well as lower toner costs for both color and monochrome pages. About Our Expert At PCMag, my focus is on printers and scanners. I started out way back in 1988 at Compute!, which still had a section of the magazine devoted to type-in programs. Since then, I’ve written more than 1,000 articles for a variety of publications, including Architectural Record, Attaché, CNET, COMDEX Daily, Computer Shopper, Digital Cinema Report, Film & Video, Hemispheres, The Leica Camera Blog, Maximum PC, Omni, PC Magazine, PC World, Sky, StudioDaily, US Airways Magazine, and ZDNET. My interest in printers stems from my interest in digital photography. Ten of my photos were featured in a solo exhibition at the Leica Store at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas. Titled “Monochrome Vegas,” the large photo prints were displayed there for more than a year. I’m also interested in technology-based music. I’ve created a large number of music videos that combine improvised music with computer graphics. You can view my photography at protozoid.com and my music videos on my YouTube channel.

item.title: US Tablet Shipments Plummet by 32% on Memory Crunch
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.80
The memory shortage appears to be sinking demand for tablets in the US. On Thursday, the research firm IDC reported that tablet shipments to the US in Q2 dropped 31.6% year-over-year. The memory crunch has been causing prices for consumer electronics to rise everywhere, and tablets have been no exception. “Samsung, Lenovo, and Apple all raised tablet prices within ten weeks of each other. The result: US tablet shipments collapsed 31.6% year over year, the worst of any region,” IDC added in a tweet. The US decline stands out since on a global basis tablet shipments only fell 12.3% year-over-year. That said, IDC says the 12.3% decrease represents “the category’s steepest year-over-year decline in this cycle.” Back in June, Apple raised prices on various iPad models by $100 to $200. Meanwhile, Samsung raised its own prices “$40 to $280 across nearly its entire Galaxy Tab lineup in April,” IDC said. “Lenovo followed with $30 to $70 increases on the Tab One, Tab Plus, and Yoga Tab during the same month.” As a result, consumer shipments for tablets fell 13.5% year over year in Q2. IDC’s report further noted that “one of the largest vendors, Amazon, has also been scaling back its tablet business due to rising costs,” pointing to the memory crunch. "Value oriented products from brands like Amazon, Walmart, and a few others have been losing steam as the market pivots to mid-high tier tablets," noted IDC analyst Jitesh Ubrani. Another factor to the big decline in the US is how vendors had shipped an abnormally high amount of tablets to get ahead of Trump's tariffs a year ago. "That provides a very tough comparison for the current quarter," Ubrani told PCMag. Over a decade ago, tablets were seen as the next big thing, briefly even outpacing notebook PCs in shipments. But now IDC wonders if tablets will eventually lose their relevancy even when the memory shortage clears, although that could take a few more years. “AI PCs are absorbing the productivity use case tablets spent a decade trying to own. Phones keep getting bigger, and foldables, still a rounding error in unit terms, are growing fast and pulling casual browsing and media consumption further into the smartphone,” the research firm noted. On the bright side, Lenovo was able to grow its tablet shipments in Q2 by 26% year-over-year. Tablet “detachables,” which include a removable keyboard, also saw only a 6% shipment decline while “slate tablets fell 19.8% year over year,” IDC said. The report adds: “The top five vendors (Apple, Samsung, Lenovo, Huawei, Xiaomi) now control roughly 79.8% of the market, up from 77.9% just one quarter earlier. Bigger vendors have the procurement leverage to secure memory allocation that smaller players simply can’t match, so the category is concentrating around the players best equipped to weather the storm.” About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. item.title: Sennheiser’s New True Wireless Earbuds Let You Easily Swap Out All 3 Batteries
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.69
What happens when your gadget's battery begins to fail? It’s unlikely you will replace the complicated and often glued-down components yourself, but Sennheiser wants to help you do so with its new flagship earbuds. The Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are designed to be more sustainable than many rivals, allowing you to replace any battery in any of the three components. That’s the battery inside each earbud, and the one used in the charging case. Unlike other battery fixes, you can do this yourself at home with an included tool to access the compartments. If you’re unhappy with the battery life on your headphones or they no longer work, you can replace each cell yourself to give them a new lease of life. Sennheiser claims the earbuds offer up to 12 hours of playtime on a single charge, with the charging case adding another 28 hours. It has yet to share how long it takes to recharge or how long each battery's predicted lifespan will be. Expect impressive audio quality and a range of new features on top of what 2024's Momentum True Wireless 4 offered, including Bluetooth 6 for better connectivity with your devices. The earbuds also come with redesigned eartips to improve bass response and enhance the seal with your ear for better noise-cancellation performance. There's also support for Dolby Atmos spatial audio to make sound more immersive. Sennheiser says, "It takes you beyond left and right, placing sound all around you—even overhead—so music, movies, and games feel bigger, clearer, and more immersive." The Momentum True Wireless 5 launches in five colors: copper, cream, denim, graphite, and lavender, with an IP54 dust and splash-resistant design. A pair cost $299.95, with a year’s warranty included if you buy directly from Sennheiser. You can preorder now, although an exact release date has yet to be confirmed. item.title: FCC: Surface Water Pool Cleaning Robots Subject to Foreign-Made Bot Ban
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.61
It looks like pool cleaning robots can fall under the US’s foreign-made robot ban if the products operate at surface water level. The FCC has updated an FAQ about the ban, which previously left it unclear if pool cleaning robots were exempt or not. The policy was first announced last month, targeting foreign-made advanced robotic devices, including those capable of autonomous locomotion. But at the time, the FAQ noted that any “unmanned underwater vehicle that is able to operate without a human occupant” fell outside the definition for advanced robots. The Commission has since added a section to the FAQ that directly addresses pool cleaning robots. Although unmanned underwater vehicles are specifically excluded from the definition, the FAQ notes “pool cleaning robots are capable of operating both underwater and at the surface level. Are these dual-use devices also excluded? “No. Such dual-use robots are not excluded. The specific exclusion of UUVs (unmanned underwater vehicles) does not exclude pool cleaning robots that satisfy the definition when operating above ground,” the FAQ’s answer says in response. An FCC spokesperson added that pool cleaning robots that operate purely underwater have been exempted from the ban — but not those that operate above ground. Still, some of the best pool cleaning robots are designed to sweep not only the floor, but also the upper walls, and skim the surface while on the waterline, meaning they would fall under the ban. Others are made only for surface skimming. That doesn’t bode well for Chinese vendors such as Dreame, Bublue and Beatbot. The FCC made the clarification after previously confirming that foreign-made robot vacuums and robot lawnmowers, in addition to humanoid robots and robot dogs, all fall under the ban. For consumers, the current prohibition only applies to future foreign-made robots, not any existing products. So US buyers can continue buying the foreign-made products already up for sale. ““Nor does it prevent retailers from continuing to sell, import, or market relevant models approved previously through the FCC’s equipment authorization process,” the Commission noted. In addition, the FCC has created a process that can temporarily exempt a company from the foreign-made device ban, which previously started with drones, and Wi-Fi routers. But so far, the Commission hasn’t issued any relief to a Chinese vendor. The White House instituted the ban citing the threat of foreign entities potentially spying or conducting sabotage through the robots. Another issue is the US becoming over-reliant on foreign-made tech. Hence, the device bans also promise to spur domestic manufacturing. But some critics fear the same policy will lead to price increases for consumers and block innovative products. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. item.title: Windows 11 Gaming Issue Linked To RGB Devices of All Things
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.40
Microsoft has discovered why this month’s Windows 11 update (KB5121003) can trigger errors and reboots when running three PC games: It turns out RGB accessories and components are involved. But the problem isn’t the hardware, or the colorful lighting. Surprisingly, Microsoft says that file name similarities in the software for the peripherals are to blame. In an update posted on Thursday, the company explained: “Ongoing investigation indicates that this issue is related to peripherals or internal device components which have RGB lighting features. Such devices may install drivers or code components with file names similar to inpoutx64. In systems where these drivers are found, the issue is then triggered by launching certain games.” Redmond didn't elaborate. There’s also not much official information about Inpoutx64.sys, but it operates as a core system file and driver that can be located in the C:\Windows\System32\drivers folder. Still, Embark Studios, a developer behind one of the affected games, told users earlier this week: “This is a crash related to the file inpoutx64.sys, which changed with the Windows update.” The problem has been affecting three games, MARVEL Tōkon: Fighting Souls along with ARC Raiders and THE FINALS, two titles from Embark Studios. The bug can cause an affected game to become unresponsive, abruptly close, display the error message “EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION,” or even cause a PC to reboot. Microsoft hasn’t issued a fix yet. For now, the company says: “We are presently working to understand the relationship between these RGB components and the games which trigger this issue. We will provide an update when more information is available.” The developer of Arc Raiders, Embark Studios, has also been telling users in the game’s Discord chat server: “We’re working towards a long-term fix but in the meantime there is a work-around solution that will safely remove the file in question and allow you to play the game without issue.” The work-around solution involves basically deleting Inpoutx64.sys, and wiping it from the OS's registry. item.title: AMD Crosses a 30% Client CPU Market Share Against Intel
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.39
For the first time, AMD’s share of the x86 client CPU market, covering both mobile and desktop, has crossed 30%, according to Mercury Research, which tracks the processor shipments. AMD’s share of client CPU for x86 processors reached 30.3% in Q2 against Intel’s 69.7%, Mercury Research said in a research note on Thursday. It represents a sizable jump from two years ago when the company’s share was at 21.1%. AMD’s share for desktop CPU shipments has already been reaching past 30% in recent quarters. Now it looks like the company’s processor shipments for notebook PCs have been increasing as well, pushing the total client CPU volume up. "Client share is just the combined desktop and mobile CPUs and nothing else," Mercury Research President Dean McCarron said. In this year’s Q2, AMD’s desktop share was at 34.9% while the company’s mobile processors made up 28.9% of the x86 shipment volume. Despite AMD’s gains, the processor market is facing newer competitors in Apple, Qualcomm and MediaTek, which have been releasing Arm-based processors for laptops that aren’t reflected in the x86 tracking from Mercury Research. Still, the research firm noted: “Our estimate of Arm-inclusive PC client CPU share for the second quarter of 2026 is 15.3 percent, a 0.9 point increase and a new record high.” In past quarters, the Arm-based PC client CPU share was around 13%. In a bad sign for the PC industry, Mercury Research found that desktop x86 CPU shipments continued to sag, leading to a “large on-year downturn in excess of 20 percent." “Desktop X86 CPU shipments in the second quarter are best described as ugly,” the report says. Although demand for desktop CPUs is usually down in the second quarter on a seasonal basis, Mercury Research’s report alluded to the ongoing memory crunch as being a major culprit to the decline. The shortage has caused prices for not only RAM and storage to soar, but also higher-end graphics cards, which require ample amounts of video memory. “We believe that higher PC prices and limited GPU supplies are having a significant impact on end demand for desktop PCs, and thus desktop CPUs, as well,” the research firm said. This follows the nearly 20% year-over-year drop in desktop CPU shipments that also occurred in Q1. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years.
