item.title: The Insta360 Luna Pro Gimbal Camera Aims to Take Down the Osmo Pocket 4
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.97
Insta360 has announced the Luna Pro, a slimmed-down, single-camera version of the Luna Ultra it launched earlier this summer. It maintains the Ultra’s biggest selling point (the detachable screen) while aiming down-market at the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 and 4. Information is somewhat limited by this China-only launch (Insta360 is yet again opting for a staggered release starting in China and coming to the rest of the globe sometime later), but the company is calling the Luna Pro its “flagship gimbal camera” that was co-engineered with Leica. It’s unclear what Insta360 thinks “flagship” means when the Ultra exists, but that’s marketing. The Luna Pro features a single Type 1 sensor — likely the same one featured in the main camera on the Luna Ultra — and promises the ability to capture 8K footage that can retain 4K resolution even when shooting vertically. The Osmo Pocket 3 and 4 can’t do that. On the Pocket 3, vertical footage has a maximum resolution of 3K (1,728 × 3,072) at up to 60p. The Osmo Pocket 4 doesn’t change that. Even the higher-end Osmo Pocket 4P can only capture up to 3K resolution footage in vertical orientation. The Luna Pro also keeps the Luna Ultra’s most attractive feature: the detachable two-inch OLED touchscreen. It features HD transmission up to 20 meters away and has a built-in microphone, just like the Ultra. The Luna Pro also pairs directly with Insta360’s dedicated microphone. Insta360 is also advertising “cinematic color” on the Pro thanks to support for Dolby Vision HDR, built-in Leica color profiles, and the ability to shoot in 10-bit I-Log with the promise of up to 14 stops of dynamic range. The company is also promising “80mm portraits” at up to 4Kp60, driven by a 4x digital zoom. Users can pull 4K live frames from that footage that can be exported as photos as well. The camera is powered by Insta360’s dual AI chip which it promises provides class-leading low light performance and accurate auto tracking for both single subjects and groups via its three-axis stabilized gimbal. As this is a China-only launch, pricing and availability in other regions has not been announced. Given the timeline of the last Luna launch, expect global availability to follow sometime in the next one to two months.

item.title: 11 Award-Winning Photos Show Science in Action
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.82
The annual 2026 BMC Ecology and Evolution and BMC Zoology photography competition offers researchers out in the field a chance to celebrate the intersection of art and science, showcasing their projects in a visually beautiful way. “The annual competition showcases the beauty and diversity of life on Earth, while also celebrating researchers and the work they undertake to understand and protect the natural world,” Springer Nature explains. This year, the judges selected an overall winner and a runner-up. They also selected winners and runners-up in three categories, along with a trio of photos that deserved a special mention. Overall Winner The overall winning photographer is Sritam Kumar Sethy, whose photo, “Windows to the Wetlands,” showcases an orange-tailed marsh dart damselfly (Ceriagrion cerinorubellum) framed by a hole in a leaf. Sethy captured the photo in a freshwater wetland in Odisha, India, while studying wetland ecosystems. Damselflies are an indicator species, as they rely on aquatic and terrestrial habitats in wetlands and are particularly sensitive to pollution, habitat loss, and the effects of climate change. “It is hard not to smile at this beautifully composed and vivid image, in which the damselfly seems to display a remarkable sense of character and presence,” says BMC Ecology and Evolution Senior Editorial Board Member David Ferrier. Runner-Up Ryan Wagner of Washington State University is this year’s runner-up for his photo of two students working at night near Portland, Oregon. The students are attaching a radio transmitter to a northern red-legged frog (Rana aurora) to better understand how these frogs move around and use their habitats. The students hope to discover ways to create safer environments for at-risk species. Category Winners Winners and runners-up were also named across the competition’s three categories: Relationships in Nature, Research in Action, and Protecting Our Planet. Victor Huertas from James Cook University in Australia took top honors in the Relationships in Nature category for his photo of two male giant Australian cuttlefish (Ascarosepion apama) competing for a female’s attention. Alwin Hardenbol of the Natural Resource Institute in Finland took second place for his photo of friarbirds (Philemon corniculatus) mobbing a brown goshawk (Tachyspiza fasciata). In Research in Action, Liam Brennan’s photo, “Intertidal Education,” won over the judges. Brennan is a student at the University of New Brunswick in Atlantic Canada, and his winning shot shows undergraduate students investigating local fish populations under a moonlit sky. Brandon Güell of Florida International University won second place for a photo of researchers monitoring aquatic life in Everglades National Park. Finally, Allen Tian won the Protecting Our Planet category with “A Bridge Between Past and Present,” a drone shot showing environmental disruption caused by prior dam construction. Tian captured the shot while his biodiversity research team studied the seaway through environmental DNA sampling and drone surveys. The team used drones to avoid disturbing resident wildlife. Abhijeet Bayani of MES Abasaheb Garware College in India is the runner-up. Bayani’s photo shows an olive ridley sea turtle (Lepidochelys olivacea)) hatchling being led to the safety of the sea by locals who are engaged in community-led conservation efforts along India’s western coast. Highly Commended Images The judges also highlighted three more entries that they believed deserved a special mention. Image creditsBMC Ecology and Evolution and BMC Zoology Photo Competition. Individual photographers are credited in the image captions.

item.title: Brightin Star’s Luxurious New 35mm f/1.7 M-Mount Lens Is Coming Soon
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.82
At CP+ 2026 in February, Brightin Star announced a new APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH. lens for Leica M-Mount cameras. The stylish new lens is finally available to order, and unlike Brightin Star’s typical lenses, it is launching first on Kickstarter. The full-frame 35mm f/1.7 ASPH. lens is just Brightin Star’s second Leica M-Mount lens, joining the 28mm f/2.8 Pancake lens that released in 2023 in black and just this week in silver. Like the company’s ultra-thin 28mm f/2.8 lens, Brightin Star makes it clear that the 35mm f/1.7 ASPH. is easily adapted to other camera systems, including Sony E, Nikon Z, Canon RF, Fujifilm X, Fujifilm GFX, and L-Mount. The manual focus lens has 307 degrees of focus throw and can focus as close as 0.3 meters (one foot). The lens supports rangefinder coupling, although in this case, the close-focusing distance is expected to be 0.7 meters, as is typical. When used on a Leica M-Mount camera with live view, or when adapted, photographers can take advantage of the closer focusing distance. The lens, which has a classic black paint-inspired finish, is 43 millimeters (1.7 inches) long and weighs 266 grams (9.4 ounces). On the inside, the Brightin Star APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH. has 11 elements arranged across seven groups. Brightin Star notes that there are six aspherical surfaces inside the lens. As the APO in the name suggests, the lens promises an apochromatic design, which means well-controlled chromatic aberrations. The lens has a circular 11-bladed aperture diaphragm. The new lens is also part of Brightin Star’s new “Apex” series. The company says this series promises “precision without compromise.” Although photographers didn’t see the new lens until earlier this year, Brightin Star says it has been working on it for more than two years. “We believe a truly exceptional M-mount lens should never have to choose between heritage and innovation,” Brightin Star explains. “The Apex Series was created with this belief at its core. It preserves the timeless, understated character of classic M lenses while bringing together advanced optics, precision mechanics, and uncompromising standards of craftsmanship.” Pricing and Availability The Brightin Star APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH. is available to back for $759, a 37 percent discount versus the eventual retail price of $1,199. Brightin Star says shipping should begin in November. Adapters are also available to backers for around 40 percent off, bringing the price down to $30 to $42, depending on the mount. item.title: Canon Has Increased Its Massive Digital Camera Market Share Lead
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.80
Thanks to the Camera and Imaging Products Association (CIPA), photographers get a lot of interesting data each month about how many cameras and lenses the Japanese manufacturers are shipping globally. However, for those who want to know who is making each of those cameras, the annual Nikkei Industry Map is the best resource. The latest edition has just arrived. As reported by Digital Camera Life, the new Nikkei Industry Map 2027 details the market shares of each publicly traded Japanese camera manufacturer in the global digital camera market. Of course, this data doesn’t capture non-Japanese camera companies like Leica or Hasselblad, though they are admittedly relatively small players in the grand scheme of things. It also doesn’t reflect Sigma’s camera sales, since the company is not public. With those caveats out of the way, the actual data itself is fascinating. Overall digital camera unit sales increased from 8.7 million units to 9.5 million units, per Nikkei, which is great news for the broader camera industry. Just like it did last year, Canon holds the top market share with a commanding lead. In fact, Canon even upped its share from 43.2 percent to 45.7 percent. Canon also increased its total annual camera sales from 3.53 million units to 4.5 million units, a massive increase. Sony, in second place yet again, held a 24.6 percent share with 2.42 million camera sales. This is a slight increase in total unit sales from 2.33 million but a drop in market share from 28.5 percent. It’s worth noting that although Sony doesn’t make Canon’s image sensors, it does make sensors for many other companies in the market, so the company benefits from a growing camera industry in more ways than one. Perhaps the biggest surprise of all in this year’s Nikkei Industry Map is that Nikon, a very historic photography company, has lost its place in the top three. After increasing its market share to 11.7 percent last year, the company sold about 80,000 fewer units in 2025, and its share dropped to 8.9 percent, a fourth-place finish. Taking Nikon’s spot on the podium is Fujifilm, which upped its unit sales from 740,000 to 1.16 million and increased its market share from nine percent to 11.8 percent. This is a significant leap in unit sales for Fujifilm, which still, over two years later, struggles to keep its popular X100VI in stock. That’s not the only Fujifilm camera model that can be hard to track down due to excess demand, though, as models like the X-M5 and X-E5 have also had bouts of backorders. Presumably, digital Instax cameras, like the Instax Wide Evo released last year, are also counted by Nikkei. It’s a long drop to fifth place, which is Panasonic. The company shipped 430,000 units last year, securing a 4.4 percent market share. This is a substantial 150,000-unit increase. Ricoh Imaging, presumably thanks to the GR IV, moved up from seventh to sixth place and shipped 210,000 units. Ricoh had a 2.1 percent market share, up from just 0.8 percent the year prior. The company tripled its shipped units as well, the largest percentage increase of any company by a huge margin. OM System dropped from sixth to seventh, finishing in last place among the charted companies. The company sold 150,000 units, a slight dip from 160,000 the year before. It will be very interesting to see if these new patterns persist in the Nikkei Industry Map 2028. Image creditsCanon. Header photo created using an asset licensed via Depositphotos.com. item.title: SmallRig’s Tribex Tripod Collab with Potato Jet is Now Also a Monopod
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.73
SmallRig has announced the Potato Jet Tribex Pro Monopod, which takes the single-handle clutch mechanism that was introduced in the Tribex Tripod and applies it to a photo or video monopod. The company says that the monopod features a “new-generation X-Clutch hydraulic technology” which puts the control of all of the leg sections into a single handle to let the user extend and automatically lock all the leg sections at once, which it says delivers a “Fast and efficient operating experience” that is both smooth and quiet. In short, the main draw is to allow a filmmaker to adjust the height quickly and seamlessly while actively capturing footage. On that note, there are two versions of the tripod: a video version with a three-prong foot and options for a video pan-tilt head, and a photo version with either that same foot design or just a single-point foot along with a more standard photo tripod ball head. The video version comes with a compact fluid head, which SmallRig says features a damping system for smooth panning. “When its center of gravity height is put at 50mm, the panning, and pre-set fixed counterbalance system can help precisely control the camera or other rigs weighing up to four kilograms (8.8 pounds) for great counterbalance,” SmallRig explains. “The video head can carry as much as six kilograms (13.2 pounds). It has a newly-designed snap-on quick-release plate mount, a more efficient mounting solution than traditional slide-on ones, which is DJI RS series quick release plate and 501PL quick release plate compatible to realize a free switch between stabilizer shooting and tripod shooting.” The monopod uses a three-section design, supports up to 25 kilograms (55.1 pounds), and weighs 2.6 kilograms (5.72 pounds). Its working height ranges from 90 to 170 centimeters (35.4 to 66.9 inches) and compresses down to a minimum of 89 centimeters (35 inches). SmallRig equipped the monopod with 1/4″-20 threaded holes for attaching accessories and the silicone feet pads have hidden spiked feet to provide better purchase in more varied environments. While there are the aforementioned two main versions of this monopod, SmallRig lists four different possible configurations. The Tribex Pro Barebone Edition (also called the Basic Edition) features just the monopod body with no head or tripod base pedal and costs $200. The Standard Edition adds a folding tripod base and is meant to pair with the DJI RS series gimbals or any heads a photographer or videographer might already own. This version costs $360. The Tribex Pro Photo kit adds a ball head to the Standard Edition configuration and costs $430. For the same price, videographers can swap that ball head for a fluid head, which is called the Video Kit. All versions are available starting today and come with a four-year warranty. item.title: The Godox P100 is a Portable Color Printer That Fits in Your Pocket
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.67
Godox has announced the P100 Portable Color Photo Printer, a pocket-sized dye-sublimation printer that promises high-quality photo prints fast while photographers are on the go. The P100 promises high quality thanks to a combination of 300 dpi high-precision output, 1,256 printhead heating elements, and support for 16.7 million colors. “Its automatic lamination process applies a protective overcoat to each finished print, helping protect it from dust, water, and fingerprints for longer-lasting preservation,” Godox says. “The P100 connects to the Godox Cam APP via Bluetooth and supports NFC tap-to-connect for quick, effortless pairing. Inside the APP, users can create ID photos and collages, capture, personalize, and print photos directly through the app, use filters, frames, stickers, and templates, and check the remaining paper count before replacing the cartridge. Compact and refined, the P100 turns favorite photos into physical keepsakes that can be held, displayed, shared, and revisited wherever life happens.” The basic premise of the P100 isn’t unique. Canon has a dye-sublimation pocket printer called the SELPHY QX20, which prints images at a similar card-sized output as the P100 and does so in about 40 seconds. For what it’s worth, Godox doesn’t clarify what “fast” actually means as far as printing speed. Xiaomi also has a pocket-sized dye sublimation printer called the Portable Photo Printer Pro. It features nearly the same specifications as Godox’s P100 does: 313 dpi and 16.7 million colors. Godox seems to be separating its product out from these and other competitors by building in app features. The app features filters, digital “stickers” and color frames that can be added to photos before printing, and the ability to create photo collages. The printer also supports NFC-based tap-to-connect as well as standard Bluetooth connectivity. Godox’s app is supported on both iOS and Android. The P100 has an 800 mAh rechargeable battery (via USB-C) and weighs about 320 grams. Godox says that the ink replacement unit is easy to swap out once it has been fully consumed and comes with a stack of 10 sheets of photo paper each. “Designed with a clean, modern aesthetic, the P100 features sleek lines and a refined finish. More than just a photo printer, it turns everyday moments into tangible keepsakes to print, collect, display, and share,” Godox says. The Godox P100 costs $119, and replacement ink/paper packs are $19. item.title: Sony’s Sensor Factory Is Back to Full Operation After Major Earthquake
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.58
Last month, a major 6.8 earthquake struck Kumamoto, Japan. It caused serious damage to multiple structures and forced the evacuation of Sony Semiconductor’s facility, which is located in the region. Nearly a month later, the factory has returned to full operating capacity. “Operations at Sony Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation’s Kumamoto Technology Center (located in Kikuyo-machi, Kumamoto Prefecture), were halted after the earthquake on July 28, and currently remain suspended. Damage to the site’s building and manufacturing lines is currently being evaluated,” Sony said shortly after the earthquake. “No significant damage to buildings or facilities has been confirmed at the company’s Nagasaki Technology Center (located in Isahaya City, Nagasaki Prefecture), Oita Technology Center (located in Oita City and Kunisaki City, Oita Prefecture), and Kagoshima Technology Center (located in Kirishima City, Kagoshima Prefecture).” There were also no casualties, but out of caution and for reasons that might be related to how manufacturing hardware operates, restarting the facility would take time. But, despite this, Sony was able to partially reopen the factory on August 4. That said, it would take weeks to get the facility up and running fully. “Sony Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation’s Kumamoto Technology Center (located in Kikuyo-machi, Kumamoto Prefecture), which temporarily was halted after the earthquake, has completed safety inspections of its buildings and facilities, and has been carrying out recovery work. As a result, the site is scheduled to resume operations in stages beginning August 4, 2026. The Kumamoto Technology Center is expected to return to its pre-earthquake operating level by mid-August 2026,” the company said on July 31. That staged re-opening appears to have been completed about on schedule, as the factory now reports that it has returned to normal operation. As reported by YOL, and spotted by Digital Camera Info, everything is back in order. It is worth pointing out that the last time a major earthquake forced the closure of Sony’s sensor plant, it caused a months-long delay that resulted in cascading supply chain issues for every camera brand that sourced its sensors from Sony Semiconductor. The fact that no machinery or building structures were damaged in this latest earthquake is likely why the factory was able to get up and running again so quickly. Still, it’s likely that losing the facility entirely for a couple of weeks and lacking full production capacity for nearly a month won’t be without its effects. It might take longer than expected to get the Sony FX5 production up to meet the high pre-order demand, for example. item.title: Old Photos Show How Air Conditioned Movie Theaters Birthed the Summer Blockbuster
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.52
“Always refreshingly cool inside,” reads a board outside the movie theater. The photo, taken around 1940, is a clue to how the summer blockbuster got started. In the 1920s, many theaters would close during the hottest months because the dark, windowless rooms were boiling hot and customers found them stifling. While Balaban and Katz opened the world’s first mechanically cooled movie theatre in Chicago in 1917, it wasn’t until 1925 that Willis Carrier, the inventor of air conditioning, installed a more sophisticated system in the Rivoli Theatre in Times Square. According to Rotten Tomatoes, Carrier persuaded Paramount Pictures to install the air con while it was still under construction. The Rivoli Theatre opened on Memorial Day weekend in 1925, and initially the air con didn’t work. As the moviegoers filed in, they got out their fans to try and cool themselves. But as the unit finally kicked in, people stopped fanning themselves, and they were able to focus on the movie far better. Adolph Zukor, who was head of Paramount Pictures, witnessed this and realized immediately what a powerful technology this was for his business. Now, instead of summer being a dead period for the nascent movie industry, the theaters could sell coolness itself by providing a place to escape from the heat and watch a film. The Blend reports that one of the first summer blockbusters was a 1943 war drama called Bombardier. It was advertised as the “blockbuster of all action-thrill service shows.” It wasn’t until the 1970s that Jaws and Star Wars became the type of quintessential summer blockbuster movie that has become a hallmark of the Hollywood calendar. By that time, air con was becoming more and more common in American homes. Nevertheless, it is possible to draw a straight line from these early photos of theaters advertising their air conditioning to the summer blockbuster phenomenon that still exists today. item.title: Magnum Photographer Spent Three Years Documenting All 42 of England’s Anglican Cathedrals
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.42
A remarkable exhibition brings together a late Magnum photographer’s images of all 42 Anglican cathedrals in England, capturing their vast, often little-seen interiors entirely in natural light. Southwark Cathedral in London, U.K. is hosting The English Cathedral, a free exhibition of photographs by renowned Magnum photojournalist Peter Marlow showing the interiors of all 42 Anglican cathedrals in England. On view through August 31, the exhibition is organized by the Peter Marlow Foundation and presents Marlow’s photographs as architectural portraits, each taken around dawn with artificial lighting switched off. The approach allows the buildings to be seen primarily through natural light entering their vast interiors. Marlow’s photograph of Southwark Cathedral, for example, shows its Gothic interior illuminated by the early morning light, emphasizing the scale and architectural details of the historic building. Marlow began the project in 2008 after being commissioned by the U.K.’s Royal Mail to photograph six Anglican cathedrals for commemorative stamps marking the 300th anniversary of the completion of St. Paul’s Cathedral. The project led Marlow to photograph all 42 Anglican cathedrals over the following three years. “What I thought was going to be incredibly simple became intricate, complicated, and utterly absorbing,” Peter Marlow, who passed away in 2016, said. “The journey was memorable and wonderfully hypnotic, a kind of reflective pilgrimage. My cathedral days involved hours of driving and thinking, with my reference Polaroids drying in the sun on the dashboard. England passed by.” How He Photographed all 42 Cathedrals The photographs may look simple, but creating them required extensive experimentation. Marlow developed a careful approach to document the vast interiors and show the architectural differences between the cathedrals. He used large-format film and only natural light, photographing almost every cathedral from the same position, facing east toward the nave and altar as morning light entered through the main window. He also made sure all artificial lights were turned off. This was unusual because many of the cathedrals keep their lights on continuously. The result was a series of photographs showing the buildings emerging from darkness, giving the interiors a sense of stillness and distance from modern life. The series can be seen as a contemporary continuation of the long tradition of photographing English churches, including the work of Frederik Evans in the late 19th century. Marlow’s photographs reveal the stunning scale and detail of the interiors of England’s Anglican cathedrals, highlighting their architectural and religious significance. More information about The English Cathedral at Southwark Cathedral in London, U.K. can be found here. item.title: Martin Parr Mural Planned at Iconic Location Where He Photographed ‘The Last Resort’
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.37
A permanent mural is being planned in tribute to the late photographer Martin Parr at the iconic location where he created his acclaimed series The Last Resort. New Brighton Creative Futures CIC has announced plans to create a major seafront mural in New Brighton in Merseyside, England, in tribute to Parr, one of Britain’s most influential photographers who died in December 2025 at age 73. New Brighton, a northern English coastal town developed as a resort modeled after the far more famous Brighton on England’s south coast, became the setting for Parr’s The Last Resort. The series of color photographs documented working-class vacationers at a seaside resort that was beginning to decline. When the series was published and exhibited in 1986, it received sharply mixed reactions, with some critics accusing Parr of portraying the working-class community in an unsympathetic light. In the years since, however, The Last Resort has come to be recognized as an important work that helped transform British documentary photography and establish Parr as one of the world’s leading photographers. According to local reports, the artwork will be created in collaboration with the Martin Parr Foundation. The mural will be located on the seafront in New Brighton, placing the tribute close to the landscape that became synonymous with Parr’s most celebrated photographs. Jenni Smith, director of the Martin Parr Foundation, describes the mural as “poignant”, as it will overlook the town of New Brighton, as the late photographer did with his camera once before. Smith says: “Martin was often asked which photographs he considered his best work; the answer was always the same: the images from The Last Resort. New Brighton, its community and the photographs he made there, always held a special place in his heart.” ‘This Mural is Our Thank You’ The project is now seeking public donations, with supporters able to contribute towards the mural and the public programme planned around it. People can donate through GoFundMe, or visit the New Brighton Creative Futures CIC’s website. Local and regional businesses can also sponsor the tribute. “Martin Parr saw something in New Brighton that the rest of the world had overlooked, and he turned it into some of the most important photographs Britain has ever produced,” Rory Wilmer, creative director and founder of New Brighton Creative Futures CIC, says. “When he passed away, we felt that loss as a town. This mural is our thank you — a way to keep him here, on the seafront he loved, for generations to come. We’d be honoured if the people of New Brighton would help us build it.” Header photo: Courtesy of the Martin Parr Foundation and Magnum Photos Affiliate Disclosure PetaPixel articles may include affiliate links; we may earn a commission if you buy through one.

item.title: The Dutch GP Has One of the Strictest Camera Policies on the F1 Calendar
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.30
The Formula 1 circus is heading to the Netherlands this weekend, the home race of driving sensation Max Verstappen. But keen photographers should know before they go: the event has a very restrictive camera policy. Motorsport photographer Jamey Price took to Instagram this week to warn fans heading to the race that unless they have media credentials to cover the race, their camera and lenses won’t be allowed in. Price says that the Dutch GP has “some of the strictest rules on cameras” and the event bans any recording device with a detachable lens. But a look at the Dutch GP website suggests it’s even stricter than that. “Selfie sticks, drones, cameras, or recording equipment are NOT permitted,” the website says under the House Rules section. Price adds that, “if you are heading to any F1 race this year, make sure you check the event-specific website. Not F1.com… They will have a list of things you can and cannot bring. And on that list, they’ll talk about cameras and lens limits. It is different for every race. Some races have no limits. Others, like the Netherlands and Vegas, do not allow any cameras with detachable lenses.” Some races have oddly specific limits on cameras. The Miami GP, for example, allows cameras with consumer-grade detachable lenses no longer than six inches. That prompted one photographer to bring a tape measure with him so that he could prove to security his gear was eligible. A lot of photographers bristle at the restrictions, with one writing under Price’s post that the rules make “absolutely no sense” while another says they only restrict “hobbyist photographers and negatively impact online fan engagement.” It is a shame too because the Dutch GP at the historic Zandvoort circuit will hold its last race this weekend for the foreseeable future. The twisty-turny track undulates around sand dunes thanks to its unusual setting on the North Sea coast. It only returned in 2021 after a 35-year absence, largely because of the meteoric rise of Max Verstappen. The Orange Army, who have followed him around the world since his debut in 2015, basically willed the event into existence. But with increasing talk that Verstappen will leave the sport, the circuit doesn’t want to commit to a long-term contract with F1. item.title: You Can Definitely Buy a ‘Banned’ DJI Osmo Pocket 4 Camera In the US
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.28
There’s been a lot of attention given to the fact that DJI has yet to officially launch its Osmo Pocket 4 and Osmo Pocket 4P gimbal cameras in the United States. However, that isn’t stopping Americans from getting them anyway. As Sean Hollister at The Verge explains, getting the Osmo Pocket 4P in the US was “cheap and easy,” even if DJI and most of its authorized retailers aren’t selling them. Over on DJI’s US website, the Osmo Pocket 4 and 4P aren’t even mentioned anywhere. It’s like they don’t even exist at all. When the company announced the cameras earlier this year, the official word was: “The Osmo Pocket 4 will not be available in the US market as the application for authorization is still pending.” That hasn’t changed. The Osmo Pocket 4 cameras have not been authorized for sale in the United States, and thus cannot be sold in the country. Or so it would seem. The effective ban means customers can’t pop onto DJI’s own store and grab an Osmo Pocket 4 in the United States. It means Best Buy is only stocking the Osmo Pocket 3. B&H doesn’t list the Osmo Pocket 4 or Osmo Pocket 4P, and neither do Adorama or Target. But as Hollister points out, there are some places where American customers can exchange their hard-earned cash for a “banned” DJI Osmo Pocket 4 or Osmo Pocket 4P gimbal camera, and it’s not quite as shady as one might think the black market would be. “As a kid, I always imagined the ‘black market’ would be like the movies: Shady vendors hawking illicit goods along dusty streets. But if you want a banned DJI Osmo Pocket 4 or Pocket 4 Pro camera in the US, you can just reach for your phone,” Hollister writes. In his case, he went on Temu and immediately bought an Osmo Pocket 4P for an all-too-reasonable price of $659.28. Just like that. It shipped in a FedEx bag from a warehouse in Oregon, and that’s it. Success. As for DJI’s thoughts on Hollister’s success, the company says it has fully complied with the FCC’s ruling. “Osmo Pocket 4P and Osmo Pocket 4 were not released in the United States when the products were launched globally,” DJI told The Verge. “DJI does not offer or sell these products through its official U.S. channels and did not distribute these products in the U.S. market. Any products that may be offered by independent third-party sellers are not products sold or distributed by DJI in the U.S. DJI has no involvement in those third-party sales.” There is no reason to doubt DJI’s claims here. The Osmo Pocket 4 series cameras are available in many places worldwide, and it’s not difficult to buy them in one place and sell them somewhere else. Companies, particularly those who don’t care to follow local rules and regulations, do it all the time. Even on Amazon, third-party resellers operate largely unchecked, and some are selling the Osmo Pocket 4 and 4P right now. As easy as it is to purchase a DJI Osmo Pocket 4 or 4P in the US, receiving service if something malfunctions or breaks is another matter altogether. This is important to consider before spending the better part of $1,000 on a new camera and accessories. As far as DJI is concerned, Americans aren’t supposed to have the Osmo Pocket 4 cameras, and they remain entirely unsupported. Americans who buy them are very much on their own, at least for now. Image creditsDJI Affiliate Disclosure PetaPixel articles may include affiliate links; we may earn a commission if you buy through one.

item.title: Aphera Is a RAW Editor for Photographers Who ‘Chase Feeling Over Formula’
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 4.21
Aphera is a new RAW photo editor built natively for macOS that prioritizes speed and handcrafted editing over complexity. Aphera features a built-from-scratch imaging pipeline and film-inspired colors, per its creators, Ryan Carver, Naz Hamid, and Juan Pablo Zambrano, who comprise the company Latent Co. Carver and Hamid are photographers, while Zambrano is a color engineer by trade and software developer. Carver and Hamid have both had bouts with VSCO, including Carver joining the company as head of product in 2015 and Hamid working on the company’s redesigned iOS app starting in 2016. Their full bios are available here, but the point is that all three of them are very experienced with imaging and all of them say they “fell out of love” with photo editing because of the complexity and preset-focused approach of many RAW photo editors. “[Aphera] features film-inspired colors, handcrafted Looks, and professional color grading without the learning curve,” the trio explain. “Built exclusively for Apple Silicon, Aphera enables real-time editing of 100MP RAW files with instant response.” The app’s key features include film-inspired colors powered by modern color science and a custom imaging pipeline, a professional color grading system informed by analog photography and professional cinema editing, real-time RAW processing, a keyboard-driven workflow, culling tools, and non-destructive RAW editing. Aphera is built for enthusiast and professional photographers who want a fast, intentional photo editing experience and who “value authentic color, efficient workflows, and native performance over bloated feature sets.” The software includes profiles for hundreds of camera and lens combinations, supports bulk editing, lets users organize their files into projects, build and save customized looks, and export across multiple formats. Complete camera and RAW format support is detailed here. The team is adamant that while Aphera is an alternative to Adobe Lightroom, a natural comparison point for any RAW photo editing application with organization tools, they aren’t trying to replace Lightroom. “We’re our own things,” they say. Pricing and Availability Aphera is available now as a lifetime license. To celebrate the software’s launch, it is 50 percent off through August 31, 2026, bringing its price down from $199 to $99. However, while users get Aphera forever if they buy it, they only receive updates for one year from the time of purchase. Updates beyond this period require a subscription, which is $99 per year. If a photographer buys Aphera for $99 and then decides, for example, in three years that they want the latest version, they’d pay another $99. A 14-day trial is also available. Image creditsLatent Co. Affiliate Disclosure PetaPixel articles may include affiliate links; we may earn a commission if you buy through one.

item.title: Nine Million Photos of People’s Faces Discovered in Exposed Database
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 3.84
A website that helps to identify people using just a photo was found to have a massive database of images unsecured on the web. ClarityCheck offers users the chance to look up people via a phone number, email, or photo by uploading one piece of information; it then searches for more info using public records and OSINT. But cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler recently discovered an exposed cache of nine million image files of people’s faces. The data, which totaled 450 gigabytes, was made up of profile images, screenshots, and photographs. Fowler found it in an unsecured Amazon S3 bucket. While ClarityCheck’s terms and conditions require users to have permission from the people in the photos when they upload, Fowler tells Wired that, in practice, there may be people in the exposed database who had no idea that their image had been uploaded to ClarityCheck. “If you’re trying to find out who a person is, you might not have authorization or permission, so people might not know that their image had been dumped into this database that was public,” Fowler says. “An AI bot could crawl it, extract faces, and use them for training. And there are lots of pictures of kids in there.” Fowler sent ClarityCheck a disclosure notice alerting them to the exposed data, which he says was accessible to anyone with an internet connection. However, the company refutes the notion that the data was “exposed”, insisting to Wired that no “ordinary member of the public” could access it. “We do not accept that data in the temporary storage location was ‘publicly exposed,’ which implies large-scale public access,” a spokesperson says. “Access required knowledge of a specific, unindexed URL that was not discoverable through ordinary use of the ClarityCheck service or a general web search.” While Fowler does not claim that the photos were accessed by any third parties, he does want to highlight the risk that images uploaded to ClarityCheck could be used for unintended purposes. “Once data is exposed in a breach, there is a possibility it could also be accessed and used by data brokers, criminals, or even nation-states without the knowledge of the individual or the organization responsible for collecting and storing the data,” he writes for the ExpressVPN blog. “As a general rule, companies should minimize the amount of biometric data they retain, securely delete records that are no longer needed, and avoid storing raw facial images whenever possible.” Photos can be used by scammers: earlier this week, PetaPixel reported on criminals who exploit vacation photos posted to social media and use them to target victims. Affiliate Disclosure PetaPixel articles may include affiliate links; we may earn a commission if you buy through one.

item.title: Lights Out in Scoresby Sund: Capturing a Total Eclipse in the High Arctic
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 3.73
“It was just breathtaking,” Wayne says, the awe unmistakable in his voice. “It was the most epic thing I’ve ever photographed in my life.” Despite leading photography workshops across the globe for years, this was the first total solar eclipse for both Marc and Wayne. Marc admits it had never really been on his bucket list—largely because those familiar telephoto shots of the corona, however technically impressive, tend to look the same no matter who’s holding the camera. “Photographically, those types of compositions were never my goal,” Marc explains. “I knew I could just go to NASA and find a beautiful close-up shot of an eclipse. For me, it was more about the light around the eclipse, and how that affects the wilderness or the landscape wherever you’re standing. If I were to shoot an eclipse, the goal was always to go somewhere unusual.” This particular eclipse was passing through multiple countries, but Greenland was Marc’s first choice of location. Having led multiple workshops to the island, he knew the landscape would be incredible, but plotting the path of totality over Scoresby Sund was a new challenge. “Marc knew of this fjord,” Wayne recalls. “We looked at the map, and it lined up perfectly, full totality right in the center for over two minutes. We knew we had the perfect spot.” The Journey to Scoresby Sund Running a workshop to Greenland is one thing, but getting a group out to Scoresby Sund takes extra planning. Commercial flights into the remote fjord only run once or twice a week, and those days didn’t line up with the timing needed to meet the ship. To make the dates work, Marc had to charter a private aircraft, adding a whole new layer of logistical complexity. His initial plan to charter a larger plane fell through, forcing him to secure two smaller aircraft instead. But with smaller planes came a stricter weight limit. To stay under the plane’s total weight ceiling, every single pound counted, including the photographers themselves. “Wayne weighs over 200 pounds—he’s all muscle, built like a wrestler,” Marc laughs. “So here we are flying over, and we’re only allowed 55 pounds between camera gear and clothes. It was tight.” To help, Marc brought his own laptop for everyone to share, letting people offload their files onto portable hard drives instead. Between that, the ship’s onboard Starlink, and a laundry service run by the crew, nobody had to leave anything crucial behind. An Eclipse in the Landscape What set this month’s eclipse apart was its low position in the sky, measuring just 25° above the horizon. For photographers, this meant that it wouldn’t just be an event happening overhead but would sit low enough to become part of a larger composition, worked into the landscape rather than shot in isolation. It was exactly the departure from the standard eclipse shot Marc had been looking for. “Wayne and I were in Utah during last year’s annular eclipse trying to figure out what 25 degrees in the sky would actually look like, just to get a mental picture of it,” Marc says. “We knew that in Greenland, 25 degrees meant the sun would be right above the mountain peaks, and the only way to compose that properly was from a ship.” To make the most of this unique celestial alignment, they chartered the Polar Front. For Marc, having the ship meant placing the eclipse into an Arctic landscape that is breathtaking even under normal conditions. “When you’re floating around on a boat, you’re right up next to building-size icebergs with arches in them, and mountains shooting 6,000 feet straight out of the water,” Marc says. “It’s indescribable.” The Lead-Up With a few days on board before the eclipse, the group had plenty of time to photograph the towering icebergs and tidewater glaciers that Scoresby Sund is known for. Sailing to the far end of the stretch still open to visitors — Greenland recently closed off roughly half of Scoresby Sund’s traditional loop to protect its resident narwhal population — they even spotted muskox along the shore. Between outings on the ship’s zodiacs, Marc and Wayne used the time to get everyone ready for the main event, including demystifying the one piece of gear many first-time eclipse shooters get wrong. When to Lose the Filter “Everyone thinks you need a solar filter,” Marc explains. While essential during the eclipse’s partial phases, solar filters must be removed the instant totality begins. Left on, a near-opaque filter blocks virtually all light from the dimmed sky, resulting in complete underexposure. As Wayne puts it: “You’re shooting through a 16 or 18-stop filter and going, ‘It’s black!’ And I’m like, yeah—you’re getting a cookie with a bite out of it. That’s all you’ll see.” To ensure no one panicked when the light dropped, Marc and Wayne ran the group through practice drills on deck so nobody was fumbling during those crucial two minutes. While larger cruise ships sailed past toward the end of the fjord, Marc and Wayne arrived at their chosen spot a full 24 hours early. “We found our place and Wayne’s like, ‘We got to park on this just in case another ship decides that this is the spot,’” Marc recalls. “So we parked on it and started watching the weather.” Lights Out On the day of the eclipse, low clouds had drifted in and threatened to obscure the 6,000-foot spires of the mountain they had planned to use as a frame. “Those three spires were meant to be on the right side of our composition, and cloud came in and covered them,” Marc says. “But that’s the beauty of being on a ship. We just repositioned a little further out in the fjord where there was no cloud, giving us an open sky with nothing obscured.” While totality lasts just over two minutes, the entire eclipse is a two-hour event. As the moon slowly took its first bites out of the sun, a quiet intensity took over the deck. For over an hour during the partial phases, the group tracked the changing light, adjusting their solar filters and checking test exposures right up until the shadow finally swept over the ship. “Darkness just—boom!” Wayne remembers. “It took about four seconds and everything went from light to dark. It went into twilight, and suddenly you could see Venus to the left, and Jupiter and Mercury to the right of the eclipse.” Marc’s own memory of it is just as visceral. The two minutes allotted by the astronomical charts felt like they passed in a blink: “What I won’t forget was how fast the lights went out, and the beauty of the light around me.” That rapid plunge into darkness caught even the most meticulous planners off guard—the deep Arctic fjord proved to be several stops darker than their calculations had suggested. Realising mid-totality that the shadow was devouring the scene faster and darker than expected, Marc and Wayne immediately bumped their ISOs and began calling out setting adjustments across the ship so the group could adapt in real time. For two minutes, the deck of the Polar Front became an arena of hyper-focused energy: photographers managing dual-camera setups, swapping between telephoto brackets of the corona and wider handheld panoramas, and even sending drones up into the sky. As the sun began to reappear, the relief and excitement on deck spilled over. “As soon as the diamond ring came out on the other side, the captain blew the foghorn on the ship, and everybody just erupted,” Marc says. “Everyone was cheering, hugging, high-fiving—it was total euphoria.” Their timing could not have been closer: “The crazy thing is, 30 minutes after totality ended, the entire sky clouded over completely. If we had been 30 minutes later we would have seen nothing.” The Photographs Pulling off those two minutes in open Arctic water came down to the captain’s seamanship as much as anything the photographers did. The fjord was over 500 feet deep—far too deep to anchor—so the captain held position purely by working the ship sideways against a 16-knot crosswind. Timing it on Marc’s radio instructions, he kept the entire vessel lined up exactly right the moment totality hit. “It was phenomenal,” Wayne says. “He timed it perfectly.” Even while managing the entire deck, both pros managed to pull off defining shots of their own, though Marc’s centerpiece image was nearly lost to distraction. Marc’s View From Above Ten minutes before totality, Marc sent his drone up to hover at around 300 feet and then got swept up in his own on-deck shooting—swapping lenses on his medium-format camera, firing off close-ups—and nearly forgot the drone was still in the sky. “I looked over at Mike, one of our participants, and he had his controller in hand, and it suddenly reminded me—I’ve still got the drone up,” Marc says. He got the shot almost by instinct; one bracketed frame of the ship, the icebergs, and the eclipse together, captured with a single tap of the controller. It wasn’t until he was home reviewing files that he realised what he’d managed to catch: a visible line between light and shadow across the frame, the edge of the moon’s shadow itself falling across the water. “I looked at it and went, oh, wow—I didn’t expect this,” he says. “It might even be my favorite shot.” “In hindsight, of course, I wished I could have just put the drone on video and watched it go into eclipse and then emerge,” he says. “Because it would have shared a little more of the experience.” Wayne’s Handheld Panorama Wayne’s own hero shot was pure improvisation. Partway through totality he realised the eclipse sat higher in the frame than he’d wished for, and that the light on the water was too good to ignore. “I thought, I’m going to try this,” he says. “And I got lucky—it was right as the diamond ring effect was happening when I swept across.” Working handheld at a high ISO, fielding client questions the entire time, Wayne pieced together a 12-image, multi-row panorama—sky, mountains, and water each shot separately and stitched together—without any idea it would actually come out. “When I got home, I had no idea it would go together. I didn’t think it was possible, to be honest. But it did.” When it came to editing, he turned to the same processing techniques he uses for astro-photography. “It’s very similar to night processing, honestly—we were shooting at bumped-up ISOs, so there was noise reduction to deal with. Once the panorama was together, I used three masks in Photoshop: one for the water, one for the mountains, one for the sky. That was it.” Crucially, he resisted the temptation to enlarge the sun in post. “A lot of people overdo the size of the eclipse because they want it to stand out. But for Marc and me, the landscape always takes precedence over what’s happening in the sky—no matter how epic it is. We preach that constantly. Everybody on that boat wanted the landscape shot.” Golden Rules for Your Next Eclipse Most people won’t get to charter a ship into an Arctic fjord for an eclipse—but Marc and Wayne’s advice travels well regardless of where you’re standing: Choose the right focal length: “Have a 35mm lens on hand, assuming the eclipse falls within that frame,” Marc says. “Go wider than 28mm and the eclipse becomes very small. A slightly longer wide-angle—35mm, even 50mm—is a lot more forgiving.” Bracket during totality: “Shoot a bracketed set, two stops apart, both under and over,” Marc says. “That alone will get you close to the overall feeling of the moment.” Stop down for the diamond ring: “Right as the sun emerges or disappears, that’s the golden, diamond light,” Marc notes. “You want to be down around f/13 to f/16 to pull out all the rays.” Don’t underestimate the corona: “People don’t realise the eclipse is actually much bigger than it looks,” Wayne adds. “When the corona appears, it can be twice the size of the moon or sun itself, sometimes more. You need to leave room for it in the frame.” Commit to your vision: Not everyone on the trip chased the wide landscape shot—one participant stayed locked on telephoto the whole time, working at 150mm and 300mm, and came away with stunning corona detail. Marc’s takeaway: pick one approach and commit to it, rather than trying to do everything in two minutes. The Afterglow The day ended in the ship’s lounge with the entire boat coming together. “We threw a big party with the captain,” Marc recalls. “And we showed a six-minute slideshow to the crew of everyone’s photos from the whole trip and the eclipse.” The sense of awe is still evident as Marc and Wayne reminisce about it, days later. “We couldn’t believe what we just experienced. We captured it. We were celebrating. It was so memorable.” “I’m the luckiest guy in the world,” Wayne says. “It was just… it was mind-blowing.” Wayne Suggs and Marc Muench are nature photographers and instructors with Muench Workshops. Marc is a third-generation photographer and son of legendary landscape photographer David Muench, while Wayne has spent more than 40 years photographing landscapes and wildlife. Founded in 2007, Muench Workshops leads small-group photography workshops and expeditions around the world. This article was also published here. Affiliate Disclosure PetaPixel articles may include affiliate links; we may earn a commission if you buy through one.

item.title: The 9 best places to visit in Portugal in 2026, from Lisbon to Madeira
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.61
The 9 best places to visit in Portugal in 2026, from Lisbon to Madeira Lisbon's tiled hills, Porto's port wine cellars, Madeira's year-round spring weather — the destinations that make a 2026 Portugal trip worth planning Portugal offers an unusually complete range of travel experiences within a genuinely small country: hillside capital, riverside wine city, fairytale palaces, terraced vineyards, and a subtropical island, all reachable within a few hours of each other, giving visitors the kind of geographic and cultural variety that larger countries typically require considerably more travel time to access. This list covers the destinations that make up the backbone of a well-planned 2026 Portugal itinerary, prioritizing the specific mix of city, coast, wine country, and island travel that defines the country's appeal. Lisbon Aayush Gupta / Unsplash Lisbon, one of the oldest cities in the world, is built across seven hills overlooking the Tagus River, its historic Alfama district climbing steep, narrow streets past colorful azulejo-tiled buildings that give the city a visual character unlike anywhere else in Western Europe. The city's soulful Fado music tradition, best experienced in small, intimate venues throughout Alfama, pairs naturally with the pastel de nata, Lisbon's beloved custard tart, and a full day of sightseeing covering the Belém Tower, São Jorge Castle, and the Jerónimos Monastery, all UNESCO-recognized sites within the city itself. Lisbon's steep hills make its iconic Tram 28 a genuinely practical way to move through the city rather than purely a tourist novelty, connecting visitors to the miradouros, the city's famous scenic overlooks, without requiring the uphill walk that seeing them independently would otherwise demand. Porto Alexjo / Pexels Porto, Portugal's second-largest city and the birthplace of port wine, sits along the Douro River's banks, its riverside Ribeira district rising in tiers of colorful buildings connected by six distinct bridges, giving the city a visual density that current guides specifically describe as picturesque enough to draw repeat visitors back. The city's wine cellars, concentrated across the river in Vila Nova de Gaia, offer tastings and tours tracing centuries of port wine production, and a Douro River cruise remains one of the most recommended single activities in the entire country for combining wine tourism with the river valley's own scenic terraced vineyards. Livraria Lello, frequently cited as one of the most beautiful bookshops in the world, sits directly in Porto's city center, giving literary-minded visitors a specific cultural landmark alongside the wine tourism and riverside architecture that otherwise define the city's core appeal. Sintra Matej Simko / Pexels Sintra, a fairytale town in the hills west of Lisbon, is defined by its extravagant palaces and gardens, with the Pena National Palace's vividly colored towers standing as the town's most photographed single landmark and a genuine architectural outlier even within a country known for distinctive palace architecture. The town's popularity means significant crowding and queues should be expected during peak visiting hours, and its steep stone steps and passages make a full palace-hopping day more physically demanding than the town's compact size might initially suggest, a specific practical consideration current travel guides flag directly for visitors planning a day trip from Lisbon. Sintra's proximity to Lisbon, roughly 30 minutes by train, makes it one of the most straightforward day-trip additions to a Lisbon-based itinerary, requiring no significant additional travel logistics beyond the short regional rail connection. Algarve Milo Deckert / Pexels The Algarve, Portugal's southernmost region, is defined by golden beaches and dramatic cliffs along its coastline, with towns throughout the region built specifically around this coastal scenery and a beach-and-golf resort culture that has made it the country's most established beach destination. Faro, the region's main gateway city, is specifically recommended by current travel guides as a strong starting point for visitors exploring the broader Algarve, offering both its own historic center and easy access to the region's most significant beach towns without requiring visitors to base themselves directly in a more purely resort-oriented location. The Algarve's cliffside coastal scenery, combined with a well-developed tourism infrastructure built up over decades, makes it the most straightforward entry on this list for visitors specifically prioritizing beach relaxation over the historical and cultural sightseeing that defines Lisbon, Porto, and Sintra. Douro Valley Rach Sam / Unsplash The Douro Valley, Portugal's most significant wine region, is defined by terraced vineyards climbing steep hillsides above the winding Douro River, a landscape current travel guides consistently rank among the most beautiful wine country settings anywhere in the world. River cruises through the valley remain one of the most recommended single activities available in Portugal, giving visitors direct access to the region's quintas, individual wine estates producing the grapes that eventually become port wine, many of which offer tastings and, at select properties, overnight stays directly among the vines. The valley's relative remoteness from Lisbon means it requires a deliberate, dedicated addition to a broader itinerary rather than a simple day trip, but its combination of dramatic terraced scenery and world-significant wine production makes it one of the most consistently recommended destinations for visitors extending beyond Portugal's major cities. Évora Magali Guimarães / Pexels Évora, a well-preserved medieval town in the Alentejo region, offers Roman heritage sites including a still-standing Roman temple alongside the Évora Cathedral, giving visitors direct access to layers of history spanning from antiquity through the medieval period within a single, compact walkable center. The town's specific appeal within a broader Portugal itinerary is historical density in a considerably less crowded setting than Lisbon or Sintra, offering the kind of significant cultural sightseeing those two destinations provide without their comparable tourist volume, a specific advantage for visitors prioritizing history over the beach or wine-focused destinations elsewhere on this list. Évora anchors the broader Alentejo region, known for its own distinct wine production and rural character, giving visitors a natural extension beyond the town itself for travelers with additional time to explore the surrounding countryside. Aveiro Marcos Túlio / Pexels Aveiro, sometimes called the Venice of Portugal for its network of scenic canals, sits about 45 miles south of Porto on the country's west coast, and current guides specifically recommend it as a stop that deserves to be on a visitor's radar despite its lower international profile relative to the country's larger cities. A canal cruise aboard one of the city's traditional moliceiro boats, once used for harvesting seaweed and now repurposed entirely for tourism, offers the clearest way to experience the city's specific character, followed by visits to the Aveiro Cathedral and the Museum of Aveiro for visitors wanting a fuller day in the city. Aveiro's proximity to Porto makes it a practical day-trip addition to a broader northern Portugal itinerary, giving visitors a genuinely distinct canal-town experience without requiring significant additional travel time beyond an already-planned Porto stay. Minho region Sergei Gussev / Pexels The Minho region, in Portugal's far north, offers the country's greenest landscapes and some of its most traditional culture, an area current travel guides specifically describe as often overlooked by tourists rushing between Porto and Lisbon despite offering a genuinely distinct regional identity. Braga's cathedral and Guimarães' historic castle anchor the region's main sightseeing, while the area's specific culinary signature, vinho verde, a light, slightly sparkling wine, gives visitors a distinct regional drink to pair with the area's food, distinguishing Minho's wine identity from the Douro Valley's port wine further south. Peneda-Gerês National Park, within the broader Minho region, adds an outdoor recreation dimension that most of the country's more historically or culturally focused destinations don't offer, making the region a specific fit for families and outdoor enthusiasts looking to extend a northern Portugal itinerary beyond Porto alone. Madeira Artem Zhukov / Pexels Madeira, a subtropical island roughly 500 miles off Portugal's mainland coast, offers genuinely spring-like weather essentially year-round, distinguishing it from every other entry on this list, all of which experience the same general seasonal patterns as the rest of mainland Portugal. The island's terrain supports extensive hiking along its network of levadas, traditional irrigation channels that double as scenic walking trails through the island's dramatic mountainous interior, alongside botanical gardens that take advantage of the island's consistently mild climate to cultivate an unusually wide range of plant species. Madeira's status as a standalone island destination, reachable by direct flight rather than requiring overland travel from the mainland, makes it a specific option either as an extension of a broader Portugal trip or as a standalone island vacation, giving visitors genuine flexibility in how it fits into an overall itinerary.

item.title: The best van life road trips in America right now — and how to actually do one
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.54
The best van life road trips in America right now — and how to actually do one The best van life road trips in America right now, from Highway 1's reopened Big Sur stretch to Utah's Mighty 5, plus how to actually plan one Van life stopped being an underground experiment once satellite internet, a mature rental market, and a well mapped legal system for overnight parking all matured around the same time. What used to require months of solitary research now runs on an established playbook. The best van life road trips in America right now reward travelers who follow that playbook rather than reinvent it from scratch. Route selection matters more than gear. A costly conversion on a cargo van will not rescue a trip built around the wrong road or the wrong season. It also will not help if the itinerary includes a national park that requires a permit reserved months out. The routes below were chosen because they hold up under real conditions. California's Highway 1 fully reopened through Big Sur in January 2026, after nearly three years of landslide repair. That reconnected the full coastal drive for the first time in years. Utah's five signature national parks link into a loop that a rented or owned van can comfortably manage in about a week. Older, quieter routes across Appalachia, the northern Rockies, and New England round out the list. They suit travelers who want scenery without the crowds that follow California and Utah in peak season. The second half of this list covers what most van life guides skip past: how any of this actually works once the romantic part of the plan is over. Choosing between a cargo van conversion, a factory built camper van, and a rental changes the entire cost structure of a trip. That decision matters before a single mile gets driven. Knowing where it is legal to park overnight for free on federal land depends on specific rules. Most first timers get those rules wrong. Staying connected well enough to work from the road, or simply to check a weather forecast in a remote canyon, now has real solutions. Those solutions did not exist a decade ago. None of the entries below require rare gear, insider access, or a fully custom van. They require picking a route that matches the season. They require understanding a small number of federal land rules. They also require building a realistic budget before departure. That is the actual difference between a van life road trip that works and one that turns into an expensive lesson. California's Highway 1 just reopened its most scenic stretch Credit: Canva Images California's Highway 1 fully reopened through Big Sur in January 2026. The reopening came after nearly three years of landslide repair work. This is the first year in a while that the entire coastal route can be driven without a detour. Highway 1, commonly called the Pacific Coast Highway, runs about 655 miles along the California coast. It stretches between Dana Point in the south and Leggett in the north, where it merges into U.S. 101. The most famous stretch cuts through Big Sur, a roughly 90-mile run of cliffside road between San Simeon and Carmel. There is no direct rail or interstate alternative nearby, which is part of why a landslide there can close the highway for years rather than weeks. A major slide near Regent's Slide had kept a section shut since 2023. Caltrans crews finished stabilizing the roadway and reopened it in January of this year. For a van life trip, Big Sur rewards a slow pace more than almost any other stretch on this list. Pullouts are frequent but small. Many of the best viewpoints, including the Bixby Creek Bridge and McWay Falls, sit right off the road with limited parking for anything longer than a standard car. A smaller van handles this better than a large Class A motorhome. Overnight options inside Big Sur itself are limited to a handful of campgrounds that book out early, so reserving ahead matters here more than on most of this list. North and south of Big Sur, the road opens up. Around Monterey and Carmel, the drive passes aquariums, golf courses, and beach towns with far more services and cell coverage. Farther south, near Santa Barbara, the highway runs close to open beaches with easier pullouts and more casual overnight options at public lots that allow self-contained vehicles. Farther north past Mendocino, the coast turns cooler and foggier, with redwood groves replacing the cliffs. A full end-to-end drive takes at least a week at a reasonable pace. Most van life travelers pick a shorter segment instead, commonly San Francisco to Los Angeles by way of Big Sur, rather than driving the full 655 miles in one trip. Given how recently the road reopened, checking Caltrans for current conditions before departure is worth doing regardless of the season. Slide risk in this stretch has not disappeared just because repairs are complete. Utah's Mighty 5 national parks make one of the best loop routes Credit: Canva Images Utah's Mighty 5 national parks are Zion, Bryce Canyon, Capitol Reef, Arches, and Canyonlands. They link together into a single loop that a van can cover comfortably in about a week. That makes this one of the most efficient national park routes in the country. A common version of the loop starts in Zion, in the southwest corner of the state. From there it heads northeast to Bryce Canyon, known for its dense fields of orange hoodoo spires. From Bryce, the route follows Scenic Byway 12, an All-American Road that cuts through the Grand Staircase-Escalante area toward Capitol Reef. Capitol Reef is the least visited of the five parks and the one most travelers underrate. From Capitol Reef, Interstate 70 and U.S. 191 lead to Moab, the gateway town for both Arches and Canyonlands. The two parks sit close enough together that both are workable from a single base. Each park suits a van trip differently. Zion's main canyon is closed to private vehicles for much of the year. Visitors ride the park shuttle and can leave the van parked at the visitor center or in nearby Springdale. Bryce Canyon's amphitheater is best seen at sunrise, which favors campers who can walk to a viewpoint before the tour buses arrive. Arches has a single scenic drive and fills its parking areas early. A timed entry reservation during the spring and fall high season now matters more than it used to. Canyonlands is split into distinct districts. It rewards visitors who treat Island in the Sky as an easy half day. That leaves more time for the rougher, more remote Needles district if the vehicle can handle it. An America the Beautiful annual pass is priced at $80 for U.S. residents as of 2026. It covers entrance to all five parks plus more than 2,000 other federal recreation sites. The pass pays for itself well before a traveler reaches the third park on this loop. Camping options range from developed campgrounds inside each park, such as Devils Garden in Arches and Fruita in Capitol Reef. Dispersed sites on the surrounding Bureau of Land Management land, outside park boundaries, offer a free alternative. Spring and fall are the better seasons for this loop. Summer pushes temperatures at Arches and Canyonlands past 100 degrees. Bryce and Cedar Breaks, both at higher elevation, stay comfortable through most of the year. The Blue Ridge Parkway connects two of the busiest national parks in the country Credit: Canva Images The Blue Ridge Parkway runs 469 miles along the crest of the Blue Ridge Mountains. It connects Shenandoah National Park in Virginia to Great Smoky Mountains National Park in North Carolina and Tennessee. There is no entrance fee and no commercial traffic allowed on the road itself. Construction began in 1935 as a Depression-era public works project. It was not finished until 1987, when the Linn Cove Viaduct closed the final gap around Grandfather Mountain. The parkway has a posted speed limit of 45 miles per hour, no traffic lights, and no billboards for its entire length. That is part of why it functions more like a linear park than a highway. It is maintained by the National Park Service. It consistently ranks among the most visited units in the entire park system, a distinction based on vehicle count rather than a single entrance gate. For a van life trip, the parkway rewards travelers who treat the drive itself as the destination rather than a connector between two national parks. Overlooks appear every few miles, and many have room for a van to park during the day, though camping directly at overlooks is not permitted. Developed campgrounds inside the parkway's boundary, including ones at Otter Creek in Virginia and Mount Pisgah in North Carolina, fill up quickly during the fall foliage season. That season generally runs from early to mid-October, depending on elevation and latitude. A full drive of the parkway takes at least three or four days at a relaxed pace. Many travelers extend the trip by detouring into Shenandoah's Skyline Drive at the northern end or into the Great Smoky Mountains at the southern end, both of which connect directly. Sections of the parkway close seasonally due to ice and snow, typically starting in November. Late fall through early spring requires checking current closures before setting out, since gates can shut with little notice. Cell service is inconsistent along long stretches, particularly in the more remote sections of North Carolina. That makes offline maps worth downloading in advance. Gas stations are not common directly on the parkway itself. Fueling up in towns along the route is the more reliable approach. It beats assuming the next exit will have a station, especially for a van with a smaller tank than a typical car. The Overseas Highway carries you 113 miles over open water to Key West Credit: Canva Images The Overseas Highway carries U.S. Route 1 for 113 miles from Key Largo to Key West. It crosses 42 bridges over the Atlantic Ocean, Florida Bay, and the Gulf of Mexico, including the famous Seven Mile Bridge. The highway was built in the 1930s on the roadbed of Henry Flagler's Overseas Railroad, after a 1935 hurricane destroyed much of the original rail line. What remained became the foundation for a highway that opened in 1938 and still follows roughly the same path today. Most of the original bridges have since been rebuilt. Despite its name, the modern Seven Mile Bridge measures just under seven miles. Driving across it, with open water on both sides and no land visible ahead for several minutes, is the single most recognizable moment on this route. For a van life trip, the Overseas Highway works well as a short, high-impact drive rather than a multi-week itinerary. The full run from Key Largo to Key West takes only about three hours without stops. Most travelers spend several days working through it slowly instead. Common stops include Islamorada for fishing charters and roadside seafood, and Marathon $MPC for the Turtle Hospital and the Seven Mile Bridge itself. The Lower Keys offer Bahia Honda $HMC State Park's beaches, among the only real sandy beaches along the entire route. Camping options are limited and popular, which makes reservations more important here than almost anywhere else on this list. State parks including Bahia Honda and John Pennekamp Coral Reef fill up months ahead during the winter high season, when travelers from colder states head south. Private campgrounds fill a similar role along the route. Space for larger vans can be tight on the smaller keys, where lots were platted decades before anyone anticipated modern RVs. Hurricane season runs from June through November. The exposed, low-lying nature of the Keys means evacuation routes can close with days or even hours of notice during a storm threat. Checking the National Hurricane Center's outlook before planning a summer or fall trip is a reasonable precaution. Open water presses in on both sides of the road for most of this drive's length. The Beartooth Highway climbs to almost 11,000 feet on the way to Yellowstone Credit: Canva Images The Beartooth Highway climbs to 10,947 feet at Beartooth Pass, making it one of the highest paved roads in the country. It connects Red Lodge, Montana, to the northeast entrance of Yellowstone National Park near Cooke City over about 68 miles of switchbacks. The road opened in 1936. It gains roughly 5,000 feet of elevation in its first 13 miles out of Red Lodge. The road climbs above the tree line into alpine tundra, where snow can fall in any month of the year. It typically operates only from late May through mid-October, closing for winter once snowfall makes the high pass impassable. Even within that window, sudden storms can force temporary closures at the summit. There are no gas stations or services along most of the route. Fueling up in Red Lodge or Cooke City before starting the drive is not optional the way it might be on a longer, better serviced highway. For a van life trip, the Beartooth Highway works best as a dramatic add-on to a Yellowstone visit rather than a standalone destination. The drive itself takes only a few hours. Travelers $TRV who budget a half day can stop at overlooks such as Rock Creek Vista Point, which sits above Rock Creek Canyon. Beartooth Lake, one of several alpine lakes visible from pullouts near the summit, is another easy stop. RVs and larger vans are permitted on the highway. The steep grades and tight switchbacks reward a smaller, more maneuverable van over a large motorhome. Camping directly on the highway is limited to a handful of campgrounds run by the Custer Gallatin and Shoshone national forests. Most sit at elevations high enough that nights stay cold even in July. Many travelers instead base themselves in Red Lodge or Cooke City and treat the pass as a day trip. That approach also solves the problem of thin cell coverage at elevation, since both towns have more reliable service than the highway itself. Because the road sits at such extreme elevation, some visitors notice symptoms such as shortness of breath or fatigue when walking to viewpoints near the pass. No strenuous hiking is required to feel it. That is worth planning around for anyone arriving directly from sea level. New Hampshire's Kancamagus Highway is the classic fall foliage drive Credit: Canva Images New Hampshire's Kancamagus Highway runs 34.5 miles through the White Mountain National Forest, between the towns of Lincoln and Conway. There are no gas stations, restaurants, or other businesses anywhere along the route, making it one of the few major American scenic drives that stays almost entirely undeveloped. Known locally as the Kanc, the road climbs to just under 3,000 feet at Kancamagus Pass. It is best known for fall foliage, when sugar maples, birches, and beeches turn the surrounding hillsides shades of red, orange, and yellow. Peak color generally arrives in the first two weeks of October, depending on elevation and that year's weather. The lack of any services along the 34.5-mile stretch means fueling up in Lincoln or Conway before starting the drive is essential, not just recommended. Running low on gas partway through leaves no realistic option but to keep driving to the other end. For a van life trip, the Kanc rewards a full day rather than a quick pass-through. Pullouts along the Swift River offer easy access to swimming holes and waterfalls, including Sabbaday Falls and Rocky Gorge, both reachable by short, flat walks from the road. The Albany covered bridge, a short detour off the main highway, adds a classic New England stop without much added driving time. Six developed campgrounds sit along or near the route, run by the White Mountain National Forest. That offers a more comfortable overnight option than dispersed camping in a region with dense forest and limited pullouts large enough for a van. Traffic during peak foliage weekends can turn what is normally an hour-long drive between the two towns into a multi-hour crawl, particularly on weekends with clear weather. Visiting on a weekday, or in the week before or after the traditional peak, generally means lighter traffic and easier parking at the most popular overlooks.
